The underlying idea is that a synergistic effect within the cluster improves the perfonnance and fault tolerance. Five networks were ini(cid:173) tially trained to perfonn the same input-output mapping. Following training, a cluster was created by computing an average of the outputs generated by the individual networks. The output of the cluster can be used as the desired output during training by feeding it back to the indi(cid:173) vidual networks. In comparison to a single BP network, a cluster of multiple BP's generalization and significant fault tolerance. It appear that cluster advantage follows from simple maxim "you can fool some of the single BP's in a cluster all of the time but you cannot fool all of them all of the time" {Lincoln}

paragraphs: The paper studies whether combining several backpropagation networks can improve performance and fault tolerance. Five networks are first trained to learn the same input-output mapping. Their outputs are then averaged to create a collective prediction, giving the group a simple way to combine the responses of its members.

The combined output can also be fed back to the individual networks as a desired output during training. This introduces an interaction between the group prediction and each member's learning. The cluster is therefore both a way to produce an averaged answer and a possible source of training targets for the networks that compose it.

The authors report improved generalization and substantial fault tolerance compared with a single backpropagation network. Their explanation is that the individual networks need not all be misled by the same inputs. Averaging can make the collective response less dependent on any one network's failure. The contribution is evidence that a simple cluster can gain useful properties from combining multiple learned versions of the same mapping.
summary.tldr: Averaging five backpropagation networks improves generalization and fault tolerance, with the collective output also usable as a training target.

title: Synergy of Clustering Multiple Back Propagation Networks

paragraphs: The paper introduces bumptrees, geometric data structures for learning, representing, and evaluating relationships from samples. Their intended uses include function approximation, classification regions, constraint surfaces, and probability densities. The common problem is how to organize geometric information so that it can be constructed, accessed, and modified efficiently.

A bumptree organizes a collection of functions over a Euclidean space in a complete binary tree. Each leaf corresponds to one of the functions, and internal nodes also have associated functions. The authors describe the structure as a generalization of several hierarchical geometric representations, including oct-trees, k-d trees, balltrees, and boxtrees.

For function approximation, the approach is related to radial basis function networks, while supporting faster construction and access and more flexible modification. The paper presents an empirical comparison on a robot arm mapping task and outlines additional applications. Its central contribution is thus a reusable organization for geometric learning, linking the representation of learned functions with the efficiency of operations performed on them.
summary.tldr: Bumptrees organize geometric functions hierarchically to support efficient learning, access, and modification across several learning tasks.

title: Bumptrees for Efficient Function, Constraint and Classification Learning

abstract: Although considerable interest has been shown in language inference and automata induction using recurrent neural networks, success of these models has mostly been limited to regular languages. We have previ(cid:173) ously demonstrated that Neural Network Pushdown Automaton (NNPDA) model is capable of learning deterministic context-free languages (e.g., anbn and parenthesis languages) from examples. However, the learning task is computationally intensive. In this paper we discus some ways in which a priori knowledge about the task and data could be used for efficient learning. We also observe that such knowledge is often an experimental prerequisite for learning nontrivial languages (eg. anbncbmam ).

paragraphs: This paper examines how prior knowledge can make neural language learning more efficient. The authors focus on a Neural Network Pushdown Automaton, a model they had previously shown could learn deterministic context-free languages from examples. Such tasks include balanced-parenthesis languages and sequences requiring matching numbers of different symbols.

The motivation is computational cost. Although the model can learn these languages, doing so is intensive, and recurrent-network language induction had mostly succeeded on regular languages. The paper discusses ways to incorporate knowledge about the task and data into learning, using what is already known to help the model acquire more demanding language structure.

The authors also observe that prior knowledge is often necessary in practice for learning nontrivial languages in their experiments. This distinguishes a model's ability to represent or learn a language in principle from the feasibility of getting learning to succeed. The contribution centers on making that learning process more effective through task-relevant knowledge, rather than relying solely on the availability of training examples.
summary.tldr: Prior knowledge helps make neural pushdown-automaton learning more efficient and is often needed experimentally for nontrivial context-free languages.

title: Using Prior Knowledge in a NNPDA to Learn Context-Free Languages

paragraphs: This paper critically examines the Bayesian evidence approximation used to choose noise and weight-penalty terms in neural network training. The supplied setup assumes independent additive Gaussian noise and a weight prior based on the sum of squared weights. The issue is how the approximation behaves in this neural network inference setting.

The author argues that the corresponding exact result is easier to use because it has a closed form, requires no computer code, and need not be recalculated for each new dataset. The paper further claims that the evidence procedure's maximum a posteriori estimate, in the analysis considered, is entirely attributable to approximation error.

The paper also examines sufficient conditions for the approximation to hold and why it can sometimes produce reasonable results. Its significance is a challenge to both the computation and interpretation of evidence-based parameter selection. In particular, it questions the inference that the procedure permits evaluating different priors against the data, making the exact analysis central to understanding what the approximation establishes.
summary.tldr: The paper challenges evidence-based neural network parameter selection through an exact analysis and an examination of approximation error.

title: On the Use of Evidence in Neural Networks

paragraphs: This paper proposes a modular account of how people learn and select movements under different environmental conditions. The architecture contains multiple pairs of models. Within each pair, an inverse model acts as a controller, while a forward model acts as a predictor. Together, the pairs provide multiple ways to control movement and anticipate its consequences.

The architecture learns both the inverse models needed for control and how to select models appropriate to the current environment. This couples acquiring motor skills with deciding when to use them. That combination matters when the same person must manipulate different objects and the correct control behavior depends on which object or conditions are currently encountered.

Object-manipulation simulations demonstrate learning for multiple objects and appropriate generalization to new ones. They also reproduce a feature of the size-weight illusion: visual cues initially activate an inappropriate motor program, followed by correction during the action. The results connect successful adaptation and a characteristic initial error to the same modular learning-and-selection architecture.
summary.tldr: Paired prediction and control models learn object-specific motor behavior, select suitable controllers, and reproduce correction in the size-weight illusion.

title: Multiple Paired Forward-Inverse Models for Human Motor Learning and Control

abstract: Training a Support Vector Machine (SVM) requires the solution of a very large quadratic programming (QP) problem. This paper proposes an al(cid:173) gorithm for training SVMs: Sequential Minimal Optimization, or SMO. SMO breaks the large QP problem into a series of smallest possible QP problems which are analytically solvable. Thus, SMO does not require a numerical QP library. SMO's computation time is dominated by eval(cid:173) uation of the kernel, hence kernel optimizations substantially quicken SMO. For the MNIST database, SMO is 1.7 times as fast as PCG chunk(cid:173) ing; while for the UCI Adult database and linear SVMs, SMO can be 1500 times faster than the PCG chunking algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Sequential Minimal Optimization, or SMO, for training support vector machines. SVM training requires solving a potentially very large quadratic programming problem. SMO divides it into a sequence of the smallest possible quadratic subproblems, each of which has an analytical solution. This makes a numerical quadratic-programming library unnecessary.

The decomposition changes where computation is spent. Kernel evaluations dominate SMO's running time, so optimizing those evaluations can substantially accelerate training. The paper thus identifies both a way to simplify the optimization machinery and the main computational operation to target for further speed improvements. Its approach turns the large optimization problem into repeated manageable steps.

Reported comparisons show that the speed advantage depends strongly on the setting. SMO is 1.7 times as fast as PCG chunking on MNIST. For the UCI Adult dataset with linear SVMs, it can be 1,500 times faster. These results demonstrate substantial practical potential, with the largest gain attached to the specific dataset and model configuration stated by the authors.
summary.tldr: SMO speeds SVM training by solving minimal quadratic subproblems analytically, with reported gains ranging from 1.7-fold to as much as 1,500-fold.

title: Using Analytic QP and Sparseness to Speed Training of Support Vector Machines

paragraphs: The Fisher score represents an observation through derivatives of a probabilistic model's log likelihood with respect to its parameters. The paper asks how class information is preserved in this representation. This matters for clustering because the usefulness of a feature space depends on whether its dimensions reflect distinctions that the clustering should recover.

The theoretical analysis finds a few dimensions carrying important class information alongside many nuisance dimensions. The authors argue that k-means-style methods are inappropriate for this situation because they use all dimensions. Their concern is the mismatch between the uneven distribution of useful information and a clustering procedure that takes the whole representation into account.

They develop a simple clustering algorithm specialized for Fisher scores that can exploit the important dimensions. The method is reported to work successfully on artificial data and on amino acid sequences. The contribution connects an analysis of where information resides in a representation to an algorithm designed around that structure, rather than assuming every coordinate is equally useful for grouping observations.
summary.tldr: An analysis of informative and nuisance Fisher-score dimensions motivates a specialized clustering algorithm tested on artificial data and amino acid sequences.

title: Clustering with the Fisher Score

We bound the dif(cid:173) ferences between the two spectra and provide a performance bound on kernel peA.

paragraphs: The paper studies the relationship between what kernel principal components analysis observes in a finite sample and the corresponding structure of the underlying data distribution. On the sample side, the relevant object is a Gram matrix containing kernel evaluations between observations. On the distribution side, the authors consider a continuous eigenvalue problem.

Both objects have eigenvalues, collectively called their spectra. The authors bound the differences between the sample matrix's spectrum and the spectrum of the continuous problem associated with the sampling density. This directly connects quantities computed from the available observations to quantities defined by the underlying process from which those observations were drawn.

The analysis also provides a performance bound for kernel PCA. Its contribution is theoretical: it turns the relationship between finite-sample spectral information and the underlying continuous spectrum into quantitative bounds. That relationship matters because the method operates on sampled data while its interpretation concerns structure beyond those particular observations. The abstract establishes the existence of these bounds without specifying their formulas or numerical size.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds differences between sample and continuous kernel spectra and derives a performance bound for kernel PCA.

title: The Stability of Kernel Principal Components Analysis and its Relation to the Process Eigenspectrum

abstract: We address the problem of learning topic hierarchies from data. The model selection problem in this domain is daunting—which of the large collection of possible trees to use? We take a Bayesian approach, gen- erating an appropriate prior via a distribution on partitions that we refer to as the nested Chinese restaurant process. This nonparametric prior al- lows arbitrarily large branching factors and readily accommodates grow- ing data collections. We build a hierarchical topic model by combining this prior with a likelihood that is based on a hierarchical variant of latent Dirichlet allocation. We illustrate our approach on simulated data and with an application to the modeling of NIPS abstracts.

paragraphs: Learning a hierarchy of topics requires choosing a tree from a very large collection of possibilities. This paper treats that structural choice as part of Bayesian modeling. Instead of fixing one tree in advance, the authors introduce a probability distribution over partitions called the nested Chinese restaurant process to provide a prior over hierarchical structure.

The prior is nonparametric and permits arbitrarily large branching factors, so the model is not tied to a preset maximum number of branches. It also accommodates growing data collections. The authors combine this structural prior with a model of observed data based on a hierarchical version of latent Dirichlet allocation, producing a hierarchical topic model.

The approach is illustrated using simulated data and NIPS abstracts. These applications show how the proposed prior and topic likelihood work together to model a document collection. The main contribution is a way to make topic-tree selection part of the probabilistic learning problem while allowing the hierarchy’s branching structure to remain flexible.
summary.tldr: The nested Chinese restaurant process supplies a flexible Bayesian prior for learning topic hierarchies from document collections.

title: Hierarchical Topic Models and the Nested Chinese Restaurant Process

abstract: Patch-based appearance models are used in a wide range of computer vision ap- plications. To learn such models it has previously been necessary to specify a suitable set of patch sizes and shapes by hand. In the jigsaw model presented here, the shape, size and appearance of patches are learned automatically from the repeated structures in a set of training images. By learning such irregularly shaped ‘jigsaw pieces’, we are able to discover both the shape and the appearance of object parts without supervision. When applied to face images, for example, the learned jigsaw pieces are surprisingly strongly associated with face parts of different shapes and scales such as eyes, noses, eyebrows and cheeks, to name a few. We conclude that learning the shape of the patch not only improves the accuracy of appearance-based part detection but also allows for shape-based part detection. This enables parts of similar appearance but different shapes to be dis- tinguished; for example, while foreheads and cheeks are both skin colored, they have markedly different shapes.

paragraphs: Patch-based appearance models describe images through smaller regions, but choosing the sizes and shapes of those regions has often required manual decisions. The paper introduces a jigsaw model that learns patch shape, size, and appearance together. It draws this information from structures that recur across a collection of training images.

The resulting patches can have irregular outlines, like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. Because both their visual content and their boundaries are learned, they can capture object parts without supervision. In the face-image example, the learned pieces are strongly associated with recognizable regions such as eyes, noses, eyebrows, and cheeks, spanning different shapes and scales.

The authors conclude that learning patch shape improves appearance-based part detection and also makes shape-based detection possible. This is useful when different parts look similar internally but have different outlines. Their example is foreheads and cheeks: both may share skin coloring, while their shapes differ. The method therefore gives the representation another basis for distinguishing parts beyond their appearance alone.
summary.tldr: The jigsaw model learns irregular image patches whose shapes and appearances reveal object parts without supervision.

title: Clustering appearance and shape by learning jigsaws

abstract: We summarize the implementation of an analog VLSI chip hosting a network of 32 integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons with spike-frequency adaptation and 2,048 Hebbian plastic bistable spike-driven stochastic synapses endowed with a self-regulating mechanism which stops unnecessary synaptic changes. The synaptic matrix can be flexibly configured and provides both recurrent and AER-based connectivity with external, AER compliant devices. We demonstrate the ability of the network to efficiently classify overlapping patterns, thanks to the self-regulating mechanism.
originalAbstract: We summarize the implementation of an analog VLSI chip hosting a network of 32 integrate-and-fire (IF) neurons with spike-frequency adaptation and 2,048 Hebbian plastic bistable spike-driven stochastic synapses endowed with a self-regulating mechanism which stops unnecessary synaptic changes. The synaptic matrix can be flexibly configured and provides both recurrent and AER-based connectivity with external, AER compliant devices. We demonstrate the ability of the network to efficiently classify overlapping patterns, thanks to the self-regulating mechanism.

paragraphs: This paper implements a learning network directly in an analog VLSI chip. The hardware contains 32 integrate-and-fire neurons with spike-frequency adaptation and 2,048 plastic synapses. Its neurons communicate through spikes, and the synapses change in response to spike activity. The implementation therefore brings neural signaling and synaptic learning together in a configurable physical circuit.

A central feature is a self-regulating mechanism that stops unnecessary synaptic changes. The synapses combine Hebbian learning, stochastic behavior, and two stable states. Self-regulation adds control over when their plasticity remains active, making the decision to stop changing connections part of the learning system itself.

The connection matrix supports recurrent connections within the network and communication with compatible external devices through an address-event representation interface. The authors demonstrate efficient classification of overlapping patterns and attribute this ability to the self-regulating mechanism. The result connects a specific hardware learning mechanism to a demonstrated classification capability, while the configurable connections allow the chip to participate in different network arrangements.
summary.tldr: An analog spiking-neuron chip uses self-regulating plastic synapses to efficiently classify overlapping patterns.

title: A configurable analog VLSI neural network with spiking neurons and self-regulating plastic synapses

abstract: Biological movement is built up of sub-blocks or motion primitives. Such primitives provide a compact representation of movement which is also desirable in robotic control applications. We analyse handwriting data to gain a better understanding of use of primitives and their timings in biological movements. Inference of the shape and the timing of primitives can be done using a factorial HMM based model, allowing the handwriting to be represented in primitive timing space. This representation provides a distribution of spikes corresponding to the primitive activations, which can also be modelled using HMM architectures. We show how the coupling of the low level primitive model, and the higher level timing model during inference can produce good reconstructions of handwriting, with shared primitives for all characters modelled. This coupled model also captures the variance profile of the dataset which is accounted for by spike timing jitter. The timing code provides a compact representation of the movement while generating a movement without an explicit timing model produces a scribbling style of output.

paragraphs: This paper investigates handwriting as a combination of reusable movement components, called motion primitives. Such components offer a compact description of movement, but their activation times also matter. The authors study both primitive shapes and timing to understand how a shared collection of movement components can account for different handwritten characters.

A factorial hidden Markov model infers the primitives and when they occur. This converts handwriting into a timing representation containing spikes that mark primitive activations. A higher-level hidden Markov model then describes those timing patterns. During inference, the lower-level movement model and higher-level timing model are coupled so that each informs the reconstruction.

The coupled system produces good handwriting reconstructions using primitives shared across all modeled characters. It also captures the dataset's pattern of variation through jitter in spike timing. Generating movement without an explicit timing model instead produces scribbling-style output. The results highlight timing as a substantive part of the compact movement representation, alongside the shapes of its constituent primitives.
summary.tldr: Coupling shared motion primitives with a model of their activation timing reconstructs handwriting and explains variation through timing jitter.

title: Modelling motion primitives and their timing in biologically executed movements

abstract: Sequential optimal design methods hold great promise for improving the efficiency of neurophysiology experiments. However, previous methods for optimal experimental design have incorporated only weak prior information about the underlying neural system (e.g., the sparseness or smoothness of the receptive field). Here we describe how to use stronger prior information, in the form of parametric models of the receptive field, in order to construct optimal stimuli and further improve the efficiency of our experiments. For example, if we believe that the receptive field is well-approximated by a Gabor function, then our method constructs stimuli that optimally constrain the Gabor parameters (orientation, spatial frequency, etc.) using as few experimental trials as possible. More generally, we may believe a priori that the receptive field lies near a known sub-manifold of the full parameter space; in this case, our method chooses stimuli in order to reduce the uncertainty along the tangent space of this sub-manifold as rapidly as possible. Applications to simulated and real data indicate that these methods may in many cases improve the experimental efficiency.

paragraphs: An informative neural experiment depends on choosing stimuli that reveal the unknown properties of a receptive field. This paper improves stimulus selection by incorporating stronger prior knowledge about the field's possible form. Instead of using only broad expectations such as smoothness or sparsity, the method uses a parameterized model to direct experimental effort.

For example, if a Gabor function is believed to approximate the receptive field, the procedure selects stimuli to constrain quantities such as orientation and spatial frequency with as few trials as possible. The broader formulation assumes that plausible receptive fields lie near a known lower-dimensional surface within the full parameter space.

The method then targets uncertainty along the local tangent space of that surface, concentrating measurement on variations associated with the assumed model. Applications to simulated and real data indicate that this strategy may improve efficiency in many cases. The significance is that structured prior knowledge can guide which uncertainties an experiment resolves, with the reported gains remaining qualified rather than universal.
summary.tldr: Parameterized receptive-field priors guide stimulus selection to reduce relevant uncertainty and may make neural experiments more efficient.

title: Designing neurophysiology experiments to optimally constrain receptive field models along parametric submanifolds

abstract: The low-rank matrix completion problem is a fundamental problem with many important applications. Recently, Candes & Recht, Keshavan et al. and Candes & Tao obtained the first non-trivial theoretical results for the problem assuming that the observed entries are sampled uniformly at random. Unfortunately, most real-world datasets do not satisfy this assumption, but instead exhibit power-law distributed samples. In this paper, we propose a graph theoretic approach to matrix completion that solves the problem for more realistic sampling models. Our method is easier to analyze than previous methods with the analysis reducing to computing the threshold for complete cascades in random graphs, a problem of independent interest. By analyzing the graph theoretic problem, we show that our method achieves exact recovery when the observed entries are sampled from the Chung-Lu-Vu model, which can generate power-law distributed graphs. We also hypothesize that our algorithm solves the matrix completion problem from an optimal number of entries for the popular preferential attachment model and provide strong empirical evidence for the claim. Furthermore, our method is easier to implement and is substantially faster than existing methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on examples when the low-rank matrix is sampled according to the prevalent random graph models for complex networks and also on the Netflix challenge dataset.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from a subset of its entries. Earlier theoretical results discussed in this paper assume uniformly random observations, while many real datasets have highly uneven sampling patterns. The authors develop a graph-theoretic approach intended to handle models that can produce power-law distributions of observed entries.

Their analysis translates recovery into a question about complete cascades in random graphs: when can a spreading process reach the whole graph? Using this connection, they establish exact recovery under the Chung-Lu-Vu sampling model. For preferential attachment sampling, they instead hypothesize that the algorithm uses an optimal number of observed entries and provide strong empirical support.

That distinction separates a proved recovery result from a supported conjecture about sample optimality. The authors also report that their method is easier to implement and substantially faster than existing methods. Demonstrations include matrices sampled using common random graph models and the Netflix challenge dataset, connecting the graph-based analysis to practical completion problems.
summary.tldr: A graph-based matrix completion method proves exact recovery under Chung-Lu-Vu sampling and empirically supports optimal sampling under preferential attachment.

title: Matrix Completion from Power-Law Distributed Samples

abstract: The problem of approximating a given probability distribution using a simpler distribution plays an important role in several areas of machine learning, e.g. variational inference and classification. Within this context, we consider the task of learning a mixture of tree distributions. Although mixtures of trees can be learned by minimizing the KL-divergence using an EM algorithm, its success depends heavily on the initialization. We propose an efficient strategy for obtaining a good initial set of trees that attempts to cover the entire observed distribution by minimizing the $\alpha$-divergence with $\alpha = \infty$. We formulate the problem using the fractional covering framework and present a convergent sequential algorithm that only relies on solving a convex program at each iteration. Compared to previous methods, our approach results in a significantly smaller mixture of trees that provides similar or better accuracies. We demonstrate the usefulness of our approach by learning pictorial structures for face recognition.

paragraphs: Approximating a complex probability distribution with simpler components is useful in tasks such as variational inference and classification. This paper focuses on mixtures of tree distributions. Such mixtures can be learned using an EM algorithm that minimizes KL divergence, but the quality of the outcome depends strongly on the trees used to initialize the procedure.

The authors propose selecting an initial collection that attempts to cover the observed distribution broadly. They express this goal through alpha-divergence with alpha equal to infinity and formulate it using fractional covering. The resulting sequential algorithm is convergent and requires solving a convex program at each iteration, providing a structured way to build the initial mixture.

Compared with previous methods, the approach produces significantly smaller tree mixtures with similar or better accuracy. This result links careful initialization to a more compact representation without a reported loss of predictive quality in the comparisons. The authors also demonstrate the method by learning pictorial structures for face recognition, showing how the distribution-approximation strategy can support a concrete visual recognition application.
summary.tldr: A coverage-oriented initialization method learns smaller mixtures of tree distributions while retaining similar or better reported accuracy.

title: Learning a Small Mixture of Trees

abstract: We describe an accelerated hardware neuron being capable of emulating the adap-tive exponential integrate-and-fire neuron model. Firing patterns of the membrane stimulated by a step current are analyzed in transistor level simulation and in silicon on a prototype chip. The neuron is destined to be the hardware neuron of a highly integrated wafer-scale system reaching out for new computational paradigms and opening new experimentation possibilities. As the neuron is dedicated as a universal device for neuroscientific experiments, the focus lays on parameterizability and reproduction of the analytical model.

paragraphs: This paper develops an accelerated hardware neuron that can emulate the adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire model. The aim is to turn a mathematical description of neuronal behavior into an adjustable physical circuit. The authors emphasize reproducing the analytical model, so the hardware is intended to support experiments whose settings can be related back to that model.

The evaluation examines firing patterns produced when the neuron receives a step current, meaning an input that changes to a sustained level. The authors analyze this response both in transistor-level simulations and on a prototype silicon chip. These two settings connect the proposed circuit design with observations from an actual manufactured device.

The neuron is intended for a highly integrated system built at wafer scale. That larger system is presented as a route toward new forms of computation and new experimental possibilities. Within this goal, the paper concentrates on a configurable neuron component: parameter adjustment and faithful model reproduction are central to its proposed usefulness across neuroscientific experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper implements an adjustable, accelerated hardware neuron and examines its firing behavior in circuit simulations and prototype silicon.

title: A VLSI Implementation of the Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire Neuron Model

abstract: In this paper, we propose a matrix-variate normal penalty with sparse inverse covariances to couple multiple tasks. Learning multiple (parametric) models can be viewed as estimating a matrix of parameters, where rows and columns of the matrix correspond to tasks and features, respectively. Following the matrix-variate normal density, we design a penalty that decomposes the full covariance of matrix elements into the Kronecker product of row covariance and column covariance, which characterizes both task relatedness and feature representation. Several recently proposed methods are variants of the special cases of this formulation. To address the overfitting issue and select meaningful task and feature structures, we include sparse covariance selection into our matrix-normal regularization via L-1 penalties on task and feature inverse covariances. We empirically study the proposed method and compare with related models in two real-world problems: detecting landmines in multiple fields and recognizing faces between different subjects. Experimental results show that the proposed framework provides an effective and flexible way to model various different structures of multiple tasks.

paragraphs: Learning several parametric models together can be viewed as estimating a matrix, with tasks along one dimension and features along the other. This paper introduces a matrix-normal penalty that couples those models. Its purpose is to represent relationships among tasks alongside structure in the features used to predict them.

The penalty decomposes the full covariance of the parameter matrix into a Kronecker product of task and feature covariances. To address overfitting and select meaningful relationships, the authors impose L1 penalties on both inverse covariance matrices. This encourages sparse structures in the relationships being learned. Several existing methods appear as variants of special cases within the formulation.

Experiments examine landmine detection across multiple fields and face recognition across different subjects, comparing the approach with related models. The reported findings support its effectiveness and flexibility for representing different task structures. The contribution is a joint framework in which task relatedness and feature representation are both learned under regularization, rather than leaving either type of structure outside the model.
summary.tldr: A matrix-normal penalty with sparse task and feature inverse covariances jointly models relationships across multiple learning tasks.

title: Learning Multiple Tasks with a Sparse Matrix-Normal Penalty

abstract: In this paper, we consider Bayesian reinforcement learning (BRL) where actions incur costs in addition to rewards, and thus exploration has to be constrained in terms of the expected total cost while learning to maximize the expected long-term total reward. In order to formalize cost-sensitive exploration, we use the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) as the model of the environment, in which we can naturally encode exploration requirements using the cost function. We extend BEETLE, a model-based BRL method, for learning in the environment with cost constraints. We demonstrate the cost-sensitive exploration behaviour in a number of simulated problems.

In order to formalize cost-sensitive exploration, we use the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) as the model of the environment, in which we can naturally encode exploration requirements using the cost function. We extend BEETLE, a model-based BRL method, for learning in the environment with cost constraints. We demonstrate the cost-sensitive exploration behaviour in a number of simulated problems.

paragraphs: Exploration in reinforcement learning gathers information through actions, but those actions can incur costs as well as deliver rewards. This paper studies Bayesian reinforcement learning under that distinction. The learner seeks high expected long-term total reward while keeping its expected total cost within a constraint. Exploration must therefore be evaluated in terms of both what it teaches and what it costs.

The authors formalize the environment as a constrained Markov decision process. Its cost function provides a way to encode requirements on exploration, making those requirements part of the learning problem. They then extend BEETLE, a model-based Bayesian reinforcement learning method, so it can learn in environments with these cost constraints.

Simulated problems demonstrate the resulting cost-sensitive exploration behavior. The contribution is a formulation and method for learning when information-gathering actions must respect an expected cost budget. The expectation qualification matters: the stated constraint concerns expected total cost, rather than a guarantee that every individual sequence of actions stays below a fixed expenditure.
summary.tldr: An extension of BEETLE learns to explore for long-term reward while accounting for constraints on expected total action cost.

title: Cost-Sensitive Exploration in Bayesian Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The expected return is a widely used objective in decision making under uncer- tainty. Many algorithms, such as value iteration, have been proposed to optimize it. In risk-aware settings, however, the expected return is often not an appropriate objective to optimize. We propose a new optimization objective for risk-aware planning and show that it has desirable theoretical properties. We also draw con- nections to previously proposed objectives for risk-aware planing: minmax, ex- ponential utility, percentile and mean minus variance. Our method applies to an extended class of Markov decision processes: we allow costs to be stochastic as long as they are bounded. Additionally, we present an efﬁcient algorithm for op- timizing the proposed objective. Synthetic and real-world experiments illustrate the effectiveness of our method, at scale.

paragraphs: Maximizing expected return is a common approach to planning under uncertainty, but an average outcome may be an unsuitable objective when risk matters. The paper proposes a different optimization objective for risk-aware planning in Markov decision processes. Its purpose is to bring risk considerations directly into what the planner optimizes.

The authors establish desirable theoretical properties of the objective and connect it to several existing approaches: minmax planning, exponential utility, percentile objectives, and mean minus variance. These connections place the proposal within a broader set of ways to express risk preferences, helping relate its formulation to alternatives already used for uncertain decisions.

The method permits stochastic costs, provided those costs are bounded, and the paper supplies an efficient optimization algorithm. Boundedness is therefore a stated condition on the extended class of decision processes it handles. Synthetic and real-world experiments illustrate effectiveness at scale. Together, the results provide a risk-aware objective, a computational procedure for optimizing it, and experimental evidence of its practical use.
summary.tldr: A new risk-aware planning objective comes with theoretical properties and an efficient algorithm for MDPs with bounded stochastic costs.

title: Risk Aversion in Markov Decision Processes via Near Optimal Chernoff Bounds

abstract: One approach to computer object recognition and modeling the brain's ventral stream involves unsupervised learning of representations that are invariant to common transformations. However, applications of these ideas have usually been limited to 2D affine transformations, e.g., translation and scaling, since they are easiest to solve via convolution. In accord with a recent theory of transformation-invariance, we propose a model that, while capturing other common convolutional networks as special cases, can also be used with arbitrary identity-preserving transformations. The model's wiring can be learned from videos of transforming objects---or any other grouping of images into sets by their depicted object. Through a series of successively more complex empirical tests, we study the invariance/discriminability properties of this model with respect to different transformations. First, we empirically confirm theoretical predictions for the case of 2D affine transformations. Next, we apply the model to non-affine transformations: as expected, it performs well on face verification tasks requiring invariance to the relatively smooth transformations of 3D rotation-in-depth and changes in illumination direction. Surprisingly, it can also tolerate clutter transformations'' which map an image of a face on one background to an image of the same face on a different background. Motivated by these empirical findings, we tested the same model on face verification benchmark tasks from the computer vision literature: Labeled Faces in the Wild, PubFig and a new dataset we gathered---achieving strong performance in these highly unconstrained cases as well."

paragraphs: A useful recognition representation should tolerate changes in an object's appearance while retaining information that distinguishes its identity. This paper proposes a model for learning such representations across identity-preserving transformations. It extends beyond the translation and scaling changes commonly handled by convolution and includes other convolutional networks as special cases.

The model's connections can be learned from videos showing objects transform, or from image groups organized by object identity. The authors examine both invariance and discriminability through increasingly complex tests. They first confirm theoretical predictions empirically for two-dimensional affine transformations, then study non-affine changes relevant to face verification.

The model performs well when faces rotate in depth or illumination direction changes. It also tolerates changes in background clutter, an empirical finding that motivates further evaluation in unconstrained settings. Tests on Labeled Faces in the Wild, PubFig, and a newly collected dataset show strong performance. These results support the usefulness of learning from identity-linked image groups, while keeping the broad modeling capability distinct from the particular transformations tested.
summary.tldr: Learning from identity-linked images produces representations that handle several appearance changes and perform strongly on face verification tasks.

title: Learning invariant representations and applications to face verification

abstract: We study the sensitivity of a MAP configuration of a discrete probabilistic graphical model with respect to perturbations of its parameters. These perturbations are global, in the sense that simultaneous perturbations of all the parameters (or any chosen subset of them) are allowed. Our main contribution is an exact algorithm that can check whether the MAP configuration is robust with respect to given perturbations. Its complexity is essentially the same as that of obtaining the MAP configuration itself, so it can be promptly used with minimal effort. We use our algorithm to identify the largest global perturbation that does not induce a change in the MAP configuration, and we successfully apply this robustness measure in two practical scenarios: the prediction of facial action units with posed images and the classification of multiple real public data sets. A strong correlation between the proposed robustness measure and accuracy is verified in both scenarios.

paragraphs: A maximum a posteriori, or MAP, configuration is the most probable joint assignment in a graphical model. This paper asks how stable that assignment is when model parameters change. Its sensitivity analysis allows simultaneous changes to all parameters or to a chosen subset, making robustness a property of coordinated perturbations.

The authors provide an exact algorithm that checks whether the MAP configuration remains unchanged under given perturbations. Its computational complexity is essentially the same as finding the MAP configuration itself. They then use this test to identify the largest global perturbation that preserves the selected configuration, producing a quantitative robustness measure.

The measure is applied to facial action-unit prediction from posed images and classification on multiple public datasets. In both settings, the authors observe a strong correlation between robustness and accuracy. This makes stability potentially informative about prediction quality in the evaluated applications. The result combines an exact check of model-output stability with empirical evidence that the resulting measure tracks a practically relevant outcome.
summary.tldr: An exact algorithm measures how much simultaneous parameter perturbation a MAP prediction tolerates, with robustness strongly correlated with accuracy in two evaluated settings.

title: Global Sensitivity Analysis for MAP Inference in Graphical Models

abstract: Scene labeling is a challenging computer vision task. It requires the use of both local discriminative features and global context information. We adopt a deep recurrent convolutional neural network (RCNN) for this task, which is originally proposed for object recognition. Different from traditional convolutional neural networks (CNN), this model has intra-layer recurrent connections in the convolutional layers. Therefore each convolutional layer becomes a two-dimensional recurrent neural network. The units receive constant feed-forward inputs from the previous layer and recurrent inputs from their neighborhoods. While recurrent iterations proceed, the region of context captured by each unit expands. In this way, feature extraction and context modulation are seamlessly integrated, which is different from typical methods that entail separate modules for the two steps. To further utilize the context, a multi-scale RCNN is proposed. Over two benchmark datasets, Standford Background and Sift Flow, the model outperforms many state-of-the-art models in accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Scene labeling needs both local visual evidence and information about the surrounding scene. This paper adapts a recurrent convolutional network, originally proposed for object recognition, to combine these sources of information within its convolutional layers. The architecture adds recurrent connections between neighboring units inside a layer.

Each unit receives a constant feed-forward input from the preceding layer together with recurrent input from nearby units. As these recurrent updates repeat, information can reach the unit from a progressively larger region. Local feature processing therefore becomes sensitive to broader context through the same computation, integrating feature extraction and contextual adjustment instead of assigning them to separate modules.

The authors also introduce a multiscale version to make further use of context. On the Stanford Background and Sift Flow benchmarks, they report better accuracy and efficiency than many leading comparison models. These results support recurrence within convolutional layers as a useful mechanism for scene labeling, with the reported gains covering both labeling quality and computational efficiency in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Recurrent connections within convolutional layers expand visual context and improve scene-labeling accuracy and efficiency on two benchmarks.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks with Intra-Layer Recurrent Connections for Scene Labeling

abstract: Neuroscience experiments often require training animals to perform tasks designed to elicit various sensory, cognitive, and motor behaviors. Training typically involves a series of gradual adjustments of stimulus conditions and rewards in order to bring about learning. However, training protocols are usually hand-designed, relying on a combination of intuition, guesswork, and trial-and-error, and often require weeks or months to achieve a desired level of task performance. Here we combine ideas from reinforcement learning and adaptive optimal experimental design to formulate methods for adaptive optimal training of animal behavior. Our work addresses two intriguing problems at once: first, it seeks to infer the learning rules underlying an animal's behavioral changes during training; second, it seeks to exploit these rules to select stimuli that will maximize the rate of learning toward a desired objective. We develop and test these methods using data collected from rats during training on a two-interval sensory discrimination task. We show that we can accurately infer the parameters of a policy-gradient-based learning algorithm that describes how the animal's internal model of the task evolves over the course of training. We then formulate a theory for optimal training, which involves selecting sequences of stimuli that will drive the animal's internal policy toward a desired location in the parameter space. Simulations show that our method can in theory provide a substantial speedup over standard training methods. We feel these results will hold considerable theoretical and practical implications both for researchers in reinforcement learning and for experimentalists seeking to train animals.

paragraphs: Training animals for neuroscience experiments often involves repeatedly adjusting stimuli and rewards until the desired behavior develops. These adjustments are usually designed by hand and can require weeks or months. This paper treats training as an adaptive decision problem: infer how an animal learns, then use that understanding to choose training stimuli that should accelerate progress.

The authors combine reinforcement learning with adaptive optimal experimental design. Using data from rats learning a two-interval sensory discrimination task, they show that they can accurately infer parameters of a policy-gradient learning model. That model describes how the animal's internal representation of the task changes during training.

They then formulate optimal training as selecting stimulus sequences that move the animal's policy toward a desired setting. Simulations suggest that this approach could substantially accelerate learning compared with standard training methods. The evidence therefore supports both learning-model inference from animal data and a theoretical route to faster training; the reported training speedup comes from simulations.
summary.tldr: Inferring how animals learn can guide adaptive training stimuli, with simulations suggesting substantial potential speedups.

title: Adaptive optimal training of animal behavior

abstract: Weighted minwise hashing (WMH) is one of the fundamental subroutine, required by many celebrated approximation algorithms, commonly adopted in industrial practice for large -scale search and learning. The resource bottleneck with WMH is the computation of multiple (typically a few hundreds to thousands) independent hashes of the data. We propose a simple rejection type sampling scheme based on a carefully designed red-green map, where we show that the number of rejected sample has exactly the same distribution as weighted minwise sampling. The running time of our method, for many practical datasets, is an order of magnitude smaller than existing methods. Experimental evaluations, on real datasets, show that for computing 500 WMH, our proposal can be 60000x faster than the Ioffe's method without losing any accuracy. Our method is also around 100x faster than approximate heuristics capitalizing on the efficient ``densified" one permutation hashing schemes~\cite{Proc:OneHashLSH ICML14,Proc:Shrivastava UAI14}. Given the simplicity of our approach and its significant advantages, we hope that it will replace existing implementations in practice.

Its cost becomes substantial when a system needs hundreds or thousands of independent hashes for each data item. This paper targets that repeated computation with a simple sampling construction.

The method uses rejection sampling based on a carefully constructed red-green map. Its key theoretical property is unusual: the number of rejected samples has exactly the distribution required by weighted minwise sampling. This distributional equivalence supports an exact sampling approach, so the proposed efficiency gain does not rely on substituting an approximate distribution.

The authors report an order-of-magnitude runtime improvement for many practical datasets. In real-data experiments computing 500 hashes, the method can be 60,000 times faster than Ioffe's method without losing accuracy, and around 100 times faster than the compared approximate heuristics. These figures describe reported comparisons rather than a universal speedup. The contribution combines a simple exact construction with substantial empirical reductions in the cost of a frequently repeated operation.
summary.tldr: A rejection-sampling construction preserves the weighted minwise sampling distribution while delivering large speedups in reported real-data experiments.

title: Simple and Efficient Weighted Minwise Hashing

abstract: This paper introduces a new encoder-decoder architecture that is trained to reconstruct images by disentangling the salient information of the image and the values of attributes directly in the latent space. As a result, after training, our model can generate different realistic versions of an input image by varying the attribute values. By using continuous attribute values, we can choose how much a specific attribute is perceivable in the generated image. This property could allow for applications where users can modify an image using sliding knobs, like faders on a mixing console, to change the facial expression of a portrait, or to update the color of some objects. Compared to the state-of-the-art which mostly relies on training adversarial networks in pixel space by altering attribute values at train time, our approach results in much simpler training schemes and nicely scales to multiple attributes. We present evidence that our model can significantly change the perceived value of the attributes while preserving the naturalness of images.

The proposed encoder-decoder learns to reconstruct images while separating salient image information from attribute values in its latent representation. This organization allows the decoder to create different versions of the same input as the supplied attributes change.

The attribute values can vary continuously, so editing can control how strongly an attribute appears rather than merely switching it on or off. The authors suggest interfaces resembling mixing-console sliders, with possible uses such as changing a portrait's expression or an object's color. These are applications enabled by the model's continuous controls.

The paper reports a simpler training scheme than approaches that largely rely on adversarial training in pixel space while changing attributes during training. It also states that the method scales well to multiple attributes. The presented evidence shows substantial changes in perceived attributes while maintaining natural-looking images, supporting the idea that separating attribute controls in latent space can make image manipulation practical.
summary.tldr: Fader Networks separate image content and attributes in latent space to enable continuous, natural-looking image edits.

title: Fader Networks:Manipulating Images by Sliding Attributes

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) aims to train a lightweight classifier suitable to provide accurate inference with constrained resources in multi-label learning. Instead of directly consuming feature-label pairs, the classifier is trained by a teacher, i.e., a high-capacity model whose training may be resource-hungry. The accuracy of the classifier trained this way is usually suboptimal because it is difficult to learn the true data distribution from the teacher. An alternative method is to adversarially train the classifier against a discriminator in a two-player game akin to generative adversarial networks (GAN), which can ensure the classifier to learn the true data distribution at the equilibrium of this game. However, it may take excessively long time for such a two-player game to reach equilibrium due to high-variance gradient updates. To address these limitations, we propose a three-player game named KDGAN consisting of a classifier, a teacher, and a discriminator. The classifier and the teacher learn from each other via distillation losses and are adversarially trained against the discriminator via adversarial losses. By simultaneously optimizing the distillation and adversarial losses, the classifier will learn the true data distribution at the equilibrium. We approximate the discrete distribution learned by the classifier (or the teacher) with a concrete distribution. From the concrete distribution, we generate continuous samples to obtain low-variance gradient updates, which speed up the training. Extensive experiments using real datasets confirm the superiority of KDGAN in both accuracy and training speed.

Experiments on real datasets report superior accuracy and training speed. The approach therefore combines teacher-based guidance with adversarial learning and a continuous approximation intended to make the resulting optimization more efficient.
summary.tldr: KDGAN combines mutual distillation and adversarial training in a three-player game, improving accuracy and training speed in reported experiments.

title: KDGAN: Knowledge Distillation with Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: We develop an efficient and provably no-regret Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithm for optimization of black-box functions in high dimensions. We assume a generalized additive model with possibly overlapping variable groups. When the groups do not overlap, we are able to provide the first provably no-regret \emph{polynomial time} (in the number of evaluations of the acquisition function) algorithm for solving high dimensional BO. To make the optimization efficient and feasible, we introduce a novel deterministic Fourier Features approximation based on numerical integration with detailed analysis for the squared exponential kernel. The error of this approximation decreases \emph{exponentially} with the number of features, and allows for a precise approximation of both posterior mean and variance. In addition, the kernel matrix inversion improves in its complexity from cubic to essentially linear in the number of data points measured in basic arithmetic operations.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to a function whose internal workings are unavailable. High-dimensional inputs make both the search and its supporting computations difficult. This paper develops an efficient algorithm under a generalized additive assumption: the function is organized into contributions from groups of variables, and those groups may overlap.

The authors establish a no-regret guarantee for their approach. When the variable groups do not overlap, they additionally provide a polynomial-time guarantee measured in acquisition-function evaluations. That distinction matters because the stronger computational result relies on a more specific structure than the general model permits.

To reduce computational cost, the method approximates the kernel using deterministic Fourier features constructed through numerical integration. For the squared exponential kernel, the analysis gives exponentially decreasing approximation error with the number of features and precise approximations to posterior mean and variance. The approach also reduces the matrix-inversion computation from cubic to essentially linear dependence on the number of observations, measured in basic arithmetic operations.
summary.tldr: Additive structure and deterministic Fourier features enable efficient high-dimensional Bayesian optimization with conditional computational and no-regret guarantees.

title: Efficient High Dimensional Bayesian Optimization with Additivity and Quadrature Fourier Features

abstract: At initialization, artificial neural networks (ANNs) are equivalent to Gaussian processes in the infinite-width limit, thus connecting them to kernel methods. We prove that the evolution of an ANN during training can also be described by a kernel: during gradient descent on the parameters of an ANN, the network function (which maps input vectors to output vectors) follows the so-called kernel gradient associated with a new object, which we call the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). This kernel is central to describe the generalization features of ANNs. While the NTK is random at initialization and varies during training, in the infinite-width limit it converges to an explicit limiting kernel and stays constant during training. This makes it possible to study the training of ANNs in function space instead of parameter space. Convergence of the training can then be related to the positive-definiteness of the limiting NTK. We then focus on the setting of least-squares regression and show that in the infinite-width limit, the network function follows a linear differential equation during training. The convergence is fastest along the largest kernel principal components of the input data with respect to the NTK, hence suggesting a theoretical motivation for early stopping. Finally we study the NTK numerically, observe its behavior for wide networks, and compare it to the infinite-width limit.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the Neural Tangent Kernel, or NTK, to describe how a neural network's predictions evolve during gradient-based training. Instead of tracking every parameter individually, the kernel describes the network's changing input-output function. This extends the connection between neural networks and kernel methods beyond their behavior at initialization.

For finite networks, the NTK is initially random and changes during training. In the infinite-width limit, the authors prove that it approaches an explicit kernel that remains fixed. This makes training dynamics accessible in function space, and connects convergence to whether the limiting kernel is positive definite.

For least-squares regression in that limit, the prediction function follows a linear differential equation. Learning proceeds fastest along the largest principal components defined by the NTK, suggesting a theoretical motivation for early stopping. Numerical studies examine wide networks and compare their kernels with the infinite-width limit. The fixed-kernel result is specifically a limiting description, while the numerical work explores its relationship to finite, wide networks.
summary.tldr: The Neural Tangent Kernel describes network training dynamics and becomes fixed at infinite width, enabling a kernel-based analysis of convergence.

title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks

abstract: Policy optimization is an effective reinforcement learning approach to solve continuous control tasks. Recent achievements have shown that alternating online and offline optimization is a successful choice for efficient trajectory reuse. However, deciding when to stop optimizing and collect new trajectories is non-trivial, as it requires to account for the variance of the objective function estimate. In this paper, we propose a novel, model-free, policy search algorithm, POIS, applicable in both action-based and parameter-based settings. We first derive a high-confidence bound for importance sampling estimation; then we define a surrogate objective function, which is optimized offline whenever a new batch of trajectories is collected. Finally, the algorithm is tested on a selection of continuous control tasks, with both linear and deep policies, and compared with state-of-the-art policy optimization methods.

paragraphs: Policy optimization for continuous control can alternate between collecting trajectories and improving a policy using the collected data. Reusing trajectories can make learning more efficient, but it raises a decision: when should offline improvement stop and new experience be gathered? The paper identifies uncertainty in the estimated objective as central to that decision.

The proposed model-free algorithm, POIS, begins with a high-confidence bound for importance-sampling estimation. The authors then use this foundation to define a surrogate objective that is optimized offline after each new batch of trajectories arrives. This connects policy improvement on reused data with an explicit treatment of the estimate's uncertainty.

POIS applies in both action-based and parameter-based settings. The authors test it on a selection of continuous-control tasks using linear and deep policies, with comparisons to state-of-the-art optimization methods. The abstract describes this evaluation without stating a performance ranking. Its main stated contribution is an uncertainty-aware foundation for policy search that repeatedly optimizes over collected experience.
summary.tldr: POIS uses a high-confidence importance-sampling bound to build an offline policy-optimization objective for reusing collected trajectories.

title: Policy Optimization via Importance Sampling

abstract: Large amounts of labeled data are typically required to train deep learning models. For many real-world problems, however, acquiring additional data can be expensive or even impossible. We present semi-supervised deep kernel learning (SSDKL), a semi-supervised regression model based on minimizing predictive variance in the posterior regularization framework. SSDKL combines the hierarchical representation learning of neural networks with the probabilistic modeling capabilities of Gaussian processes. By leveraging unlabeled data, we show improvements on a diverse set of real-world regression tasks over supervised deep kernel learning and semi-supervised methods such as VAT and mean teacher adapted for regression.

paragraphs: Regression models predict numerical outputs, but obtaining enough labeled examples to train a deep model can be expensive or impossible. This paper proposes semi-supervised deep kernel learning, or SSDKL, to make use of examples whose output values are unavailable. Its central mechanism is to minimize predictive variance within a posterior-regularization framework.

The model combines neural networks' ability to learn hierarchical representations with Gaussian processes' probabilistic modeling capabilities. This pairing supplies both learned features and a predictive distribution. Unlabeled data enter through the variance-based learning criterion, giving those examples a role in shaping the model even though they do not supply target values for ordinary supervised regression.

The authors evaluate SSDKL on a diverse collection of real-world regression tasks. They report improvements over supervised deep kernel learning and over VAT and mean teacher methods adapted for regression. The findings support predictive-variance minimization as a useful way to incorporate unlabeled data in these tasks, connecting probabilistic prediction to the practical problem of limited labeled training data.
summary.tldr: SSDKL combines neural representations and Gaussian processes, using predictive variance to learn from unlabeled regression examples.

title: Semi-supervised Deep Kernel Learning: Regression with Unlabeled Data by Minimizing Predictive Variance

abstract: Neyshabur and Srebro proposed SIMPLE-LSH, which is the state-of-the-art hashing based algorithm for maximum inner product search (MIPS). We found that the performance of SIMPLE-LSH, in both theory and practice, suffers from long tails in the 2-norm distribution of real datasets. We propose NORM-RANGING LSH, which addresses the excessive normalization problem caused by long tails by partitioning a dataset into sub-datasets and building a hash index for each sub-dataset independently. We prove that NORM-RANGING LSH achieves lower query time complexity than SIMPLE-LSH under mild conditions. We also show that the idea of dataset partitioning can improve another hashing based MIPS algorithm. Experiments show that NORM-RANGING LSH probes much less items than SIMPLE-LSH at the same recall, thus significantly benefiting MIPS based applications.

paragraphs: Maximum inner product search seeks dataset vectors with large inner products against a query. The paper identifies a weakness in SIMPLE-LSH, a leading hashing approach: long tails in the distribution of vector lengths can cause excessive normalization. The authors show that this affects both the method's theoretical behavior and its practical performance.

NORM-RANGING LSH addresses the issue by splitting the dataset into subsets and building an independent hash index for each. Partitioning changes the scope over which indexing and normalization operate, directly targeting the problem created by a long-tailed norm distribution. The paper also shows that dataset partitioning can improve another hashing-based method for maximum inner product search.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove lower query-time complexity than SIMPLE-LSH. Experiments show that the proposed method examines substantially fewer items while achieving the same recall. Keeping recall fixed makes the reported benefit especially clear: the method reduces search work at a comparable retrieval level. The theoretical improvement remains conditional on the assumptions of the result.
summary.tldr: Partitioning vectors into separately indexed subsets improves inner-product search when long-tailed vector norms hinder normalization.

title: Norm-Ranging LSH for Maximum Inner Product Search

abstract: This paper focuses on two fundamental tasks of graph analysis: community detection and node representation learning, which capture the global and local structures of graphs respectively. In existing literature, these two tasks are usually independently studied while they are actually highly correlated. We propose a probabilistic generative model called vGraph to learn community membership and node representation collaboratively. Specifically, we assume that each node can be represented as a mixture of communities, and each community is defined as a multinomial distribution over nodes. Both the mixing coefficients and the community distribution are parameterized by the low-dimensional representations of the nodes and communities. We designed an effective variational inference algorithm for the optimization through backpropagation, which regularizes the community membership of neighboring nodes to be similar in the latent space. Experimental results on multiple real-world graphs show that vGraph is very effective in both community detection and node representation learning, outperforming many competitive baselines in both tasks. We show that the framework of vGraph is quite flexible and can be easily extended to detect hierarchical communities.

paragraphs: Community detection describes a graph's broader group structure, while node representation learning captures information about individual nodes and local structure. These tasks are often studied separately despite their close relationship. vGraph combines them in a probabilistic generative model so that community membership and node representations are learned collaboratively.

The model assumes each node is a mixture of communities and each community is a multinomial distribution over nodes. Low-dimensional representations of nodes and communities parameterize both the mixture coefficients and community distributions. A variational inference algorithm trains the model through backpropagation while encouraging neighboring nodes to have similar community memberships in the latent space.

Experiments on multiple real-world graphs show strong performance on both tasks, exceeding many competitive baselines. The framework can also be extended to identify hierarchical communities. The contribution is a shared probabilistic account of group membership and node representation, supported by results on both outputs rather than treating one solely as a preliminary step for the other.
summary.tldr: vGraph jointly learns community memberships and node representations through a generative mixture model, improving both tasks on evaluated real-world graphs.

title: vGraph: A Generative Model for Joint Community Detection and Node Representation Learning

abstract: The present paper develops a novel aggregated gradient approach for distributed machine learning that adaptively compresses the gradient communication. The key idea is to first quantize the computed gradients, and then skip less informative quantized gradient communications by reusing outdated gradients. Quantizing and skipping result in 'lazy' worker-server communications, which justifies the term Lazily Aggregated Quantized gradient that is henceforth abbreviated as LAQ. Our LAQ can provably attain the same linear convergence rate as the gradient descent in the strongly convex case, while effecting major savings in the communication overhead both in transmitted bits as well as in communication rounds. Empirically, experiments with real data corroborate a significant communication reduction compared to existing gradient- and stochastic gradient-based algorithms.

The key idea is to first quantize the computed gradients, and then skip less informative quantized gradient communications by reusing outdated gradients. Quantizing and skipping result in 'lazy' worker-server communications, which justifies the term Lazily Aggregated Quantized gradient that is henceforth abbreviated as LAQ. Our LAQ can provably attain the same linear convergence rate as the gradient descent in the strongly convex case, while effecting major savings in the communication overhead both in transmitted bits as well as in communication rounds. Empirically, experiments with real data corroborate a significant communication reduction compared to existing gradient- and stochastic gradient-based algorithms.

paragraphs: Distributed learning requires workers to communicate information used to update a shared model. This paper targets that communication burden through two complementary decisions: how much information each gradient message contains, and whether a new message is informative enough to send. Its method is called Lazily Aggregated Quantized gradients, or LAQ.

LAQ first quantizes computed gradients, reducing the information needed to represent them. It then skips some less informative communications and reuses older gradients instead. Combining these steps can save both transmitted bits and communication rounds. The adaptive skipping mechanism makes communication depend on the usefulness of an update rather than simply sending every newly computed gradient.

For strongly convex problems, the authors prove that LAQ can retain the same linear convergence rate as gradient descent while substantially reducing communication overhead. Experiments on real data also show significant communication reductions relative to existing gradient and stochastic-gradient methods. The theoretical result is specifically tied to the strongly convex case, while the experiments provide evidence of practical communication savings.
summary.tldr: LAQ compresses gradient messages and skips less informative updates, reducing communication while retaining a linear convergence rate in strongly convex problems.

title: Communication-Efficient Distributed Learning via Lazily Aggregated Quantized Gradients

abstract: It is well known that in stochastic multi-armed bandits (MAB), the sample mean of an arm is typically not an unbiased estimator of its true mean. In this paper, we decouple three different sources of this selection bias: adaptive \emph{sampling} of arms, adaptive \emph{stopping} of the experiment, and adaptively \emph{choosing} which arm to study. Through a new notion called ``optimism'' that captures certain natural monotonic behaviors of algorithms, we provide a clean and unified analysis of how optimistic rules affect the sign of the bias. The main takeaway message is that optimistic sampling induces a negative bias, but optimistic stopping and optimistic choosing both induce a positive bias. These results are derived in a general stochastic MAB setup that is entirely agnostic to the final aim of the experiment (regret minimization or best-arm identification or anything else). We provide examples of optimistic rules of each type, demonstrate that simulations confirm our theoretical predictions, and pose some natural but hard open problems.
