In this paper, we decouple three different sources of this selection bias: adaptive \emph{sampling} of arms, adaptive \emph{stopping} of the experiment, and adaptively \emph{choosing} which arm to study. Through a new notion called ``optimism'' that captures certain natural monotonic behaviors of algorithms, we provide a clean and unified analysis of how optimistic rules affect the sign of the bias. The main takeaway message is that optimistic sampling induces a negative bias, but optimistic stopping and optimistic choosing both induce a positive bias. These results are derived in a general stochastic MAB setup that is entirely agnostic to the final aim of the experiment (regret minimization or best-arm identification or anything else). We provide examples of optimistic rules of each type, demonstrate that simulations confirm our theoretical predictions, and pose some natural but hard open problems.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit experiment, the observations collected from an option can influence subsequent decisions about the experiment. Its sample average therefore need not be an unbiased estimate of its true average reward. The paper separates three places where this dependence arises: choosing which arm to sample, deciding when to stop, and choosing which arm's estimate to examine.

The authors introduce a mathematical notion of optimism that captures particular monotonic behaviors in these decisions. Under the corresponding optimistic rules, the sources of bias point in different directions. Adaptive sampling induces negative bias, while adaptive stopping and adaptive selection of an arm induce positive bias. These conclusions concern the defined rule classes, rather than every possible adaptive procedure.

The analysis uses a general stochastic bandit setting and does not depend on whether the experiment aims to minimize regret or identify the best arm. Examples illustrate each rule type, and simulations support the predicted bias directions. The practical lesson is that interpreting an estimate requires distinguishing how observations, stopping, and final selection were determined.
summary.tldr: For defined optimistic bandit rules, adaptive sampling biases sample means downward, while adaptive stopping and arm selection bias them upward.

title: Are sample means in multi-armed bandits positively or negatively biased?

abstract: We study the task of smoothing a circuit, i.e., ensuring that all children of a plus-gate mention the same variables. Circuits serve as the building blocks of state-of-the-art inference algorithms on discrete probabilistic graphical models and probabilistic programs. They are also important for discrete density estimation algorithms. Many of these tasks require the input circuit to be smooth. However, smoothing has not been studied in its own right yet, and only a trivial quadratic algorithm is known. This paper studies efficient smoothing for structured decomposable circuits. We propose a near-linear time algorithm for this task and explore lower bounds for smoothing decomposable circuits, using existing results on range-sum queries. Further, for the important case of All-Marginals, we show a more efficient linear-time algorithm. We validate experimentally the performance of our methods.

However, smoothing has not been studied in its own right yet, and only a trivial quadratic algorithm is known. This paper studies efficient smoothing for structured decomposable circuits. paragraphs: Probabilistic inference and density-estimation algorithms often require smooth circuits: every child of a plus gate must mention the same variables. Although this property is operationally important, the paper notes that the previously available general smoothing procedure was a straightforward quadratic-time algorithm.

The authors study smoothing as an algorithmic problem for structured decomposable circuits and propose a near-linear-time solution. They also examine lower bounds for smoothing decomposable circuits by connecting the task with existing results about range-sum queries.

For the important all-marginals case, they obtain a more efficient linear-time algorithm. Experiments validate the performance of the proposed methods. The different claims apply to different tasks and circuit assumptions; the abstract does not say that every arbitrary circuit can be smoothed in linear time. Its contribution is a sharper understanding of this preprocessing requirement together with faster algorithms in the specified settings.
summary.tldr: Near-linear smoothing and linear-time all-marginals computation improve structured probabilistic circuits.

title: Smoothing Structured Decomposable Circuits

abstract: This paper introduces MDP homomorphic networks for deep reinforcement learning. MDP homomorphic networks are neural networks that are equivariant under symmetries in the joint state-action space of an MDP. Current approaches to deep reinforcement learning do not usually exploit knowledge about such structure. By building this prior knowledge into policy and value networks using an equivariance constraint, we can reduce the size of the solution space. We specifically focus on group-structured symmetries (invertible transformations). Additionally, we introduce an easy method for constructing equivariant network layers numerically, so the system designer need not solve the constraints by hand, as is typically done. We construct MDP homomorphic MLPs and CNNs that are equivariant under either a group of reflections or rotations. We show that such networks converge faster than unstructured baselines on CartPole, a grid world and Pong.

Current approaches to deep reinforcement learning do not usually exploit knowledge about such structure. By building this prior knowledge into policy and value networks using an equivariance constraint, we can reduce the size of the solution space. We specifically focus on group-structured symmetries (invertible transformations). Additionally, we introduce an easy method for constructing equivariant network layers numerically, so the system designer need not solve the constraints by hand, as is typically done. We construct MDP homomorphic MLPs and CNNs that are equivariant under either a group of reflections or rotations. We show that such networks converge faster than unstructured baselines on CartPole, a grid world and Pong.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning problems contain known symmetries relating states and actions. This paper builds that knowledge into policy and value networks through equivariance: when a state-action configuration undergoes a symmetry transformation, the network responds in the corresponding structured way. The resulting architectures are called MDP homomorphic networks.

Constraining networks in this way reduces the space of solutions learning must consider. The paper specifically studies group-structured symmetries, which involve invertible transformations. It also introduces a numerical method for constructing equivariant layers, easing the designer's task by avoiding the need to solve the symmetry constraints by hand. The authors construct both multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks with reflection or rotation symmetries.

On CartPole, a grid world, and Pong, these structured networks converge faster than unstructured baselines. The results support incorporating applicable prior knowledge into reinforcement learning architectures. The contribution combines a way to restrict networks according to known state-action structure with a practical construction method and empirical evidence of faster convergence in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: MDP homomorphic networks encode known state-action symmetries and converge faster than unstructured baselines in the reported reinforcement learning tasks.

title: MDP Homomorphic Networks: Group Symmetries in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Adam is a widely used optimization method for training deep learning models. It computes individual adaptive learning rates for different parameters. In this paper, we propose a generalization of Adam, called Adambs, that allows us to also adapt to different training examples based on their importance in the model's convergence. To achieve this, we maintain a distribution over all examples, selecting a mini-batch in each iteration by sampling according to this distribution, which we update using a multi-armed bandit algorithm. This ensures that examples that are more beneficial to the model training are sampled with higher probabilities. We theoretically show that Adambs improves the convergence rate of Adam---$O(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{T} })$ instead of $O(\sqrt{\frac{n}{T}})$ in some cases. Experiments on various models and datasets demonstrate Adambs's fast convergence in practice.

paragraphs: Adam adapts learning rates separately for different model parameters. This paper adds another kind of adaptation: choosing which training examples to use more often. The proposed method, Adambs, treats examples as having different levels of usefulness for making progress toward convergence, rather than giving every example the same sampling probability throughout training.

Adambs maintains a probability distribution over the training examples and draws each mini-batch from that distribution. A multi-armed bandit algorithm updates the probabilities as training proceeds. Examples that contribute more to training receive higher sampling probabilities, making the selection of data part of the optimization procedure alongside Adam's parameter-specific updates.

The theoretical analysis improves the convergence rate from O(sqrt(n/T)) to O(sqrt(log n/T)) in some cases. The qualification matters: the abstract does not claim this improvement for every training problem. Experiments across several models and datasets also demonstrate fast convergence. Together, the results support adapting both parameter updates and example selection as a way to improve training efficiency.
summary.tldr: Adambs extends Adam with bandit-based example sampling, improving convergence guarantees in some cases and showing fast convergence experimentally.

title: Adam with Bandit Sampling for Deep Learning

abstract: We develop a method for generating causal post-hoc explanations of black-box classifiers based on a learned low-dimensional representation of the data. The explanation is causal in the sense that changing learned latent factors produces a change in the classifier output statistics. To construct these explanations, we design a learning framework that leverages a generative model and information-theoretic measures of causal influence. Our objective function encourages both the generative model to faithfully represent the data distribution and the latent factors to have a large causal influence on the classifier output. Our method learns both global and local explanations, is compatible with any classifier that admits class probabilities and a gradient, and does not require labeled attributes or knowledge of causal structure. Using carefully controlled test cases, we provide intuition that illuminates the function of our causal objective. We then demonstrate the practical utility of our method on image recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Post-hoc explanations should clarify which changes in an input affect a classifier’s decision. This paper learns a low-dimensional generative representation whose latent factors influence the output statistics of a trained classifier. The stated causal meaning concerns interventions on these learned factors and their effect on the classifier.

The training objective balances faithful modeling of the data distribution with information-theoretic measures of causal influence on predictions. It produces both global and local explanations without requiring labeled attributes or a known causal structure. The classifier must provide class probabilities and a gradient.

Controlled test cases illustrate how the objective behaves, followed by image-recognition demonstrations. The abstract does not report numerical explanation-quality scores. Its causal claim should remain tied to changes within the learned generative representation; it does not by itself establish the real-world causal relationships that originally produced the observed data.
summary.tldr: A generative model learns latent factors whose changes influence a classifier’s output.

title: Generative causal explanations of black-box classifiers

abstract: Many learning algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent, are affected by the order in which training examples are used. It is often observed that sampling the training examples without-replacement, also known as random reshuffling, causes learning algorithms to converge faster. We give a counterexample to the Operator Inequality of Noncommutative Arithmetic and Geometric Means, a longstanding conjecture that relates to the performance of random reshuffling in learning algorithms (Recht and Ré, "Toward a noncommutative arithmetic-geometric mean inequality: conjectures, case-studies, and consequences," COLT 2012). We use this to give an example of a learning task and algorithm for which with-replacement random sampling actually outperforms random reshuffling.

We use this to give an example of a learning task and algorithm for which with-replacement random sampling actually outperforms random reshuffling.

paragraphs: The order of training examples can influence how quickly a learning algorithm converges. Random reshuffling samples without replacement, avoiding repeated selection within a pass through the data. Sampling with replacement allows examples to be selected again. Although reshuffling often performs better in practice, this paper asks whether its advantage can be treated as a general mathematical rule.

The authors construct a counterexample to a longstanding conjecture called the Operator Inequality of Noncommutative Arithmetic and Geometric Means. That conjecture is connected to the performance of random reshuffling in learning algorithms. Disproving it removes a proposed mathematical relationship that could support a broad ordering of the two sampling strategies.

They then use the counterexample to construct a learning task and algorithm for which sampling with replacement outperforms reshuffling. The conclusion is deliberately specific: an often observed advantage of reshuffling has exceptions. The work does not establish that replacement sampling is generally preferable. Its significance is to show that comparisons must account for the learning problem and algorithm, because a universal preference for reshuffling would exclude a demonstrated case.
summary.tldr: A mathematical counterexample yields a learning problem where sampling with replacement outperforms random reshuffling.

title: Random Reshuffling is Not Always Better

abstract: Several works have aimed to explain why overparameterized neural networks generalize well when trained by Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). The consensus explanation that has emerged credits the randomized nature of SGD for the bias of the training process towards low-complexity models and, thus, for implicit regularization. We take a careful look at this explanation in the context of image classification with common deep neural network architectures. We find that if we do not regularize \emph{explicitly}, then SGD can be easily made to converge to poorly-generalizing, high-complexity models: all it takes is to first train on a random labeling on the data, before switching to properly training with the correct labels. In contrast, we find that in the presence of explicit regularization, pretraining with random labels has no detrimental effect on SGD. We believe that our results give evidence that explicit regularization plays a far more important role in the success of overparameterized neural networks than what has been understood until now. Specifically, in suppressing complicated models that got lucky with the training data, regularization not only makes simple models that fit the data well the global optima, but it also clears the way to make them discoverable by local methods, such as SGD.

This paper tests that explanation in image classification using common deep architectures. It asks whether the optimizer's implicit preferences are enough to prevent highly complex solutions that generalize poorly.

The authors first train networks with randomly assigned labels, then switch to the correct labels. Without explicit regularization, this procedure can readily lead SGD to poorly generalizing, high-complexity models. In the reported experiments with explicit regularization, the same random-label pretraining has no detrimental effect. The training history therefore exposes an important difference between these two settings.

The authors interpret the results as evidence that explicit regularization contributes more to successful generalization than an explanation centered on SGD alone suggests. Their account gives regularization two roles: favoring simpler solutions that fit the data and making those solutions discoverable by local optimization. The experiments challenge the sufficiency of optimizer randomness as an explanation without claiming that SGD always finds bad solutions.
summary.tldr: Random-label pretraining can steer unregularized SGD toward poorly generalizing models, highlighting the importance of explicit regularization.

title: Bad Global Minima Exist and SGD Can Reach Them

abstract: Learning-based photometric stereo methods predict the surface normal either in a per-pixel or an all-pixel manner. Per-pixel methods explore the inter-image intensity variation of each pixel but ignore features from the intra-image spatial domain. All-pixel methods explore the intra-image intensity variation of each input image but pay less attention to the inter-image lighting variation. In this paper, we present a Graph-based Photometric Stereo Network, which unifies per-pixel and all-pixel processings to explore both inter-image and intra-image information. For per-pixel operation, we propose the Unstructured Feature Extraction Layer to connect an arbitrary number of input image-light pairs into graph structures, and introduce Structure-aware Graph Convolution filters to balance the input data by appropriately weighting shadows and specular highlights. For all-pixel operation, we propose the Normal Regression Network to make efficient use of the intra-image spatial information for predicting a surface normal map with rich details. Experimental results on the real-world benchmark show that our method achieves excellent performance under both sparse and dense lighting distributions.

paragraphs: Photometric stereo predicts surface orientation from images captured under different lighting. The paper describes two complementary sources of information: how one pixel changes across images and how intensities vary spatially within each image. Existing learning approaches tend to emphasize one source while making less use of the other.

GPS-Net combines both forms of processing. For the per-pixel component, an Unstructured Feature Extraction Layer connects an arbitrary number of image-light pairs into graphs. Structure-aware graph convolution then weights the observations to account appropriately for shadows and specular highlights. This graph representation provides a way to process lighting observations without requiring a fixed number of input pairs.

For the spatial component, a Normal Regression Network uses information within images to predict a detailed surface normal map. Experiments on a real-world benchmark report excellent performance with both sparse and dense lighting distributions. The findings support combining variation across lighting conditions with spatial context, so the prediction can draw on evidence about both individual pixels and the surrounding surface.
summary.tldr: GPS-Net combines graph-based processing of lighting observations with spatial image features to predict detailed surface normals.

title: GPS-Net: Graph-based Photometric Stereo Network

abstract: Reasoning about the physical world requires models that are endowed with the right inductive biases to learn the underlying dynamics. Recent works improve generalization for predicting trajectories by learning the Hamiltonian or Lagrangian of a system rather than the differential equations directly. While these methods encode the constraints of the systems using generalized coordinates, we show that embedding the system into Cartesian coordinates and enforcing the constraints explicitly with Lagrange multipliers dramatically simplifies the learning problem. We introduce a series of challenging chaotic and extended-body systems, including systems with $N$-pendulums, spring coupling, magnetic fields, rigid rotors, and gyroscopes, to push the limits of current approaches. Our experiments show that Cartesian coordinates with explicit constraints lead to a 100x improvement in accuracy and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics can benefit from representing a system through its Hamiltonian or Lagrangian rather than directly learning its differential equations. The paper examines a design choice within these physics-informed models: how to represent the system's coordinates and constraints. Earlier approaches encode constraints through generalized coordinates.

The authors instead embed the system in Cartesian coordinates and enforce constraints explicitly using Lagrange multipliers. They show that this formulation dramatically simplifies the learning problem. The choice concerns how physical structure enters the model: the coordinate representation and the enforcement of constraints become explicit parts of the learning setup.

The evaluation includes challenging chaotic and extended-body systems involving multiple pendulums, spring coupling, magnetic fields, rigid rotors, and gyroscopes. In these experiments, the authors report a 100-fold improvement in accuracy and data efficiency from using Cartesian coordinates with explicit constraints. These results make coordinate choice a substantive modeling consideration, showing that retaining Hamiltonian or Lagrangian structure while changing how constraints are expressed can substantially improve the evaluated learning problems.
summary.tldr: Using Cartesian coordinates with explicit constraints simplifies Hamiltonian and Lagrangian learning and yields reported 100-fold experimental gains in accuracy and data efficiency.

title: Simplifying Hamiltonian and Lagrangian Neural Networks via Explicit Constraints

abstract: One-shot weight sharing methods have recently drawn great attention in neural architecture search due to high efficiency and competitive performance. However, weight sharing across models has an inherent deficiency, i.e., insufficient training of subnetworks in the hypernetwork. To alleviate this problem, we present a simple yet effective architecture distillation method. The central idea is that subnetworks can learn collaboratively and teach each other throughout the training process, aiming to boost the convergence of individual models. We introduce the concept of prioritized path, which refers to the architecture candidates exhibiting superior performance during training. Distilling knowledge from the prioritized paths is able to boost the training of subnetworks. Since the prioritized paths are changed on the fly depending on their performance and complexity, the final obtained paths are the cream of the crop. We directly select the most promising one from the prioritized paths as the final architecture, without using other complex search methods, such as reinforcement learning or evolution algorithms. The experiments on ImageNet verify such path distillation method can improve the convergence ratio and performance of the hypernetwork, as well as boosting the training of subnetworks. The discovered architectures achieve superior performance compared to the recent MobileNetV3 and EfficientNet families under aligned settings. Moreover, the experiments on object detection and more challenging search space show the generality and robustness of the proposed method. Code and models are available at \url{https://github.com/neurips-20/cream.git}.

paragraphs: One-shot architecture search saves training effort by letting candidate networks share weights inside a larger hypernetwork. A drawback is that individual subnetworks can receive insufficient training, weakening the candidates being considered. This paper introduces architecture distillation to improve their training through collaboration among subnetworks.

The method maintains prioritized paths: candidate architectures that perform well during training. These candidates teach other subnetworks by transferring knowledge, with the aim of improving individual convergence. The prioritized set changes as candidate performance and complexity change. At the end, the method selects the most promising prioritized path directly, avoiding an additional search procedure based on reinforcement learning or evolutionary algorithms.

Under aligned settings, the discovered architectures outperform the compared MobileNetV3 and EfficientNet families. Experiments on object detection and a more challenging search space further support the method’s generality and robustness. The results suggest that improving how shared-weight candidates learn can benefit both architecture selection and the resulting models.
summary.tldr: Distilling knowledge from dynamically prioritized subnetworks improves one-shot architecture search and enables direct selection of a strong final architecture.

title: Cream of the Crop: Distilling Prioritized Paths For One-Shot Neural Architecture Search

abstract: There has been recent interest in using machine-learned predictions to improve the worst-case guarantees of online algorithms. In this paper we continue this line of work by studying the online knapsack problem, but with very weak predictions: in the form of knowing an upper and lower bound for the number of items of each value. We systematically derive online algorithms that attain the best possible competitive ratio for any fixed prediction; we also extend the results to more general settings such as generalized one-way trading and two-stage online knapsack. Our work shows that even seemingly weak predictions can be utilized effectively to provably improve the performance of online algorithms.

In this paper we continue this line of work by studying the online knapsack problem, but with very weak predictions: in the form of knowing an upper and lower bound for the number of items of each value. We systematically derive online algorithms that attain the best possible competitive ratio for any fixed prediction; we also extend the results to more general settings such as generalized one-way trading and two-stage online knapsack. Our work shows that even seemingly weak predictions can be utilized effectively to provably improve the performance of online algorithms.

paragraphs: Online knapsack requires making allocation choices as items arrive, before the entire input is known. This paper asks how much help predictions can provide when they contain very limited information. Its predictions specify only lower and upper bounds on the number of items at each value, rather than describing the complete future sequence.

For any fixed prediction of this form, the authors systematically derive algorithms achieving the best possible competitive ratio. That ratio measures worst-case performance relative to an optimal solution with advance knowledge. The result therefore connects the strength of an online guarantee to the particular frequency information supplied, rather than requiring a detailed forecast.

The paper extends its results to generalized one-way trading and two-stage online knapsack. Across these formulations, the central finding is that coarse predictions can still improve provable online performance. The optimality claim is tied to each fixed prediction and the studied setting. This makes the contribution useful for understanding the value of partial information: even interval bounds on frequencies can support stronger decisions.
summary.tldr: Bounds on item frequencies suffice to derive online knapsack algorithms with the best possible competitive ratio for each fixed prediction.

title: Online Knapsack with Frequency Predictions

abstract: Graph Neural Networks are perfectly suited to capture latent interactions between various entities in the spatio-temporal domain (e.g. videos). However, when an explicit structure is not available, it is not obvious what atomic elements should be represented as nodes. Current works generally use pre-trained object detectors or fixed, predefined regions to extract graph nodes. Improving upon this, our proposed model learns nodes that dynamically attach to well-delimited salient regions, which are relevant for a higher-level task, without using any object-level supervision. Constructing these localized, adaptive nodes gives our model inductive bias towards object-centric representations and we show that it discovers regions that are well correlated with objects in the video. In extensive ablation studies and experiments on two challenging datasets, we show superior performance to previous graph neural networks models for video classification.

When the video supplies no explicit graph, earlier approaches commonly use pretrained object detectors or fixed regions. Those choices determine the elements whose interactions the network can learn.

This paper instead learns nodes that attach dynamically to clearly bounded, salient regions relevant to the higher-level task. It does so without object-level supervision. The localized, adaptive construction encourages an object-centered representation, while allowing the training task to influence which regions become graph nodes rather than fixing them in advance.

The authors show that the discovered regions correlate well with objects in the videos. That finding supports the intended object-centered bias without claiming that every learned node is a perfectly identified object. Ablation studies and experiments on two challenging datasets report better video-classification performance than previous graph neural network models. Together, the results connect the learned choice of graph elements with improved performance on the task those elements are meant to support.
summary.tldr: Learning adaptive video regions as graph nodes improves classification without requiring object-level supervision.

title: Discovering Dynamic Salient Regions for Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We propose several schemes for upper bounding the optimal value of the constrained most probable explanation (CMPE) problem. Given a set of discrete random variables, two probabilistic graphical models defined over them and a real number $q$, this problem involves finding an assignment of values to all the variables such that the probability of the assignment is maximized according to the first model and is bounded by $q$ w.r.t. the second model. In prior work, it was shown that CMPE is a unifying problem with several applications and special cases including the nearest assignment problem, the decision preserving most probable explanation task and robust estimation. It was also shown that CMPE is NP-hard even on tractable models such as bounded treewidth networks and is hard for integer linear programming methods because it includes a dense global constraint. The main idea in our approach is to simplify the problem via Lagrange relaxation and decomposition to yield either a knapsack problem or the unconstrained most probable explanation (MPE) problem, and then solving the two problems, respectively using specialized knapsack algorithms and mini-buckets based upper bounding schemes. We evaluate our proposed scheme along several dimensions including quality of the bounds and computation time required on various benchmark graphical models and how it can be used to find heuristic, near-optimal feasible solutions in an example application pertaining to robust estimation and adversarial attacks on classifiers.

paragraphs: The constrained most probable explanation problem asks for an assignment of discrete variables that is as probable as possible under one graphical model while meeting a probability bound under another. This combines a preference with a global constraint. The problem remains NP-hard even for some graphical models that otherwise support tractable inference.

The paper develops upper bounds on the best achievable objective value. Its approach uses Lagrange relaxation and decomposition to simplify the constrained problem into either a knapsack problem or an unconstrained most probable explanation problem. Specialized knapsack algorithms handle the first route, while mini-bucket upper-bounding schemes handle the second.

The authors evaluate both bound quality and computation time on benchmark graphical models. They also examine how the schemes help find heuristic, near-optimal feasible solutions in an application involving robust estimation and adversarial attacks on classifiers. The contribution supplies ways to assess and approach a difficult constrained optimum, preserving the distinction between bounding the optimum and obtaining a feasible assignment that approximates it.
summary.tldr: Relaxation and decomposition yield new upper bounds for constrained probabilistic inference and support finding near-optimal feasible assignments.

title: Novel Upper Bounds for the Constrained Most Probable Explanation Task

abstract: We propose the use of the vector-valued distance to compute distances and extract geometric information from the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices (SPD), and develop gyrovector calculus, constructing analogs of vector space operations in this curved space. We implement these operations and showcase their versatility in the tasks of knowledge graph completion, item recommendation, and question answering. In experiments, the SPD models outperform their equivalents in Euclidean and hyperbolic space. The vector-valued distance allows us to visualize embeddings, showing that the models learn to disentangle representations of positive samples from negative ones.

paragraphs: This paper develops tools for learning representations in the curved space of symmetric positive definite matrices. It proposes a vector-valued distance for computing distances and extracting geometric information. Keeping distance information in vector form also provides a way to examine how learned representations are organized.

The authors complement this distance with gyrovector calculus, constructing counterparts of familiar vector-space operations for the matrix manifold. They implement these operations and use them in knowledge graph completion, item recommendation, and question answering. The combined contribution supplies both a way to compare representations and operations for working with them in the chosen geometry.

In the reported experiments, the symmetric positive definite models outperform their corresponding models in Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces. Visualizations based on the vector-valued distance show learned separation between representations of positive and negative samples. These results demonstrate practical uses for the proposed geometry across the evaluated tasks. They also connect predictive performance with an interpretable view of how the embedding space distinguishes the two kinds of samples.
summary.tldr: Vector-valued distances and gyrovector operations enable effective SPD-matrix embeddings and reveal learned separation between positive and negative samples.

title: Vector-valued Distance and Gyrocalculus on the Space of Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices

abstract: We show a generic reduction from multiclass differentially private PAC learning to binary private PAC learning. We apply this transformation to a recently proposed binary private PAC learner to obtain a private multiclass learner with sample complexity that has a polynomial dependence on the multiclass Littlestone dimension and a poly-logarithmic dependence on the number of classes. This yields a doubly exponential improvement in the dependence on both parameters over learners from previous work. Our proof extends the notion of $\Psi$-dimension defined in work of Ben-David et al. [JCSS, 1995] to the online setting and explores its general properties.

This yields a doubly exponential improvement in the dependence on both parameters over learners from previous work. Our proof extends the notion of $\Psi$-dimension defined in work of Ben-David et al. [JCSS, 1995] to the online setting and explores its general properties.

paragraphs: Private learning must learn from examples while satisfying a differential privacy requirement. This paper asks how learning with many possible classes relates to learning with only two. It establishes a generic reduction that turns a binary differentially private PAC learner into a multiclass private learner, connecting the two problems through a reusable theoretical transformation.

Applying the reduction to an existing binary learner produces a sample-complexity bound with polynomial dependence on the multiclass Littlestone dimension and polylogarithmic dependence on the number of classes. These quantities describe different aspects of the problem: the complexity of the hypothesis class and the size of the label set. The paper reports a doubly exponential improvement in both dependencies over previous learners.

The proof extends the notion of Psi-dimension to an online setting and studies its properties. This supplies the mathematical structure needed for the reduction and its improved bounds. The result concerns how many examples private multiclass learning requires, showing that strong binary learning guarantees can yield substantially better multiclass sample guarantees.
summary.tldr: A reduction from private multiclass learning to private binary learning yields sharply improved sample-complexity bounds.

title: Multiclass versus Binary Differentially Private PAC Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of preference bandits in the contextual setting. At each round, the learner is presented with a context set of $K$ items, chosen randomly from a potentially infinite set of arms $\mathcal D \subseteq \mathbf R^d$. However, unlike classical contextual bandits, our framework only allows the learner to receive feedback in terms of item preferences: At each round, the learner is allowed to play a subset of size $q$ (any $q \in \{2,\ldots,K\}$) upon which only a (noisy) winner of the subset is revealed. Yet, same as the classical setup, the goal is still to compete against the best context arm at each round. The problem is relevant in various online decision-making scenarios, including recommender systems, information retrieval, tournament ranking--typically any application where it's easier to elicit the items' relative strength instead of their absolute scores. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to consider preference-based stochastic contextual bandits for potentially infinite decision spaces. We start with presenting two algorithms for the special case of pairwise preferences $(q=2)$: The first algorithm is simple and easy to implement with an $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T})$ regret guarantee, while the second algorithm is shown to achieve the optimal $\tilde O(\sqrt{dT})$ regret, as follows from our $\Omega(\sqrt {dT})$ matching lower bound analysis. We then proceed to analyze the problem for any general $q$-subsetwise preferences ($q \ge 2$), where surprisingly, our lower bound proves the fundamental performance limit to be $\Omega(\sqrt{d T})$ yet again, independent of the subsetsize $q$. Following this, we propose a matching upper bound algorithm justifying the tightness of our results. This implies having access to subsetwise preferences does not help in faster information aggregation for our feedback model. All the results are corroborated empirically against existing baselines.

summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal contextual preference-bandit rates and shows that larger winner-only comparison sets do not improve the fundamental rate.

title: Optimal Algorithms for Stochastic Contextual Preference Bandits

abstract: While Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to train an agent from a reward function in a given environment, Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) seeks to recover the reward function from observing an expert's behavior. It is well known that, in general, various reward functions can lead to the same optimal policy, and hence, IRL is ill-defined. However, \cite{cao2021identifiability} showed that, if we observe two or more experts with different discount factors or acting in different environments, the reward function can under certain conditions be identified up to a constant. This work starts by showing an equivalent identifiability statement from multiple experts in tabular MDPs based on a rank condition, which is easily verifiable and is shown to be also necessary. We then extend our result to various different scenarios, i.e., we characterize reward identifiability in the case where the reward function can be represented as a linear combination of given features, making it more interpretable, or when we have access to approximate transition matrices. Even when the reward is not identifiable, we provide conditions characterizing when data on multiple experts in a given environment allows to generalize and train an optimal agent in a new environment. Our theoretical results on reward identifiability and generalizability are validated in various numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards from an expert's behavior. The difficulty is that multiple reward functions can produce the same optimal policy. Observing several experts with different discount factors or environments can resolve that ambiguity under certain conditions, identifying rewards up to an additive constant.

This paper gives an equivalent identifiability statement for multiple experts in tabular Markov decision processes using an easily checked rank condition. The condition is also necessary, so it characterizes when recovery is possible in the analyzed setting. The authors extend their results to rewards expressed as linear combinations of known features and to cases with approximate transition matrices.

The paper separately studies whether expert behavior can support an optimal agent in a new environment when the reward itself remains ambiguous. It supplies conditions characterizing when that generalization is possible. This separates two questions that need not have the same answer: whether one can recover the reward and whether one can act optimally elsewhere. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical results on both questions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when multiple experts identify a reward function and when their behavior supports optimal transfer even without reward identifiability.

title: Identifiability and generalizability from multiple experts in Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Imperfect-Information Extensive-Form Games (IIEFGs) is a prevalent model for real-world games involving imperfect information and sequential plays. The Extensive-Form Correlated Equilibrium (EFCE) has been proposed as a natural solution concept for multi-player general-sum IIEFGs. However, existing algorithms for finding an EFCE require full feedback from the game, and it remains open how to efficiently learn the EFCE in the more challenging bandit feedback setting where the game can only be learned by observations from repeated playing. This paper presents the first sample-efficient algorithm for learning the EFCE from bandit feedback. We begin by proposing $K$-EFCE---a generalized definition that allows players to observe and deviate from the recommended actions for $K$ times. The $K$-EFCE includes the EFCE as a special case at $K=1$, and is an increasingly stricter notion of equilibrium as $K$ increases. We then design an uncoupled no-regret algorithm that finds an $\varepsilon$-approximate $K$-EFCE within $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\max_{i}X_iA_i^{K}/\varepsilon^2)$ iterations in the full feedback setting, where $X_i$ and $A_i$ are the number of information sets and actions for the $i$-th player. Our algorithm works by minimizing a wide-range regret at each information set that takes into account all possible recommendation histories. Finally, we design a sample-based variant of our algorithm that learns an $\varepsilon$-approximate $K$-EFCE within $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\max_{i}X_iA_i^{K+1}/\varepsilon^2)$ episodes of play in the bandit feedback setting. When specialized to $K=1$, this gives the first sample-efficient algorithm for learning EFCE from bandit feedback.

paragraphs: In sequential games with imperfect information, players must learn while observing only part of what happens. This paper studies extensive-form correlated equilibrium, a solution concept for multiplayer games with potentially different objectives. Its main contribution is an algorithm that learns such an equilibrium efficiently from repeated play, using bandit feedback instead of full game feedback.

The authors introduce K-EFCE, which allows a player to observe and deviate from recommendations K times. The usual equilibrium appears at K = 1, while larger K imposes stronger requirements. Their uncoupled no-regret algorithm accounts for possible recommendation histories when minimizing regret at each information set, the collection of situations a player cannot distinguish.

For approximation error ε, the full-feedback iteration bound scales, up to logarithmic factors, as the largest X_i A_i^K/ε² across players. The bandit version uses X_i A_i^(K+1)/ε² episodes, where X_i and A_i count information sets and actions. Setting K = 1 yields the stated first sample-efficient bandit-feedback algorithm for EFCE, while the dependence on K quantifies the cost of stronger equilibrium requirements.
summary.tldr: A sample-based no-regret algorithm efficiently learns extensive-form correlated equilibria from bandit feedback, with extensions to stronger recommendation-deviation guarantees.

title: Sample-Efficient Learning of Correlated Equilibria in Extensive-Form Games

abstract: Off-policy evaluation often refers to two related tasks: estimating the expected return of a policy and estimating its value function (or other functions of interest, such as density ratios). While recent works on marginalized importance sampling (MIS) show that the former can enjoy provable guarantees under realizable function approximation, the latter is only known to be feasible under much stronger assumptions such as prohibitively expressive discriminators. In this work, we provide guarantees for off-policy function estimation under only realizability, by imposing proper regularization on the MIS objectives. Compared to commonly used regularization in MIS, our regularizer is much more flexible and can account for an arbitrary user-specified distribution, under which the learned function will be close to the groundtruth. We provide exact characterization of the optimal dual solution that needs to be realized by the discriminator class, which determines the data-coverage assumption in the case of value-function learning. As another surprising observation, the regularizer can be altered to relax the data-coverage requirement, and completely eliminate it in the ideal case with strong side information.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation uses data collected under one policy to assess another. Estimating a single expected return and learning an entire value function are related but different tasks. Previous guarantees for marginalized importance sampling supported return estimation under realizability, while function estimation had required stronger assumptions. Realizability means that the chosen function classes can represent the relevant targets.

The paper introduces a more flexible regularizer for marginalized importance-sampling objectives. It establishes function-estimation guarantees under realizability and lets the user specify the distribution under which estimation errors matter. This makes the accuracy objective explicit: a learned function can be judged according to a chosen distribution rather than only the weighting implicit in a conventional objective.

The authors also characterize the optimal dual solution that the discriminator class must represent. For value-function learning, that characterization determines the required data coverage. Changing the regularizer can weaken the coverage requirement, and can remove it in an ideal case with strong side information. That last conclusion depends on the additional information, rather than applying to arbitrary datasets.
summary.tldr: Flexible regularization enables off-policy function-estimation guarantees under realizability while allowing users to choose how estimation error is weighted.

title: Beyond the Return: Off-policy Function Estimation under User-specified Error-measuring Distributions

abstract: Nonlinear dynamics are ubiquitous in science and engineering applications, but the physics of most complex systems is far from being fully understood. Discovering interpretable governing equations from measurement data can help us understand and predict the behavior of complex dynamic systems. Although extensive work has recently been done in this field, robustly distilling explicit model forms from very sparse data with considerable noise remains intractable. Moreover, quantifying and propagating the uncertainty of the identified system from noisy data is challenging, and relevant literature is still limited. To bridge this gap, we develop a novel Bayesian spline learning framework to identify parsimonious governing equations of nonlinear (spatio)temporal dynamics from sparse, noisy data with quantified uncertainty. The proposed method utilizes spline basis to handle the data scarcity and measurement noise, upon which a group of derivatives can be accurately computed to form a library of candidate model terms. The equation residuals are used to inform the spline learning in a Bayesian manner, where approximate Bayesian uncertainty calibration techniques are employed to approximate posterior distributions of the trainable parameters. To promote the sparsity, an iterative sequential-threshold Bayesian learning approach is developed, using the alternative direction optimization strategy to systematically approximate L0 sparsity constraints. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on multiple nonlinear dynamical systems governed by canonical ordinary and partial differential equations, and the merit/superiority of the proposed method is demonstrated by comparison with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Discovering governing equations from measurements can make a dynamical system easier to understand and predict. Sparse observations and substantial noise make that task difficult, especially when the goal includes quantifying uncertainty. This paper develops a Bayesian spline framework that seeks compact equations for dynamics evolving over time or across both space and time.

Splines provide a representation of the measurements from which derivatives can be computed and used to build candidate equation terms. Learning also uses equation residuals, so the proposed dynamics help inform the spline representation. Approximate Bayesian techniques estimate posterior distributions over trainable parameters, attaching uncertainty to the learned system rather than returning only a single fitted description.

To favor concise equations, the method iteratively thresholds terms within a Bayesian learning procedure and uses alternating optimization to approximate a constraint on the number of retained terms. Evaluations cover nonlinear systems governed by ordinary and partial differential equations. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate the approach's reported advantages in these settings, supporting the combination of data fitting, equation discovery, and uncertainty estimation.
summary.tldr: Bayesian spline learning discovers compact nonlinear governing equations from sparse, noisy measurements while estimating uncertainty in the learned system.

title: Bayesian Spline Learning for Equation Discovery of Nonlinear Dynamics with Quantified Uncertainty

abstract: Recent self-supervised advances in medical computer vision exploit the global and local anatomical self-similarity for pretraining prior to downstream tasks such as segmentation. However, current methods assume i.i.d. image acquisition, which is invalid in clinical study designs where follow-up longitudinal scans track subject-specific temporal changes. Further, existing self-supervised methods for medically-relevant image-to-image architectures exploit only spatial or temporal self-similarity and do so via a loss applied only at a single image-scale, with naive multi-scale spatiotemporal extensions collapsing to degenerate solutions. To these ends, this paper makes two contributions: (1) It presents a local and multi-scale spatiotemporal representation learning method for image-to-image architectures trained on longitudinal images. It exploits the spatiotemporal self-similarity of learned multi-scale intra-subject image features for pretraining and develops several feature-wise regularizations that avoid degenerate representations; (2) During finetuning, it proposes a surprisingly simple self-supervised segmentation consistency regularization to exploit intra-subject correlation. Benchmarked across various segmentation tasks, the proposed framework outperforms both well-tuned randomly-initialized baselines and current self-supervised techniques designed for both i.i.d. and longitudinal datasets. These improvements are demonstrated across both longitudinal neurodegenerative adult MRI and developing infant brain MRI and yield both higher performance and longitudinal consistency.

paragraphs: Repeated brain scans of the same person contain relationships across both space and time. Treating scans as independent observations overlooks this structure. The paper develops self-supervised learning for longitudinal image analysis, where useful representations should capture anatomy while accounting for subject-specific changes across follow-up scans.

The pretraining method uses local features at multiple image scales and exploits their spatiotemporal self-similarity within a subject. Feature-level regularizations prevent degenerate representations, a problem the authors identify in naive multiscale extensions. During finetuning, a separate self-supervised segmentation-consistency regularizer uses correlations between scans from the same person.

The framework is evaluated on several segmentation tasks involving adult MRI in neurodegenerative settings and developing infant brain MRI. It outperforms well-tuned models trained from random initialization and existing self-supervised approaches designed for independent or longitudinal data. The reported gains include both segmentation performance and longitudinal consistency. Together, the two training stages make repeated observations useful for learning features and for producing more consistent segmentations over time.
summary.tldr: Multiscale spatiotemporal pretraining and segmentation-consistency regularization improve longitudinal brain MRI segmentation.

title: Local Spatiotemporal Representation Learning for Longitudinally-consistent Neuroimage Analysis

abstract: Modern statistical estimation is often performed in a distributed setting where each sample belongs to single user who shares their data with a central server. Users are typically concerned with preserving the privacy of their sample, and also with minimizing the amount of data they must transmit to the server. We give improved private and communication-efficient algorithms for estimating several popular measures of the entropy of a distribution. All of our algorithms have constant communication cost and satisfy local differential privacy. For a joint distribution on many variables whose conditional independence graph is a tree, we describe algorithms for estimating Shannon entropy that require a number of samples that is linear in the number of variables, compared to the quadratic sample complexity of prior work. We also describe an algorithm for estimating Gini entropy whose sample complexity has no dependence on the support size of the distribution and can be implemented using a single round of concurrent communication between the users and the server, while the previously best-known algorithm has high communication cost and requires the server to facilitate interaction between the users. Finally, we describe an algorithm for estimating collision entropy that matches the space and sample complexity of the best known algorithm but generalizes it to the private and communication-efficient setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies entropy estimation when individual users each hold a sample and communicate with a central server. The algorithms must protect each user’s information while limiting transmitted data. The authors develop estimators for several entropy measures that all satisfy local differential privacy and have constant communication cost.

For Shannon entropy, the result concerns joint distributions whose conditional independence graph is a tree. Under that structural assumption, the required sample count grows linearly with the number of variables, improving on earlier quadratic dependence. For Gini entropy, the proposed estimator’s sample complexity does not depend on how many possible outcomes the distribution has.

The Gini estimator also needs only one concurrent communication round, whereas the previously best-known approach required costly communication and server-facilitated interaction between users. For collision entropy, the authors preserve the best-known space and sample complexity while adding privacy and communication efficiency. These are complementary results: one exploits tree structure, another removes support-size dependence, and another extends an existing efficiency guarantee to private distributed estimation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops locally private entropy estimators with constant communication cost and improved or preserved sample-complexity guarantees.

title: Private and Communication-Efficient Algorithms for Entropy Estimation

abstract: Conventional saliency maps highlight input features to which neural network predictions are highly sensitive. We take a different approach to saliency, in which we identify and analyze the network parameters, rather than inputs, which are responsible for erroneous decisions. We first verify that identified salient parameters are indeed responsible for misclassification by showing that turning these parameters off improves predictions on the associated samples more than turning off the same number of random or least salient parameters. We further validate the link between salient parameters and network misclassification errors by observing that fine-tuning a small number of the most salient parameters on a single sample results in error correction on other samples which were misclassified for similar reasons -- nearest neighbors in the saliency space. After validating our parameter-space saliency maps, we demonstrate that samples which cause similar parameters to malfunction are semantically similar. Further, we introduce an input-space saliency counterpart which reveals how image features cause specific network components to malfunction.

paragraphs: Conventional saliency maps highlight input features that strongly affect a model's prediction. This paper instead investigates which network parameters are associated with incorrect decisions. Its parameter-space saliency maps aim to locate internal components involved in errors, providing a different perspective on why a model misclassifies particular samples.

The authors validate the identified parameters through interventions. Disabling salient parameters improves predictions on the associated samples more than disabling an equal number of randomly chosen or least-salient parameters. They also find that fine-tuning a small set of highly salient parameters on one sample can correct errors on other samples nearby in saliency space.

Those neighboring samples were misclassified for similar reasons, linking shared parameter involvement to related failures. The authors further demonstrate that samples associated with similar malfunctioning parameters are semantically similar. An additional input-space saliency method reveals which image features cause particular network components to malfunction. Together, these analyses connect observable image content, internal parameters, and patterns of prediction error.
summary.tldr: Parameter-space saliency identifies network components involved in errors and links them to semantically related failures across samples.

title: Where do Models go Wrong? Parameter-Space Saliency Maps for Explainability

abstract: Nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) aims to recover the underlying independent latent sources from their observable nonlinear mixtures. How to make the nonlinear ICA model identifiable up to certain trivial indeterminacies is a long-standing problem in unsupervised learning. Recent breakthroughs reformulate the standard independence assumption of sources as conditional independence given some auxiliary variables (e.g., class labels and/or domain/time indexes) as weak supervision or inductive bias. However, nonlinear ICA with unconditional priors cannot benefit from such developments. We explore an alternative path and consider only assumptions on the mixing process, such as Structural Sparsity. We show that under specific instantiations of such constraints, the independent latent sources can be identified from their nonlinear mixtures up to a permutation and a component-wise transformation, thus achieving nontrivial identifiability of nonlinear ICA without auxiliary variables. We provide estimation methods and validate the theoretical results experimentally. The results on image data suggest that our conditions may hold in a number of practical data generating processes.

Recent breakthroughs reformulate the standard independence assumption of sources as conditional independence given some auxiliary variables (e.g., class labels and/or domain/time indexes) as weak supervision or inductive bias. However, nonlinear ICA with unconditional priors cannot benefit from such developments. We explore an alternative path and consider only assumptions on the mixing process, such as Structural Sparsity. We show that under specific instantiations of such constraints, the independent latent sources can be identified from their nonlinear mixtures up to a permutation and a component-wise transformation, thus achieving nontrivial identifiability of nonlinear ICA without auxiliary variables. We provide estimation methods and validate the theoretical results experimentally. The results on image data suggest that our conditions may hold in a number of practical data generating processes.

paragraphs: Nonlinear independent component analysis tries to recover independent hidden sources from observations that mix them nonlinearly. A central difficulty is identifiability: whether the observations determine those sources, apart from accepted ambiguities. Recent approaches use auxiliary information such as labels or time indices, but that route does not address models with unconditional source priors.

This paper instead imposes assumptions on the mixing process, including structural sparsity. Under specific forms of these constraints, the authors prove that the latent sources can be identified up to reordering and a separate transformation of each source. The result provides nontrivial identifiability without requiring auxiliary variables, while explicitly retaining those remaining ambiguities.

The authors also provide estimation methods and test their theoretical findings experimentally. Results on image data suggest that the proposed conditions may occur in practical data-generating processes. The contribution is an alternative set of sufficient structural conditions for source recovery, with experimental evidence supporting their possible relevance beyond purely theoretical constructions.
summary.tldr: Specific structural constraints on nonlinear mixing make independent sources identifiable without auxiliary variables, up to stated ambiguities.

title: On the Identifiability of Nonlinear ICA: Sparsity and Beyond

abstract: Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) is a widely-used machine learning algorithm that has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art results on many standard data science problems. We are interested in its application to multioutput problems when the output is highly multidimensional. Although there are highly effective GBDT implementations, their scalability to such problems is still unsatisfactory. In this paper, we propose novel methods aiming to accelerate the training process of GBDT in the multioutput scenario. The idea behind these methods lies in the approximate computation of a scoring function used to find the best split of decision trees. These methods are implemented in SketchBoost, which itself is integrated into our easily customizable Python-based GPU implementation of GBDT called Py-Boost. Our numerical study demonstrates that SketchBoost speeds up the training process of GBDT by up to over 40 times while achieving comparable or even better performance.

paragraphs: Gradient-boosted decision trees are effective on many data-science tasks, but training can scale poorly when each example has a highly multidimensional output. This paper focuses on that multioutput setting. It targets the computation used to choose tree splits, an operation that must compare possible ways of dividing the training data.

The method therefore reduces work within tree construction while continuing to learn a boosted tree model. The numerical study reports training speedups reaching more than 40 times, with comparable or sometimes better predictive performance. That figure describes the upper end of the reported gains, rather than an expected acceleration on every task. The findings show that approximate split scoring can offer substantial computational savings in the studied multioutput problems without necessarily sacrificing the quality of the resulting predictions.
summary.tldr: SketchBoost approximates tree-split scores to accelerate multioutput gradient boosting, with reported speedups exceeding 40 times in some cases.

title: SketchBoost: Fast Gradient Boosted Decision Tree for Multioutput Problems

abstract: Consider making a prediction over new test data without any opportunity to learn from a training set of labelled data - instead given access to a set of expert models and their predictions alongside some limited information about the dataset used to train them. In scenarios from finance to the medical sciences, and even consumer practice, stakeholders have developed models on private data they either cannot, or do not want to, share. Given the value and legislation surrounding personal information, it is not surprising that only the models, and not the data, will be released - the pertinent question becoming: how best to use these models? Previous work has focused on global model selection or ensembling, with the result of a single final model across the feature space. Machine learning models perform notoriously poorly on data outside their training domain however, and so we argue that when ensembling models the weightings for individual instances must reflect their respective domains - in other words models that are more likely to have seen information on that instance should have more attention paid to them. We introduce a method for such an instance-wise ensembling of models, including a novel representation learning step for handling sparse high-dimensional domains. Finally, we demonstrate the need and generalisability of our method on classical machine learning tasks as well as highlighting a real world use case in the pharmacological setting of vancomycin precision dosing.

paragraphs: Sometimes predictions must be made without a labeled training set, using only existing expert models and limited information about their original training data. Those data may remain private even when the models are shared. This paper asks how to combine such models when their experience covers different parts of the input space.

The proposed method assigns ensemble weights separately for each test instance. Its guiding idea is to give more influence to models whose training domains are more relevant to that particular instance. This differs from selecting one model or one global combination for every input. The method also includes a representation-learning step designed for sparse, high-dimensional domains.

The authors demonstrate the approach on classical machine learning tasks and a real-world application involving vancomycin precision dosing. These evaluations support the usefulness and generalizability of instance-wise combination. The contribution is a way to use a collection of privately trained experts while recognizing that the most relevant expert can change from one prediction to the next.
summary.tldr: Synthetic Model Combination weights expert models separately for each input using their domain relevance, without requiring a labeled training set.

title: Synthetic Model Combination: An Instance-wise Approach to Unsupervised Ensemble Learning

abstract: Recently, adversarial imitation learning has shown a scalable reward acquisition method for inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) problems. However, estimated reward signals often become uncertain and fail to train a reliable statistical model since the existing methods tend to solve hard optimization problems directly. Inspired by a first-order optimization method called mirror descent, this paper proposes to predict a sequence of reward functions, which are iterative solutions for a constrained convex problem. IRL solutions derived by mirror descent are tolerant to the uncertainty incurred by target density estimation since the amount of reward learning is regulated with respect to local geometric constraints. We prove that the proposed mirror descent update rule ensures robust minimization of a Bregman divergence in terms of a rigorous regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ for step sizes $\{\eta_t\}_{t=1}^{T}$. Our IRL method was applied on top of an adversarial framework, and it outperformed existing adversarial methods in an extensive suite of benchmarks.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to recover reward signals that explain demonstrated behavior. Adversarial imitation methods provide a scalable approach, but the paper argues that directly tackling difficult optimization problems can produce uncertain rewards and unreliable learning. Its proposed remedy is to learn a sequence of reward functions through updates inspired by mirror descent.

Each reward update is an iterative solution to a constrained convex problem. Local geometric constraints regulate how much reward learning occurs, making the resulting inverse-reinforcement-learning solutions tolerant of uncertainty in target-density estimation. The method therefore ties robustness to the way updates are controlled, rather than treating reward estimation as a single direct optimization task.

The authors prove that their mirror-descent update robustly minimizes a Bregman divergence, a measure of discrepancy used in the analysis, with an O(1/T) regret bound for the considered step-size sequence. They then place the method within an adversarial learning framework and report improvements over existing adversarial methods across an extensive benchmark suite. The contribution connects a controlled reward-learning procedure with both a formal robustness result and empirical imitation performance.
summary.tldr: Mirror-descent reward updates improve robustness to estimation uncertainty in inverse reinforcement learning, with a regret guarantee and stronger benchmark performance.

title: Robust Imitation via Mirror Descent Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Ensembling neural networks is an effective way to increase accuracy, and can often match the performance of individual larger models. This observation poses a natural question: given the choice between a deep ensemble and a single neural network with similar accuracy, is one preferable over the other? Recent work suggests that deep ensembles may offer distinct benefits beyond predictive power: namely, uncertainty quantification and robustness to dataset shift. In this work, we demonstrate limitations to these purported benefits, and show that a single (but larger) neural network can replicate these qualities. First, we show that ensemble diversity, by any metric, does not meaningfully contribute to an ensemble's ability to detect out-of-distribution (OOD) data, but is instead highly correlated with the relative improvement of a single larger model. Second, we show that the OOD performance afforded by ensembles is strongly determined by their in-distribution (InD) performance, and - in this sense - is not indicative of any "effective robustness." While deep ensembles are a practical way to achieve improvements to predictive power, uncertainty quantification, and robustness, our results show that these improvements can be replicated by a (larger) single model.

paragraphs: Combining several neural networks often improves accuracy. This paper asks whether an ensemble provides additional advantages over a larger single network with similar predictive performance. It focuses on uncertainty estimation and behavior under dataset shift, two properties often presented as distinctive reasons to use ensembles.

The authors find limitations to those claims. In their analysis, diversity among ensemble members does not meaningfully explain the ability to detect out-of-distribution inputs. Instead, diversity is strongly correlated with the relative improvement obtainable from a larger single model. This challenges the interpretation that variation between members is itself responsible for the detection advantage.

They also find that an ensemble's out-of-distribution performance is strongly determined by its in-distribution performance. In that sense, the improvement does not demonstrate additional effective robustness beyond the relationship with ordinary predictive performance. The findings leave ensembles as a practical way to improve accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and robustness, while showing that a larger single network can reproduce these benefits in the studied comparisons.
summary.tldr: The study finds that larger single networks can reproduce ensemble benefits in uncertainty estimation and robustness, challenging their presumed uniqueness.

title: Deep Ensembles Work, But Are They Necessary?

abstract: While distributional reinforcement learning (DistRL) has been empirically effective, the question of when and why it is better than vanilla, non-distributional RL has remained unanswered.This paper explains the benefits of DistRL through the lens of small-loss bounds, which are instance-dependent bounds that scale with optimal achievable cost.Particularly, our bounds converge much faster than those from non-distributional approaches if the optimal cost is small.As warmup, we propose a distributional contextual bandit (DistCB) algorithm, which we show enjoys small-loss regret bounds and empirically outperforms the state-of-the-art on three real-world tasks.In online RL, we propose a DistRL algorithm that constructs confidence sets using maximum likelihood estimation. We prove that our algorithm enjoys novel small-loss PAC bounds in low-rank MDPs.As part of our analysis, we introduce the $\ell_1$ distributional eluder dimension which may be of independent interest. Then, in offline RL, we show that pessimistic DistRL enjoys small-loss PAC bounds that are novel to the offline setting and are more robust to bad single-policy coverage.
