Then, in offline RL, we show that pessimistic DistRL enjoys small-loss PAC bounds that are novel to the offline setting and are more robust to bad single-policy coverage.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning has shown empirical success, but understanding when it offers an advantage requires more specific guarantees. This paper provides small-loss bounds: guarantees that depend on the optimal achievable cost of the problem. When that cost is small, the derived bounds converge much faster than those from non-distributional approaches.

The analysis begins with a distributional contextual-bandit algorithm, DistCB. It receives small-loss regret guarantees and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approach on three real-world tasks. For online reinforcement learning, the authors build confidence sets through maximum likelihood estimation and prove small-loss learning guarantees in low-rank Markov decision processes. They also introduce a distributional complexity measure to support the analysis.

For offline reinforcement learning, a pessimistic distributional method obtains small-loss guarantees that are more robust to poor single-policy coverage. The contribution therefore spans bandits and both online and offline learning, with different constructions for each setting. Its central explanation is conditional: distributional methods can obtain especially favorable guarantees when the best achievable cost is already low.
summary.tldr: Small-loss bounds explain a distributional reinforcement-learning advantage when the optimal achievable cost is low.

title: The Benefits of Being Distributional: Small-Loss Bounds for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) refers to learning general-purpose skills that aim to reach diverse goals. In particular, offline GCRL only requires purely pre-collected datasets to perform training tasks without additional interactions with the environment. Although offline GCRL has become increasingly prevalent and many previous works have demonstrated its empirical success, the theoretical understanding of efficient offline GCRL algorithms is not well established, especially when the state space is huge and the offline dataset only covers the policy we aim to learn. In this paper, we provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of an existing empirically successful offline GCRL algorithm. We prove that under slight modification, this algorithm enjoys an $\tilde{O}(\text{poly}(1/\epsilon))$ sample complexity (where $\epsilon$ is the desired suboptimality of the learned policy) with general function approximation thanks to the property of (semi-)strong convexity of the objective functions. We only require nearly minimal assumptions on the dataset (single-policy concentrability) and the function class (realizability). Moreover, this algorithm consists of two uninterleaved optimization steps, which we refer to as $V$-learning and policy learning, and is computationally stable since it does not involve minimax optimization. We also empirically validate our theory by showing that the modified algorithm outperforms the previous algorithm in various real-world environments.To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that is both provably efficient with general function approximation and single-policy concentrability, and empirically successful without requiring solving minimax optimization problems.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains an agent to reach different goals using only previously collected data. Its theoretical analysis becomes difficult when the state space is large and the data cover only the policy of interest. This paper gives guarantees for a slightly modified version of an existing empirically successful algorithm.

The proof establishes sample complexity polynomial in the inverse of the desired policy suboptimality, up to logarithmic factors, with general function approximation. It relies on strong or semi-strong convexity of the objectives. The assumptions include single-policy concentrability, concerning dataset coverage of the relevant policy, and realizability, concerning the expressive adequacy of the chosen function class.

The algorithm separates training into two uninterleaved stages: V-learning and policy learning. It avoids minimax optimization, which the authors identify as supporting computational stability. Experiments in several real-world environments show that the modification outperforms the earlier algorithm. The contribution therefore combines a conditional efficiency guarantee under limited coverage assumptions with empirical evidence that the theoretically motivated change improves performance.
summary.tldr: A modified offline goal-learning algorithm gains polynomial sample-complexity guarantees under single-policy coverage and realizability assumptions, alongside empirical improvements.

title: Provably Efficient Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning with General Function Approximation and Single-Policy Concentrability

abstract: The evaluation of generative models has received significant attention in the machine learning community. When applied to a multi-modal distribution which is common among image datasets, an intuitive evaluation criterion is the number of modes captured by the generative model. While several scores have been proposed to evaluate the quality and diversity of a model's generated data, the correspondence between existing scores and the number of modes in the distribution is unclear. In this work, we propose an information-theoretic diversity evaluation method for multi-modal underlying distributions. We utilize the R\'enyi Kernel Entropy (RKE) as an evaluation score based on quantum information theory to measure the number of modes in generated samples. To interpret the proposed evaluation method, we show that the RKE score can output the number of modes of a mixture of sub-Gaussian components. We also prove estimation error bounds for estimating the RKE score from limited data, suggesting a fast convergence of the empirical RKE score to the score for the underlying data distribution. Utilizing the RKE score, we conduct an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art generative models over standard image datasets. The numerical results indicate that while the recent algorithms for training generative models manage to improve the mode-based diversity over the earlier architectures, they remain incapable of capturing the full diversity of real data. Our empirical results provide a ranking of widely-used generative models based on the RKE score of their generated samples.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce convincing examples while missing substantial parts of a dataset’s variety. This paper evaluates diversity through modes, the distinct components of a multimodal distribution. Its motivation is that existing quality and diversity scores do not have a clear correspondence with how many such components a model captures.

The authors propose using Rényi Kernel Entropy, or RKE, as an information-theoretic diversity score. In these evaluations, newer training approaches improve mode-based diversity relative to earlier architectures but still fall short of the diversity in real data. The resulting rankings therefore concern diversity as measured by RKE, connecting an interpretable statistical quantity to an empirical comparison of generated samples.
summary.tldr: The paper uses Rényi Kernel Entropy to evaluate mode coverage and finds that tested generative models still miss some real-data diversity.

title: An Information-Theoretic Evaluation of Generative Models in Learning Multi-modal Distributions

abstract: The tremendous success of large models trained on extensive datasets demonstrates that scale is a key ingredient in achieving superior results. Therefore, the reflection on the rationality of designing knowledge distillation (KD) approaches for limited-capacity architectures solely based on small-scale datasets is now deemed imperative. In this paper, we identify the small data pitfall that presents in previous KD methods, which results in the underestimation of the power of vanilla KD framework on large-scale datasets such as ImageNet-1K. Specifically, we show that employing stronger data augmentation techniques and using larger datasets can directly decrease the gap between vanilla KD and other meticulously designed KD variants. This highlights the necessity of designing and evaluating KD approaches in the context of practical scenarios, casting off the limitations of small-scale datasets. Our investigation of the vanilla KD and its variants in more complex schemes, including stronger training strategies and different model capacities, demonstrates that vanilla KD is elegantly simple but astonishingly effective in large-scale scenarios. Without bells and whistles, we obtain state-of-the-art ResNet-50, ViT-S, and ConvNeXtV2-T models for ImageNet, which achieve 83.1%, 84.3%, and 85.0% top-1 accuracy, respectively. PyTorch code and checkpoints can be found at https://github.com/Hao840/vanillaKD.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge into models with limited capacity, but many proposed improvements are designed and judged on small datasets. This paper argues that such evaluations can underestimate ordinary, or vanilla, distillation. Its central question is how the relative value of elaborate distillation methods changes when data and training conditions become more substantial.

The authors find that larger datasets and stronger data augmentation directly reduce the performance gap between vanilla distillation and more carefully engineered variants. They also compare approaches under stronger training strategies and different model capacities. These investigations make the training setting part of the comparison, rather than assuming conclusions from small-scale experiments carry over unchanged.

Using vanilla distillation, the paper reports ImageNet top-1 accuracies of 83.1% for ResNet-50, 84.3% for ViT-S, and 85.0% for ConvNeXtV2-T, described as state-of-the-art results. The findings establish vanilla distillation as a strong option in the studied large-scale settings and motivate evaluating proposed improvements under conditions that reflect their intended use.
summary.tldr: Larger datasets and stronger augmentation narrow the gap between vanilla knowledge distillation and specialized variants in the paper’s evaluations.

title: Revisit the Power of Vanilla Knowledge Distillation: from Small Scale to Large Scale

abstract: We consider offline reinforcement learning (RL) where we only have only access to offline data. In contrast to numerous offline RL algorithms that necessitate the uniform coverage of the offline data over state and action space, we propose value-based algorithms with PAC guarantees under partial coverage, specifically, coverage of offline data against a single policy, and realizability of soft Q-function (a.k.a., entropy-regularized Q-function) and another function, which is defined as a solution to a saddle point of certain minimax optimization problem). Furthermore, we show the analogous result for Q-functions instead of soft Q-functions. To attain these guarantees, we use novel algorithms with minimax loss functions to accurately estimate soft Q-functions and Q-functions with -convergence guarantees measured on the offline data. We introduce these loss functions by casting the estimation problems into nonlinear convex optimization problems and taking the Lagrange functions.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset without collecting new interactions. Many algorithms require that this dataset cover the state-action space uniformly. This paper develops value-based methods with learning guarantees under a narrower coverage requirement: the offline data need only provide coverage relative to a single policy.

The guarantees also require realizability of an entropy-regularized Q-function and an additional function defined through a minimax saddle-point problem. Realizability means that the selected function classes can represent the functions required by the analysis. The authors establish an analogous result for ordinary Q-functions, extending the treatment beyond the entropy-regularized setting.

To build the algorithms, the authors express value estimation as nonlinear convex optimization and derive minimax losses through Lagrange functions. These losses support convergence guarantees measured on the offline data and probabilistic approximate-correctness guarantees for learning. The contribution is a conditional theoretical route to offline learning with partial coverage. Its weaker coverage requirement remains paired with the stated representation assumptions, rather than eliminating assumptions about the data and function classes altogether.
summary.tldr: Minimax value-learning methods obtain offline reinforcement learning guarantees under single-policy coverage and stated realizability assumptions.

title: Offline Minimax Soft-Q-learning Under Realizability and Partial Coverage

abstract: In a carbon auction, licenses for CO2 emissions are allocated among multiple interested players. Inspired by this setting, we consider repeated multi-unit auctions with uniform pricing, which are widely used in practice. Our contribution is to analyze these auctions in both the offline and online settings, by designing efficient bidding algorithms with low regret and giving regret lower bounds. We also analyze the quality of the equilibria in two main variants of the auction, finding that one variant is susceptible to collusion among the bidders while the other is not.

Our contribution is to analyze these auctions in both the offline and online settings, by designing efficient bidding algorithms with low regret and giving regret lower bounds. We also analyze the quality of the equilibria in two main variants of the auction, finding that one variant is susceptible to collusion among the bidders while the other is not.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated auctions that allocate multiple units using uniform pricing, motivated by auctions for carbon-emission licenses. Such settings involve several interested bidders and repeated opportunities to choose bids. The research connects two questions: how bidders can learn effective bidding strategies, and how the auction's rules affect the outcomes that emerge.

For both offline and online settings, the authors design computationally efficient bidding algorithms with low regret. Regret measures the shortfall relative to a comparison strategy, so these guarantees characterize the cost of learning how to bid. The paper also supplies regret lower bounds, addressing limits on achievable performance rather than presenting algorithms alone.

A separate equilibrium analysis compares two main auction variants. The authors find that one is susceptible to collusion among bidders while the other is not. This distinction shows why evaluating bidder learning and evaluating auction design are complementary tasks. An effective bidding algorithm addresses a participant's decision problem; the equilibrium results address whether the surrounding rules permit coordinated behavior that changes the auction's outcome.
summary.tldr: The paper develops low-regret bidding algorithms and distinguishes two uniform-price auction variants by their susceptibility to bidder collusion.

title: Learning and Collusion in Multi-unit Auctions

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is arguably the most important single algorithm in modern machine learning. Although SGD with unbiased gradient estimators has been studied extensively over at least half a century, SGD variants relying on biased estimators are rare. Nevertheless, there has been an increased interest in this topic in recent years. However, existing literature on SGD with biased estimators lacks coherence since each new paper relies on a different set of assumptions, without any clear understanding of how they are connected, which may lead to confusion. We address this gap by establishing connections among the existing assumptions, and presenting a comprehensive map of the underlying relationships. Additionally, we introduce a new set of assumptions that is provably weaker than all previous assumptions, and use it to present a thorough analysis of BiasedSGD in both convex and non-convex settings, offering advantages over previous results. We also provide examples where biased estimators outperform their unbiased counterparts or where unbiased versions are simply not available. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through experimental results that validate our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent updates a model using estimates of the direction in which its objective improves. Much of its theory concerns unbiased estimates, but useful estimates can also be biased. This paper addresses a fragmented literature in which different analyses impose different assumptions, making their results difficult to compare.

The authors map the relationships between existing assumptions and introduce a new set that they prove is weaker than the previous ones. Weaker assumptions expand the situations covered by an analysis. Using this framework, they study biased SGD for both convex and non-convex objectives and obtain advantages over earlier theoretical results.

The paper also gives examples where biased estimates outperform unbiased alternatives, or where an unbiased version is unavailable. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore both organizational and analytical: it makes existing guarantees easier to relate and provides a broader framework for studying biased updates. The examples establish that bias can be useful, rather than that it is always beneficial.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies assumptions for biased SGD and develops a broader theoretical framework covering convex and non-convex optimization.

title: A Guide Through the Zoo of Biased SGD

abstract: In this paper, we present Motion-X, a large-scale 3D expressive whole-body motion dataset. Existing motion datasets predominantly contain body-only poses, lacking facial expressions, hand gestures, and fine-grained pose descriptions. Moreover, they are primarily collected from limited laboratory scenes with textual descriptions manually labeled, which greatly limits their scalability. To overcome these limitations, we develop a whole-body motion and text annotation pipeline, which can automatically annotate motion from either single- or multi-view videos and provide comprehensive semantic labels for each video and fine-grained whole-body pose descriptions for each frame. This pipeline is of high precision, cost-effective, and scalable for further research. Based on it, we construct Motion-X, which comprises 15.6M precise 3D whole-body pose annotations (i.e., SMPL-X) covering 81.1K motion sequences from massive scenes. Besides, Motion-X provides 15.6M frame-level whole-body pose descriptions and 81.1K sequence-level semantic labels. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the accuracy of the annotation pipeline and the significant benefit of Motion-X in enhancing expressive, diverse, and natural motion generation, as well as 3D whole-body human mesh recovery.

paragraphs: Motion-X expands human motion data beyond body-only poses to include facial expressions, hand gestures, and detailed pose descriptions. The paper identifies restricted laboratory scenes and manually written text annotations as obstacles to scaling existing datasets. Its contribution combines a whole-body motion dataset with an automated annotation pipeline.

The pipeline accepts single-view or multiview videos. It produces whole-body motion annotations, semantic labels for each sequence, and fine-grained pose descriptions for individual frames. Motion-X contains 15.6 million SMPL-X whole-body pose annotations across 81.1 thousand motion sequences, alongside matching frame-level descriptions and sequence-level semantic labels.

They also find improvements in three-dimensional whole-body human mesh recovery. The dataset's value therefore spans both generating motion and recovering detailed human shape and pose from visual information.
summary.tldr: Motion-X pairs large-scale whole-body motion annotations with detailed language labels to support motion generation and human mesh recovery.

title: Motion-X: A Large-scale 3D Expressive Whole-body Human Motion Dataset

abstract: Recent advances in graph neural networks (GNNs) have enabled more comprehensive modeling of molecules and molecular systems, thereby enhancing the precision of molecular property prediction and molecular simulations. Nonetheless, as the field has been progressing to bigger and more complex architectures, state-of-the-art GNNs have become largely prohibitive for many large-scale applications. In this paper, we explore the utility of knowledge distillation (KD) for accelerating molecular GNNs. To this end, we devise KD strategies that facilitate the distillation of hidden representations in directional and equivariant GNNs, and evaluate their performance on the regression task of energy and force prediction. We validate our protocols across different teacher-student configurations and datasets, and demonstrate that they can consistently boost the predictive accuracy of student models without any modifications to their architecture. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive optimization of various components of our framework, and investigate the potential of data augmentation to further enhance performance. All in all, we manage to close the gap in predictive accuracy between teacher and student models by as much as 96.7\% and 62.5\% for energy and force prediction respectively, while fully preserving the inference throughput of the more lightweight models.

paragraphs: Molecular graph neural networks have become more accurate as their architectures have grown more complex, but that complexity makes large-scale applications expensive. This paper investigates whether knowledge distillation can transfer useful information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. The goal is to improve the students’ predictions while retaining the inference speed of their existing architectures.

The authors develop strategies for transferring hidden representations in directional and equivariant graph neural networks. They evaluate these strategies on energy and force prediction, testing different teacher–student combinations and datasets. They also optimize components of the distillation framework and investigate whether data augmentation can further improve performance. The approach changes how students learn without modifying their architectures.

Across the evaluated configurations, distillation consistently improves student accuracy. The reported improvements close as much as 96.7% of the teacher–student accuracy gap for energy prediction and 62.5% for force prediction, while preserving student inference throughput. These percentages describe reductions in an accuracy gap, not absolute accuracy scores. The results show that lightweight molecular models can gain substantially from richer models during training.
summary.tldr: Distilling hidden representations improves lightweight molecular models’ energy and force predictions while preserving their inference throughput.

title: Accelerating Molecular Graph Neural Networks via Knowledge Distillation

abstract: The success of contrastive learning is well known to be dependent on data augmentation.Although the degree of data augmentations has been well controlled by utilizing pre-defined techniques in some domains like vision, time-series data augmentation is less explored and remains a challenging problem due to the complexity of the data generation mechanism, such as the intricate mechanism involved in the cardiovascular system.Moreover, there is no widely recognized and general time-series augmentation method that can be applied across different tasks.In this paper, we propose a novel data augmentation method for time-series tasks that aims to connect intra-class samples together, and thereby find order in the latent space.Our method builds upon the well-known data augmentation technique of mixup by incorporating a novel approach that accounts for the non-stationary nature of time-series data.Also, by controlling the degree of chaos created by data augmentation, our method leads to improved feature representations and performance on downstream tasks.We evaluate our proposed method on three time-series tasks, including heart rate estimation, human activity recognition, and cardiovascular disease detection. Extensive experiments against the state-of-the-art methods show that the proposed method outperforms prior works on optimal data generation and known data augmentation techniques in three tasks, reflecting the effectiveness of the presented method. The source code is available at double-blind policy.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning depends heavily on how training data are augmented. For time series, suitable transformations are difficult to design because the processes generating the observations can be complex and can change over time. This paper proposes an augmentation method intended to connect examples from the same class and organize their learned representations.

The method builds on mixup while accounting for the non-stationary nature of time-series data. It also controls the degree of disruption introduced by augmentation, described by the authors as controlling chaos. The aim is to make the augmented data useful for learning better features while bringing related examples together in the latent space where the model represents them.

The authors evaluate the approach on heart-rate estimation, human-activity recognition, and cardiovascular-disease detection. Across these three tasks, they report improvements over prior work on optimal data generation and established augmentation techniques. These findings support the proposed augmentation strategy across the evaluated applications and connect its treatment of time-series variation to better downstream performance.
summary.tldr: A mixup-based augmentation method accounts for changing time-series behavior and improves representation learning across three evaluated tasks.

title: Finding Order in Chaos: A Novel Data Augmentation Method for Time Series in Contrastive Learning

abstract: We study structure-preserving low-dimensional representation of a data manifold embedded in a high-dimensional observation space based on variational auto-encoders (VAEs). We approach this by decomposing the data manifold $\mathcal{M}$ as $\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{M} / G \times G$, where $G$ and $\mathcal{M} / G$ are a group of symmetry transformations and a quotient space of $\mathcal{M}$ up to $G$, respectively. From this perspective, we define the structure-preserving representation of such a manifold as a latent space $\mathcal{Z}$ which is isometrically isomorphic (i.e., distance-preserving) to the quotient space $\mathcal{M} / G$ rather $\mathcal{M}$ (i.e., symmetry-preserving). To this end, we propose a novel auto-encoding framework, named isometric quotient VAEs (IQVAEs), that can extract the quotient space from observations and learn the Riemannian isometry of the extracted quotient in an unsupervised manner. Empirical proof-of-concept experiments reveal that the proposed method can find a meaningful representation of the learned data and outperform other competitors for downstream tasks.

paragraphs: The paper asks what a low-dimensional representation should preserve when observations contain symmetry transformations. Its starting point decomposes a data manifold into a symmetry group and a quotient space that identifies observations up to those transformations. This provides a mathematical way to separate the underlying structure from the variations introduced by symmetry.

The desired latent representation preserves distances in that quotient space. Accordingly, the goal is to capture the geometry remaining after symmetry-related observations are treated together. The proposed isometric quotient variational auto-encoder, or IQVAE, learns to extract the quotient from observations and represent its Riemannian geometry through a distance-preserving mapping. The framework learns this structure without supervision.

Proof-of-concept experiments show that IQVAEs can discover meaningful representations and outperform competing methods on downstream tasks. These results provide empirical support for the proposed definition of structure preservation. The broader contribution is a representation-learning objective that specifies which geometry should be retained: the geometry of the quotient, with symmetry transformations factored into the formulation.
summary.tldr: IQVAEs learn unsupervised representations that preserve distances in a data manifold's quotient space after accounting for symmetries.

title: Isometric Quotient Variational Auto-Encoders for Structure-Preserving Representation Learning

abstract: Many approaches to draping individual garments on human body models are realistic, fast, and yield outputs that are differentiable with respect to the body shape on which they are draped. However, they are either unable to handle multi-layered clothing, which is prevalent in everyday dress, or restricted to bodies in T-pose. In this paper, we introduce a parametric garment representation model that addresses these limitations. As in models used by clothing designers, each garment consists of individual 2D panels. Their 2D shape is defined by a Signed Distance Function and 3D shape by a 2D to 3D mapping. The 2D parameterization enables easy detection of potential collisions and the 3D parameterization handles complex shapes effectively. We show that this combination is faster and yields higher quality reconstructions than purely implicit surface representations, and makes the recovery of layered garments from images possible thanks to its differentiability. Furthermore, it supports rapid editing of garment shapes and texture by modifying individual 2D panels.

paragraphs: Realistic digital clothing needs to handle several garments layered on a body, including bodies outside a fixed T-pose. Existing draping approaches described in the paper fall short on one or both requirements. ISP introduces a parametric garment representation that uses individual two-dimensional panels, following the structure of sewing patterns.

Each panel's flat shape is represented by a signed distance function, while a mapping from two to three dimensions describes its spatial shape. These complementary representations serve different purposes. The two-dimensional structure makes potential collisions easier to detect, and the three-dimensional mapping supports complex garment shapes.

The authors show that this combination is faster and produces higher-quality reconstructions than purely implicit surface representations. Its differentiability also makes recovering layered garments from images possible. Because the model retains editable panels, users can rapidly change garment shape and texture through those panels. The result connects reconstruction, layered draping, and editing within a representation that preserves an explicit relationship between flat garment pieces and their three-dimensional form.
summary.tldr: ISP combines implicit two-dimensional sewing panels with three-dimensional mappings to support layered garment reconstruction, draping, and editing.

title: ISP: Multi-Layered Garment Draping with Implicit Sewing Patterns

abstract: This paper presents the official release of the Digital Typhoon dataset, the longest typhoon satellite image dataset for 40+ years aimed at benchmarking machine learning models for long-term spatio-temporal data. To build the dataset, we developed a workflow to create an infrared typhoon-centered image for cropping using Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection referring to the best track data. We also address data quality issues such as inter-satellite calibration to create a homogeneous dataset. To take advantage of the dataset, we organized machine learning tasks by the types and targets of inference, with other tasks for meteorological analysis, societal impact, and climate change. The benchmarking results on the analysis, forecasting, and reanalysis for the intensity suggest that the dataset is challenging for recent deep learning models, due to many choices that affect the performance of various models. This dataset reduces the barrier for machine learning researchers to meet large-scale real-world events called tropical cyclones and develop machine learning models that may contribute to advancing scientific knowledge on tropical cyclones as well as solving societal and sustainability issues such as disaster reduction and climate change. The dataset is publicly available at http://agora.ex.nii.ac.jp/digital-typhoon/dataset/ and https://github.com/kitamoto-lab/digital-typhoon/.

paragraphs: Digital Typhoon provides more than forty years of satellite imagery for studying tropical cyclones with machine learning. The paper presents its official release as a benchmark for data that vary across both space and time. Its long record supports research that must consider storms across many observations and across changing satellite measurement conditions.

The dataset construction workflow produces infrared images centered on each typhoon. It uses best-track information and a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection to prepare the image crops. The authors also address quality issues, including calibration between satellites, to make the collection homogeneous. These processing choices matter because comparability across the record is central to using a long-term dataset.

The paper organizes potential tasks by inference type and target, including meteorological analysis and questions about societal impacts and climate change. Benchmarks on intensity analysis, forecasting, and reanalysis suggest that recent deep learning models still find the dataset challenging, with performance affected by many choices. Public release lowers the access barrier for researchers, with possible contributions to cyclone science and disaster reduction.
summary.tldr: Digital Typhoon releases a calibrated, typhoon-centered satellite image record spanning over forty years for challenging spatial and temporal machine learning tasks.

title: Digital Typhoon: Long-term Satellite Image Dataset for the Spatio-Temporal Modeling of Tropical Cyclones

abstract: With ever increasing parameters and computation, vision-language pre-trained (VLP) models exhibit prohibitive expenditure in downstream task adaption. Recent endeavors mainly focus on parameter efficient transfer learning (PETL) for VLP models by only updating a small number of parameters. However, excessive computational overhead still plagues the application of VLPs. In this paper, we aim at parameter and computation efficient transfer learning (PCETL) for VLP models. In particular, PCETL not only needs to limit the number of trainable parameters in VLP models, but also to reduce the computational redundancy during inference, thus enabling a more efficient transfer. To approach this target, we propose a novel dynamic architecture skipping (DAS) approach towards effective PCETL. Instead of directly optimizing the intrinsic architectures of VLP models, DAS first observes the significances of their modules to downstream tasks via a reinforcement learning (RL) based process, and then skips the redundant ones with lightweight networks, i.e. adapters, according to the obtained rewards. In this case, the VLP model can well maintain the scale of trainable parameters while speeding up its inference on downstream tasks. To validate DAS, we apply it to two representative VLP models, namely ViLT and METER, and conduct extensive experiments on a bunch of VL tasks. The experimental results not only show the great advantages of DAS in reducing computational complexity, e.g. -11.97% FLOPs of METER on VQA2.0, but also confirm its competitiveness against existing PETL methods in terms of parameter scale and performance. Our source code is given in our appendix.

paragraphs: Adapting a large vision-language model can involve training only a small number of parameters while still leaving inference expensive. This paper targets both costs together. Its objective is transfer learning that limits trainable parameters and also removes computation that is redundant for a downstream task, so adaptation efficiency carries through to using the resulting model.

The proposed dynamic architecture skipping method first uses reinforcement learning to assess how important different model modules are for the target task. It then uses the resulting rewards to skip redundant modules with lightweight adapter networks. This connects decisions about which computation to retain with the task being learned, while keeping the trainable parameter scale controlled.

The authors apply the method to ViLT and METER and evaluate it on several vision-language tasks. They report competitive performance and parameter counts relative to existing parameter-efficient methods, alongside reduced computational complexity. One stated result is an 11.97% reduction in METER's FLOPs on VQA2.0. The evidence supports treating inference computation as a separate adaptation objective alongside the number of parameters updated.
summary.tldr: Dynamic architecture skipping adapts vision-language models with few trainable parameters while reducing task-specific inference computation.

title: Parameter and Computation Efficient Transfer Learning for Vision-Language Pre-trained Models

abstract: Search is an important technique in program synthesis that allows for adaptive strategies such as focusing on particular search directions based on execution results. Several prior works have demonstrated that neural models are effective at guiding program synthesis searches. However, a common drawback of those approaches is the inability to handle iterative loops, higher-order functions, or lambda functions, thus limiting prior neural searches from synthesizing longer and more general programs. We address this gap by designing a search algorithm called LambdaBeam that can construct arbitrary lambda functions that compose operations within a given DSL. We create semantic vector representations of the execution behavior of the lambda functions and train a neural policy network to choose which lambdas to construct during search, and pass them as arguments to higher-order functions to perform looping computations. Our experiments show that LambdaBeam outperforms neural, symbolic, and LLM-based techniques in an integer list manipulation domain.

paragraphs: Program synthesis searches for programs that perform a desired computation. Neural models can guide that search using information from candidate executions, but several earlier approaches cannot handle loops, higher-order functions, or lambda functions. Those restrictions limit the kinds of longer and more general programs they can construct.

LambdaBeam introduces a search algorithm that builds arbitrary lambda functions by composing operations available in a given domain-specific language. It represents the execution behavior of these functions as semantic vectors. A neural policy then uses these representations to choose which lambdas to construct during the search, connecting the search decisions to what candidate functions actually do.

The constructed lambdas can be passed to higher-order functions to carry out looping computations. This extends neural program search beyond candidates that lack these functional building blocks. In an integer-list-manipulation domain, LambdaBeam outperforms the tested neural, symbolic, and language-model-based techniques. The results support its approach within that domain, while the construction capability remains defined by the operations available in the chosen language.
summary.tldr: LambdaBeam guides program search with execution-based representations of lambda functions, enabling higher-order looping computations.

title: LambdaBeam: Neural Program Search with Higher-Order Functions and Lambdas

abstract: The rapid advancement of chat-based language models has led to remarkable progress in complex task-solving. However, their success heavily relies on human input to guide the conversation, which can be challenging and time-consuming. This paper explores the potential of building scalable techniques to facilitate autonomous cooperation among communicative agents, and provides insight into their “cognitive” processes. To address the challenges of achieving autonomous cooperation, we propose a novel communicative agent framework named role-playing . Our approach involves using inception prompting to guide chat agents toward task completion while maintaining consistency with human intentions. We showcase how role-playing can be used to generate conversational data for studying the behaviors and capabilities of a society of agents, providing a valuable resource for investigating conversational language models. In particular, we conduct comprehensive studies on instruction-following cooperation in multi-agent settings. Our contributions include introducing a novel communicative agent framework, offering a scalable approach for studying the cooperative behaviors and capabilities of multi-agent systems, and open-sourcing our library to support research on communicative agents and beyond: https://github.com/camel-ai/camel.

paragraphs: Chat-based language models can tackle complex tasks, but their conversations often require substantial human guidance. CAMEL explores how multiple communicating agents might cooperate more autonomously while remaining directed toward human intentions. It also treats those interactions as material for studying the behavior of groups of language-model agents.

The proposed framework uses role-playing and inception prompting to guide agents toward task completion. The prompts establish the intended cooperation, and the resulting conversations provide data for investigating how agents follow instructions and interact. This makes the framework both a way to organize cooperation and a way to generate evidence about that cooperation.

The authors showcase conversational data generation and conduct studies of instruction-following cooperation in multi-agent settings. They also release a library to support further research. The stated contribution is a scalable framework for examining cooperative behaviors and capabilities, alongside demonstrations of its use. References to agent cognition describe the research motivation; the concrete work concerns prompted conversations, task-oriented interaction, and observable agent behavior.
summary.tldr: CAMEL uses prompted role-playing to organize agent cooperation and generate conversations for studying multi-agent language-model behavior.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for "Mind" Exploration of Large Language Model Society

abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) is a rapidly evolving area of research that seeks to optimize the sparse initialization of a neural network by adapting its topology during training. It has been shown that under specific conditions, DST is able to outperform dense models. The key components of this framework are the pruning and growing criteria, which are repeatedly applied during the training process to adjust the network’s sparse connectivity. While the growing criterion's impact on DST performance is relatively well studied, the influence of the pruning criterion remains overlooked. To address this issue, we design and perform an extensive empirical analysis of various pruning criteria to better understand their impact on the dynamics of DST solutions. Surprisingly, we find that most of the studied methods yield similar results. The differences become more significant in the low-density regime, where the best performance is predominantly given by the simplest technique: magnitude-based pruning.
originalAbstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) is a rapidly evolving area of research that seeks to optimize the sparse initialization of a neural network by adapting its topology during training. It has been shown that under specific conditions, DST is able to outperform dense models. The key components of this framework are the pruning and growing criteria, which are repeatedly applied during the training process to adjust the network’s sparse connectivity. While the growing criterion's impact on DST performance is relatively well studied, the influence of the pruning criterion remains overlooked. To address this issue, we design and perform an extensive empirical analysis of various pruning criteria to better understand their impact on the dynamics of DST solutions. Surprisingly, we find that most of the studied methods yield similar results. The differences become more significant in the low-density regime, where the best performance is predominantly given by the simplest technique: magnitude-based pruning.

paragraphs: Dynamic Sparse Training trains a neural network while repeatedly changing which connections are active. It starts with sparse connectivity and alternates between removing weights and growing connections elsewhere. Under particular conditions, this approach has been shown to outperform dense models. Its behavior therefore depends on both how new connections are selected and how existing ones are removed.

This paper focuses on the removal step, which has received less attention than connection growth. The authors conduct an extensive empirical comparison of pruning criteria to study how they affect the dynamics and outcomes of sparse training. The question is whether more elaborate rules for deciding which weights to discard produce meaningful improvements.

Most of the investigated criteria give similar results. Differences become more pronounced when very few connections remain active, and simple magnitude-based pruning predominantly delivers the best performance in that low-density regime. This finding gives practical weight to a straightforward criterion. It remains an empirical conclusion about the studied methods and settings, rather than a universal ranking of every possible pruning rule.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds that pruning criteria often perform similarly in dynamic sparse training, with magnitude pruning predominantly best at low density.

title: Fantastic Weights and How to Find Them: Where to Prune in Dynamic Sparse Training

abstract: Tone mapping aims to convert high dynamic range (HDR) images to low dynamic range (LDR) representations, a critical task in the camera imaging pipeline. In recent years, 3-Dimensional LookUp Table (3D LUT) based methods have gained attention due to their ability to strike a favorable balance between enhancement performance and computational efficiency. However, these methods often fail to deliver satisfactory results in local areas since the look-up table is a global operator for tone mapping, which works based on pixel values and fails to incorporate crucial local information. To this end, this paper aims to address this issue by exploring a novel strategy that integrates global and local operators by utilizing closed-form Laplacian pyramid decomposition and reconstruction. Specifically, we employ image-adaptive 3D LUTs to manipulate the tone in the low-frequency image by leveraging the specific characteristics of the frequency information. Furthermore, we utilize local Laplacian filters to refine the edge details in the high-frequency components in an adaptive manner. Local Laplacian filters are widely used to preserve edge details in photographs, but their conventional usage involves manual tuning and fixed implementation within camera imaging pipelines or photo editing tools. We propose to learn parameter value maps progressively for local Laplacian filters from annotated data using a lightweight network. Our model achieves simultaneous global tone manipulation and local edge detail preservation in an end-to-end manner. Extensive experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods.

summary.tldr: A learned pyramid reconstruction method combines adaptive lookup tables for global tone with local Laplacian filters for edge preservation.

title: Lookup Table meets Local Laplacian Filter: Pyramid Reconstruction Network for Tone Mapping

abstract: Language models (LMs) often exhibit undesirable text generation behaviors, including generating false, toxic, or irrelevant outputs. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)---where human preference judgments on LM outputs are transformed into a learning signal---has recently shown promise in addressing these issues. However, such holistic feedback conveys limited information on long text outputs; it does not indicate which aspects of the outputs influenced user preference; e.g., which parts contain what type(s) of errors. In this paper, we use fine-grained human feedback (e.g., which sentence is false, which sub-sentence is irrelevant) as an explicit training signal. We introduce Fine-Grained RLHF, a framework that enables training and learning from reward functions that are fine-grained in two respects: (1) density, providing a reward after every segment (e.g., a sentence) is generated; and (2) incorporating multiple reward models associated with different feedback types (e.g., factual incorrectness, irrelevance, and information incompleteness). We conduct experiments on detoxification and long-form question answering to illustrate how learning with this reward function leads to improved performance, supported by both automatic and human evaluation. Additionally, we show that LM behaviors can be customized using different combinations of fine-grained reward models. We release all data, collected human feedback, and codes at https://FineGrainedRLHF.github.io.

paragraphs: A preference judgment about an entire language-model response gives limited guidance about what went wrong within it. This becomes especially restrictive for long answers, where factual mistakes, irrelevant passages, and missing information may coexist. The paper uses more detailed human feedback to turn those separate problems into explicit training signals.

Fine-Grained RLHF makes rewards more specific in two ways. It supplies rewards after individual segments, such as sentences, and uses multiple reward models for different feedback categories. Consequently, training can receive information about both where an issue occurs and what kind of issue it is, instead of relying only on a single judgment of the complete response.

Experiments on detoxification and long-form question answering show improvements supported by automatic measures and human evaluations. The authors also demonstrate that changing the combination of reward models can customize model behavior. The findings indicate that the structure of feedback matters: richer annotations can guide improvements along distinct dimensions and make those dimensions available as controls during language-model training.
summary.tldr: Segment-level, error-specific human feedback improves language-model training and enables behavior customization through different reward combinations.

title: Fine-Grained Human Feedback Gives Better Rewards for Language Model Training

abstract: We study the convergence to local Nash equilibria of gradient methods for two-player zero-sum differentiable games.It is well-known that, in the continuous-time setting, such dynamics converge locally when $S \succ 0$ and may diverge when $S=0$, where $S\succeq 0$ is the symmetric part of the Jacobian at equilibrium that accounts for the "potential" component of the game. We show that these dynamics also converge as soon as $S$ is nonzero (*partial curvature*) and the eigenvectors of the antisymmetric part $A$ are in general position with respect to the kernel of $S$.We then study the convergence rate when $S \ll A$ and prove that it typically depends on the *average* of the eigenvalues of $S$, instead of the minimum as an analogy with minimization problems would suggest.To illustrate our results, we consider the problem of computing mixed Nash equilibria of continuous games. We show that, thanks to partial curvature, conic particle methods -- which optimize over both weights and supports of the mixed strategies -- generically converge faster than fixed-support methods.For min-max games, it is thus beneficial to add degrees of freedom "with curvature": this can be interpreted as yet another benefit of over-parameterization.

paragraphs: This paper studies local convergence of gradient dynamics in differentiable two-player zero-sum games. Near an equilibrium, the relevant Jacobian separates into a symmetric component S and an antisymmetric component A. Earlier continuous-time results establish local convergence when S is positive definite, while dynamics may diverge when S is zero.

The authors show that partial curvature can suffice: S may be merely nonzero and positive semidefinite, provided the eigenvectors of A are in general position relative to the kernel of S. They also analyze cases where S is small compared with A. There, the convergence rate typically depends on the average eigenvalue of S, rather than its smallest eigenvalue.

An application considers computing mixed Nash equilibria in continuous games. Methods that optimize both the weights and locations of strategy particles generically converge faster than methods with fixed locations, thanks to partial curvature. The result gives a conditional explanation for why adding degrees of freedom can help: those extra freedoms can introduce curvature that improves local game dynamics.
summary.tldr: Partial curvature suffices for local convergence of continuous-time game dynamics under a general-position condition.

title: Local Convergence of Gradient Methods for Min-Max Games: Partial Curvature Generically Suffices

abstract: We study the problem of $(\epsilon,\delta)$-certified machine unlearning for minimax models. Most of the existing works focus on unlearning from standard statistical learning models that have a single variable and their unlearning steps hinge on the direct Hessian-based conventional Newton update. We develop a new $(\epsilon,\delta)$-certified machine unlearning algorithm for minimax models. It proposes a minimax unlearning step consisting of a total Hessian-based complete Newton update and the Gaussian mechanism borrowed from differential privacy. To obtain the unlearning certification, our method injects calibrated Gaussian noises by carefully analyzing the ''sensitivity'' of the minimax unlearning step (i.e., the closeness between the minimax unlearning variables and the retraining-from-scratch variables). We derive the generalization rates in terms of population strong and weak primal-dual risk for three different cases of loss functions, i.e., (strongly-)convex-(strongly-)concave losses. We also provide the deletion capacity to guarantee that a desired population risk can be maintained as long as the number of deleted samples does not exceed the derived amount. With training samples $n$ and model dimension $d$, it yields the order $\mathcal O(n/d^{1/4})$, which shows a strict gap over the baseline method of differentially private minimax learning that has $\mathcal O(n/d^{1/2})$. In addition, our rates of generalization and deletion capacity match the state-of-the-art rates derived previously for standard statistical learning models.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples. This paper develops a certified unlearning algorithm for minimax models, where learning involves coupled minimization and maximization variables. That coupling motivates an update designed for the full minimax problem rather than the single-variable setting emphasized in earlier work.

The algorithm combines a complete Newton update based on a total Hessian with calibrated Gaussian noise. Its analysis measures how close the updated variables are to those obtained by retraining from scratch. This sensitivity calculation determines the noise required for the stated epsilon-delta unlearning certification. The authors also derive population risk guarantees across three cases involving convex-concave and strongly convex-concave losses.

The deletion-capacity result specifies how many samples can be removed while maintaining a desired population risk. With n samples and dimension d, its order is n divided by d to the one-quarter power, improving on the stated differentially private minimax baseline. The rates also match previously established rates for standard statistical learning models.
summary.tldr: A minimax-specific Newton update with calibrated Gaussian noise enables certified unlearning with improved deletion capacity over the stated privacy-based baseline.

title: Certified Minimax Unlearning with Generalization Rates and Deletion Capacity

abstract: We present a multi-temporal, multi-modal remote-sensing dataset for predicting how active wildfires will spread at a resolution of 24 hours. The dataset consists of 13607 images across 607 fire events in the United States from January 2018 to October 2021. For each fire event, the dataset contains a full time series of daily observations, containing detected active fires and variables related to fuel, topography and weather conditions. The dataset is challenging due to: a) its inputs being multi-temporal, b) the high number of 23 multi-modal input channels, c) highly imbalanced labels and d) noisy labels, due to smoke, clouds, and inaccuracies in the active fire detection. The underlying complexity of the physical processes adds to these challenges. Compared to existing public datasets in this area, WildfireSpreadTS allows for multi-temporal modeling of spreading wildfires, due to its time series structure. Furthermore, we provide additional input modalities and a high spatial resolution of 375m for the active fire maps. We publish this dataset to encourage further research on this important task with multi-temporal, noise-resistant or generative methods, uncertainty estimation or advanced optimization techniques that deal with the high-dimensional input space.

paragraphs: WildfireSpreadTS is a remote-sensing dataset for predicting wildfire spread at 24-hour intervals. It contains 13,607 images covering 607 United States fire events from January 2018 through October 2021. Each event includes a daily observation sequence, allowing researchers to study how a fire develops over time.

The inputs combine detected active fires with information about fuel, terrain, and weather across 23 channels. Active-fire maps have a spatial resolution of 375 meters. The time-series organization and additional input modalities distinguish the dataset from existing public resources described in the paper and support models that use multiple observations of a spreading fire.

The dataset presents several stated challenges: many input channels, temporal structure, highly imbalanced labels, and noisy fire detections affected by smoke, clouds, and detection inaccuracies. Complex physical processes add further difficulty. The release is intended to support research on temporal modeling, noise resistance, generative methods, uncertainty estimation, and optimization for many input dimensions; its contribution is the dataset and the research opportunities it enables.
summary.tldr: WildfireSpreadTS provides daily multimodal observations of 607 fire events to support 24-hour wildfire spread prediction.

title: WildfireSpreadTS: A dataset of multi-modal time series for wildfire spread prediction

abstract: Visual anomaly detection, the task of detecting abnormal characteristics in images, is challenging due to the rarity and unpredictability of anomalies. In order to reliably model the distribution of normality and detect anomalies, a few works have attempted to exploit the density estimation ability of normalizing flow (NF). However, previous NF-based methods have relied solely on the capability of NF and forcibly transformed the distribution of all features to a single distribution (e.g., unit normal distribution), when features can have different semantic information and thus follow different distributions. We claim that forcibly learning to transform such diverse distributions to a single distribution with a single network will cause the learning difficulty, limiting the capacity of a network to discriminate normal and abnormal data. As such, we propose to transform the distribution of features at each location of a given image to different distributions. In particular, we train NF to map normal data distribution to distributions with the same mean but different variances at each location of the given image. To enhance the discriminability, we also train NF to map abnormal data distribution to a distribution with a mean that is different from that of normal data, where abnormal data is synthesized with data augmentation. The experimental results outline the effectiveness of the proposed framework in improving the density modeling and thus anomaly detection performance.

paragraphs: Visual anomaly detection requires modeling normal appearance well enough to identify unusual image characteristics. Normalizing flows offer a way to model feature distributions, but earlier approaches mapped diverse features into one shared target distribution. This paper argues that forcing semantically different features through that same target makes learning harder and weakens anomaly discrimination.

SANFlow instead assigns different target distributions to features at different image locations. For normal data, those distributions share a mean but have location-dependent variances. This lets the model retain differences in how features vary across locations while keeping a common reference for normal appearance. The design explicitly accommodates diversity within normal image features.

The method also creates artificial abnormal data through augmentation and trains the flow to map it to a distribution with a different mean. This adds a separate training signal for distinguishing abnormal from normal features. Experiments show improved density modeling and anomaly detection. The contribution combines a more flexible representation of normality with explicit separation encouraged by synthesized anomalies.
summary.tldr: SANFlow improves anomaly detection by giving normal features location-specific distributions and separating synthesized abnormal features.

title: SANFlow: Semantic-Aware Normalizing Flow for Anomaly Detection

abstract: Targeted protein degradation techniques, such as PROteolysis TArgeting Chimeras (PROTACs), have emerged as powerful tools for selectively removing disease-causing proteins. One challenging problem in this field is designing a linker to connect different molecular fragments to form a stable drug-candidate molecule. Existing models for linker design assume that the relative positions of the fragments are known, which may not be the case in real scenarios. In this work, we address a more general problem where the poses of the fragments are *unknown* in 3D space. We develop a 3D equivariant diffusion model that jointly learns the generative process of both fragment poses and the 3D structure of the linker. By viewing fragments as rigid bodies, we design a fragment pose prediction module inspired by the Newton-Euler equations in rigid body mechanics. Empirical studies on ZINC and PROTAC-DB datasets demonstrate that our model can generate chemically valid, synthetically-accessible, and low-energy molecules under both unconstrained and constrained generation settings.

paragraphs: Linker design seeks a molecular connection between fragments that together form a stable candidate molecule. This is a challenging part of targeted protein degradation approaches such as PROTACs. Existing models assume that the fragments' relative positions are already known, even though that information may be unavailable in practical design settings.

LinkerNet tackles the joint problem of placing the fragments and generating the linker's three-dimensional structure. It uses a 3D equivariant diffusion model to learn both processes together. The model treats each fragment as a rigid body, and its pose-prediction module draws inspiration from the Newton-Euler equations used in rigid-body mechanics.

Experiments on ZINC and PROTAC-DB show that the method can generate molecules with chemical validity, synthetic accessibility, and low energy in both constrained and unconstrained settings. These findings support treating fragment arrangement and linker structure as coupled design choices. The demonstrated contribution is molecular generation under this broader setup, including cases where fragment poses are not supplied in advance.
summary.tldr: LinkerNet jointly generates molecular linkers and fragment poses, allowing linker design when relative fragment positions are unknown.

title: LinkerNet: Fragment Poses and Linker Co-Design with 3D Equivariant Diffusion

abstract: Recommending out-of-vocabulary (OOV) items is a challenging problem since the in-vocabulary (IV) items have well-trained behavioral embeddings but the OOV items only have content features. Current OOV recommendation models often generate 'makeshift' embeddings for OOV items from content features and then jointly recommend with the `makeshift' OOV item embeddings and the behavioral IV item embeddings. However, merely using the 'makeshift' embedding will result in suboptimal recommendation performance due to the substantial gap between the content feature and the behavioral embeddings. To bridge the gap, we propose a novel **User Sequence IMagination (USIM)** fine-tuning framework, which first imagines the user sequences and then refines the generated OOV embeddings with the user behavioral embeddings. Specifically, we frame the user sequence imagination as a reinforcement learning problem and develop a recommendation-focused reward function to evaluate to what extent a user can help recommend the OOV items. Besides, we propose an embedding-driven transition function to model the embedding transition after imaging a user. USIM has been deployed on a prominent e-commerce platform for months, offering recommendations for millions of OOV items and billions of users. Extensive experiments demonstrate that USIM outperforms traditional generative models in OOV item recommendation performance across traditional collaborative filtering and GNN-based collaborative filtering models.

paragraphs: Recommenders represent established items using learned patterns of user behavior. Out-of-vocabulary items have only content features, so their representations must be generated from a different source of information. The paper argues that directly mixing these generated representations with established behavioral representations leaves a substantial gap that hurts recommendation quality.

User Sequence IMagination, or USIM, adds a fine-tuning stage that imagines user sequences and uses user behavioral embeddings to refine the generated item embeddings. It formulates this process as reinforcement learning. A recommendation-focused reward assesses how much a user can help recommend an unfamiliar item, while an embedding-driven transition function models how the item representation changes after imagining a user.

Experiments show improvements over traditional generative approaches across both conventional and graph-neural-network-based collaborative filtering models. The authors also report deployment for months on a prominent e-commerce platform serving millions of unfamiliar items and billions of users. The results support refining content-derived embeddings through behavioral information as a useful addition to generating those embeddings in the first place.
summary.tldr: USIM uses imagined user sequences to refine content-derived item embeddings and improve recommendations for out-of-vocabulary items.

title: Fine Tuning Out-of-Vocabulary Item Recommendation with User Sequence Imagination

abstract: In this paper, we introduce the first learning-free model reuse task within the non-Euclidean domain, termed as Deep Graph Mating (Grama). We strive to create a child Graph Neural Network (GNN) that integrates knowledge from pre-trained parent models without requiring re-training, fine-tuning, or annotated labels. To this end, we begin by investigating the permutation invariance property of GNNs, which leads us to develop two vanilla approaches for Grama: Vanilla Parameter Interpolation (VPI) and Vanilla Alignment Prior to Interpolation (VAPI), both employing topology-independent interpolation in the parameter space. However, neither approach has achieved the anticipated results. Through theoretical analysis of VPI and VAPI, we identify critical challenges unique to Grama, including increased sensitivity to parameter misalignment and further the inherent topology-dependent complexities. Motivated by these findings, we propose the Dual-Message Coordination and Calibration (DuMCC) methodology, comprising the Parent Message Coordination (PMC) scheme to optimise the permutation matrices for parameter interpolation by coordinating aggregated messages, and the Child Message Calibration (CMC) scheme to mitigate over-smoothing identified in PMC by calibrating the message statistics within child GNNs. Experiments across diverse domains, including node and graph property prediction, 3D object recognition, and large-scale semantic parsing, demonstrate that the proposed DuMCC effectively enables training-free knowledge transfer, yielding results on par with those of pre-trained models.

paragraphs: Deep Graph Mating asks whether pretrained graph neural networks can contribute their knowledge to a child model without retraining, fine-tuning, or annotated labels. The authors first examine direct parameter interpolation and interpolation preceded by alignment. Both approaches operate independently of graph topology and fail to deliver the expected results.

Their analysis identifies sensitivity to parameter misalignment and complications that depend on graph structure. The proposed Dual-Message Coordination and Calibration method addresses these through the messages exchanged within graph neural networks. Parent Message Coordination optimizes the permutations used to align parameters by coordinating aggregated messages. Child Message Calibration then adjusts message statistics in the combined model to mitigate the over-smoothing identified in the coordination stage.

Experiments cover node and graph property prediction, three-dimensional object recognition, and large-scale semantic parsing. Across these domains, the authors report training-free knowledge transfer with results comparable to pretrained models. The findings support message-aware coordination and calibration as a way to reuse graph models where straightforward parameter interpolation is inadequate.
summary.tldr: Deep Graph Mating combines pretrained GNN knowledge through message-based alignment and calibration without retraining or labeled data.

title: Deep Graph Mating

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have become the dominant paradigm of generative modeling in a variety of domains by learning stochastic processes from noise to data. Recently, diffusion denoising bridge models (DDBMs), a new formulation of generative modeling that builds stochastic processes between fixed data endpoints based on a reference diffusion process, have achieved empirical success across tasks with coupled data distribution, such as image-to-image translation. However, DDBM's sampling process typically requires hundreds of network evaluations to achieve decent performance, which may impede their practical deployment due to high computational demands. In this work, inspired by the recent advance of consistency models in DMs, we tackle this problem by learning the consistency function of the probability-flow ordinary differential equation (PF-ODE) of DDBMs, which directly predicts the solution at a starting step given any point on the ODE trajectory. Based on a dedicated general-form ODE solver, we propose two paradigms: consistency bridge distillation and consistency bridge training, which is flexible to apply on DDBMs with broad design choices. Experimental results show that our proposed method could sample $4\times$ to $50\times$ faster than the base DDBM and produce better visual quality given the same step in various tasks with pixel resolution ranging from $64 \times 64$ to $256 \times 256$, as well as supporting downstream tasks such as semantic interpolation in the data space.
originalAbstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have become the dominant paradigm of generative modeling in a variety of domains by learning stochastic processes from noise to data. Recently, diffusion denoising bridge models (DDBMs), a new formulation of generative modeling that builds stochastic processes between fixed data endpoints based on a reference diffusion process, have achieved empirical success across tasks with coupled data distribution, such as image-to-image translation. However, DDBM's sampling process typically requires hundreds of network evaluations to achieve decent performance, which may impede their practical deployment due to high computational demands. In this work, inspired by the recent advance of consistency models in DMs, we tackle this problem by learning the consistency function of the probability-flow ordinary differential equation (PF-ODE) of DDBMs, which directly predicts the solution at a starting step given any point on the ODE trajectory. Based on a dedicated general-form ODE solver, we propose two paradigms: consistency bridge distillation and consistency bridge training, which is flexible to apply on DDBMs with broad design choices. Experimental results show that our proposed method could sample $4\times$ to $50\times$ faster than the base DDBM and produce better visual quality given the same step in various tasks with pixel resolution ranging from $64 \times 64$ to $256 \times 256$, as well as supporting downstream tasks such as semantic interpolation in the data space.

paragraphs: Diffusion bridge models construct stochastic paths between data endpoints, making them useful for tasks such as image-to-image translation. Their sampling procedures can require hundreds of network evaluations, creating a substantial computational burden. This paper develops consistency-based methods to obtain results with fewer evaluations while retaining the bridge formulation.

The central idea is to learn a function associated with the bridge model’s probability-flow ordinary differential equation. Given a point along its trajectory, this function predicts the solution at a designated starting step. Learning that relationship provides a way to bypass much of the repeated numerical progression normally required during sampling.

Using a dedicated general-form solver, the authors introduce consistency bridge distillation and consistency bridge training, accommodating broad choices in bridge-model design. Experiments report sampling speedups of 4× to 50× over the base model and better visual quality at the same sampling-step count. These results span tasks at resolutions from 64 × 64 to 256 × 256, and the method also supports semantic interpolation in data space.
summary.tldr: Consistency functions accelerate diffusion bridge sampling, with reported speedups of 4× to 50× and better quality at equal step counts.

title: Consistency Diffusion Bridge Models

abstract: High-quality, large-scale corpora are the cornerstone of building foundation models. In this work, we introduce MathPile, a diverse and high-quality math-centric corpus comprising about 9.5 billion tokens. Throughout its creation, we adhered to the principle of “less is more”, firmly believing in the supremacy of data quality over quantity, even in the pre-training phase. Our meticulous data collection and processing efforts included a complex suite of preprocessing, prefiltering, language identification, cleaning, filtering, and deduplication, ensuring the high quality of our corpus. Furthermore, we performed data contamination detection on downstream benchmark test sets to eliminate duplicates and conducted continual pre-training experiments, booting the performance on common mathematical reasoning benchmarks. We aim for our MathPile to boost language models’ mathematical reasoning abilities and open-source its different versions and processing scripts to advance the field.
