paragraphs: MathPile is a mathematics-focused corpus containing approximately 9.5 billion tokens for language-model pretraining. The project emphasizes the quality and diversity of training material, treating careful selection and processing as central parts of dataset construction. Its intended use is to strengthen mathematical reasoning in language models.

The creation pipeline includes preprocessing, preliminary filtering, language identification, cleaning, further filtering, and deduplication. The authors also check for overlap with downstream benchmark test sets and remove detected duplicates. This benchmark-contamination step addresses a concrete concern when evaluating models trained on large collections: test material may otherwise appear within the training corpus.

The authors conduct continual-pretraining experiments and report improvements on common mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Those results provide empirical support for the corpus’s usefulness in the tested training setting. They also release different corpus versions and the processing scripts, making both the training material and its preparation methods available to others. The contribution thus combines a substantial mathematical resource, a quality-focused preparation workflow, and experimental evidence of benefits.
summary.tldr: MathPile offers roughly 9.5 billion carefully processed mathematics tokens and reports reasoning gains from continual pretraining.

title: MathPile: A Billion-Token-Scale Pretraining Corpus for Math

abstract: Curvature information -- particularly, the largest eigenvalue of the lossHessian, known as the sharpness -- often forms the basis for learning ratetuners. However, recent work has shown that the curvature information undergoescomplex dynamics during training, going from a phase of increasing sharpness toeventual stabilization. We analyze the closed-loop feedback effect betweenlearning rate tuning and curvature. We find that classical learning rate tunersmay yield greater one-step loss reduction, yet they ultimately underperform inthe long term when compared to constant learning rates in the full batch regime.These models break the stabilization of the sharpness, which we explain using asimplified model of the joint dynamics of the learning rate and the curvature.To further investigate these effects, we introduce a new learning rate tuningmethod, Curvature Dynamics Aware Tuning (CDAT), which prioritizes long termcurvature stabilization over instantaneous progress on the objective. In thefull batch regime, CDAT shows behavior akin to prefixed warm-up schedules on deeplearning objectives, outperforming tuned constant learning rates. In the minibatch regime, we observe that stochasticity introduces confounding effects thatexplain the previous success of some learning rate tuners at appropriate batchsizes. Our findings highlight the critical role of understanding the jointdynamics of the learning rate and curvature, beyond greedy minimization, todiagnose failures and design effective adaptive learning rate tuners.

paragraphs: Learning-rate tuners often use loss curvature, especially the largest Hessian eigenvalue, called sharpness. But sharpness changes during training, and the learning rate itself influences those changes. This paper studies that feedback loop, asking whether a step that immediately reduces loss most effectively also supports good longer-term training.

In full-batch training, the authors find that classical tuners can achieve greater one-step loss reduction yet ultimately underperform constant learning rates. Their explanation is that these tuners disrupt the stabilization of sharpness. A simplified model of learning-rate and curvature dynamics motivates Curvature Dynamics Aware Tuning, which prioritizes longer-term curvature stabilization over immediate objective improvement.

In the full-batch setting, the proposed method behaves similarly to predefined warm-up schedules and outperforms tuned constant learning rates on deep learning objectives. In minibatch training, stochasticity complicates the feedback and helps explain why some existing tuners succeed at suitable batch sizes. The findings make training dynamics, including batch-dependent effects, central to assessing curvature-based learning-rate adaptation.
summary.tldr: CDAT tunes learning rates to stabilize long-term curvature dynamics, improving full-batch training over tuned constant learning rates.

title: Stepping on the Edge: Curvature Aware Learning Rate Tuners

abstract: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) and their variants are popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques that closely match full model fine-tune performance while requiring only a small number of additional parameters. These additional LoRA parameters are specific to the base model being adapted. When the base model needs to be deprecated and replaced with a new one, all the associated LoRA modules need to be re-trained. Such re-training requires access to the data used to train the LoRA for the original base model. This is especially problematic for commercial cloud applications where the LoRA modules and the base models are hosted by service providers who may not be allowed to host proprietary client task data. To address this challenge, we propose $\textit{Trans-LoRA}$ --- a novel method for lossless, nearly data-free transfer of LoRAs across base models. Our approach relies on synthetic data to transfer LoRA modules. Using large language models, we design a synthetic data generator to approximate the data-generating process of the $\textit{observed}$ task data subset. Training on the resulting synthetic dataset transfers LoRA modules to new models. We show the effectiveness of our approach using both LLama and Gemma model families. Our approach achieves lossless (mostly improved) LoRA transfer between models within and across different base model families, and even between different PEFT methods, on a wide variety of tasks.

paragraphs: LoRA adapters provide economical task adaptation, but their parameters are tied to the base model used during training. Replacing that model normally requires retraining its adapters using the original task data. This is problematic when a service provider hosts the models but cannot retain a client’s proprietary training data.

Trans-LoRA transfers adaptation through synthetic data. A language-model-based generator approximates the data-generating process of an observed subset of task examples. Training on the generated dataset then transfers the adaptation to another model. The observed subset is an important qualification: the abstract describes the method as nearly data-free, rather than requiring no task-data exposure at all.

Across the evaluated tasks, the authors report lossless, and mostly improved, transfer within and between the Llama and Gemma model families. They also demonstrate transfer between different parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. These results suggest that synthetic task data can preserve useful adaptation when the underlying model changes, reducing dependence on access to the original training collection.
summary.tldr: Trans-LoRA uses synthetic data derived from an observed task subset to transfer adapters across models with no reported performance loss in its evaluations.

title: $\textit{Trans-LoRA}$: towards data-free Transferable Parameter Efficient Finetuning

abstract: In human-AI collaborative tasks, the distribution of human behavior, influenced by mental models, is non-stationary, manifesting in various levels of initiative and different collaborative strategies. A significant challenge in human-AI collaboration is determining how to collaborate effectively with humans exhibiting non-stationary dynamics. Current collaborative agents involve initially running self-play (SP) multiple times to build a policy pool, followed by training the final adaptive policy against this pool. These agents themselves are a single policy network, which is $\textbf{insufficient for handling non-stationary human dynamics}$. We discern that despite the inherent diversity in human behaviors, the $\textbf{underlying meta-tasks within specific collaborative contexts tend to be strikingly similar}$. Accordingly, we propose $\textbf{C}$ollaborative $\textbf{B}$ayesian $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{R}$euse ($\textbf{CBPR}$), a novel Bayesian-based framework that $\textbf{adaptively selects optimal collaborative policies matching the current meta-task from multiple policy networks}$ instead of just selecting actions relying on a single policy network. We provide theoretical guarantees for CBPR's rapid convergence to the optimal policy once human partners alter their policies. This framework shifts from directly modeling human behavior to identifying various meta-tasks that support human decision-making and training meta-task playing (MTP) agents tailored to enhance collaboration. Our method undergoes rigorous testing in a well-recognized collaborative cooking simulator, $\textit{Overcooked}$. Both empirical results and user studies demonstrate CBPR's superior competitiveness compared to existing baselines.

paragraphs: Human collaborators can change their initiative and strategy during a shared task. An AI partner therefore faces a moving target: behavior that worked with one collaboration style may become less suitable when the person changes approach. This paper argues that representing the final collaborative agent with a single policy network is insufficient for handling these changing dynamics.

Collaborative Bayesian Policy Reuse, or CBPR, draws on the observation that different human behaviors can involve similar underlying meta-tasks. It trains agents for those meta-tasks and uses Bayesian reasoning to select among multiple policy networks as collaboration unfolds. Adaptation thus includes choosing an appropriate collaborative policy, rather than relying entirely on action selection within one network.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for rapid convergence to the optimal policy after a human partner changes policies. Experiments and user studies in the Overcooked cooking simulator show stronger performance than the evaluated baselines. Together, these results support organizing collaborative expertise around recurring meta-tasks as a useful approach to partners whose behavior changes over time.
summary.tldr: CBPR adapts to changing human partners by selecting among policies trained for recurring collaborative meta-tasks.

title: Beyond Single Stationary Policies: Meta-Task Players as Naturally Superior Collaborators

abstract: Current techniques for detecting AI-generated text are largely confined to manual feature crafting and supervised binary classification paradigms. These methodologies typically lead to performance bottlenecks and unsatisfactory generalizability. Consequently, these methods are often inapplicable for out-of-distribution (OOD) data and newly emerged large language models (LLMs). In this paper, we revisit the task of AI-generated text detection. We argue that the key to accomplishing this task lies in distinguishing writing styles of different authors, rather than simply classifying the text into human-written or AI-generated text. To this end, we propose DeTeCtive, a multi-task auxiliary, multi-level contrastive learning framework. DeTeCtive is designed to facilitate the learning of distinct writing styles, combined with a dense information retrieval pipeline for AI-generated text detection. Our method is compatible with a range of text encoders. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method enhances the ability of various text encoders in detecting AI-generated text across multiple benchmarks and achieves state-of-the-art results. Notably, in OOD zero-shot evaluation, our method outperforms existing approaches by a large margin. Moreover, we find our method boasts a Training-Free Incremental Adaptation (TFIA) capability towards OOD data, further enhancing its efficacy in OOD detection scenarios. We will open-source our code and models in hopes that our work will spark new thoughts in the field of AI-generated text detection, ensuring safe application of LLMs and enhancing compliance.

paragraphs: Detecting AI-generated text becomes harder when the writing comes from unfamiliar data distributions or newly introduced language models. The authors argue that conventional handcrafted features and supervised human-versus-AI classification can generalize poorly in these situations. They recast detection as a problem of learning differences between authors' writing styles.

DeTeCtive combines auxiliary learning tasks with contrastive learning at multiple levels to develop representations that distinguish those styles. It then uses a dense information retrieval pipeline for detection. This connects the learned representation to a retrieval-based decision process, and the framework can work with a range of text encoders.

Across multiple benchmarks, the method improves the detection performance of various encoders and achieves state-of-the-art results. The authors report particularly large gains in zero-shot evaluation on out-of-distribution data. They also identify a capability for incremental adaptation to such data without further training. Together, these findings support style-oriented representation learning and retrieval as a useful approach to detection when the evaluated writing differs from the training distribution.
summary.tldr: DeTeCtive learns writing-style representations and uses retrieval to improve AI-text detection, especially on the evaluated out-of-distribution data.

title: DeTeCtive: Detecting AI-generated Text via Multi-Level Contrastive Learning

abstract: Learning the intents of an agent, defined by its goals or motion style, is often extremely challenging from just a few examples. We refer to this problem as task concept learning and present our approach, Few-Shot Task Learning through Inverse Generative Modeling (FTL-IGM), which learns new task concepts by leveraging invertible neural generative models. The core idea is to pretrain a generative model on a set of basic concepts and their demonstrations. Then, given a few demonstrations of a new concept (such as a new goal or a new action), our method learns the underlying concepts through backpropagation without updating the model weights, thanks to the invertibility of the generative model. We evaluate our method in five domains -- object rearrangement, goal-oriented navigation, motion caption of human actions, autonomous driving, and real-world table-top manipulation. Our experimental results demonstrate that via the pretrained generative model, we successfully learn novel concepts and generate agent plans or motion corresponding to these concepts in (1) unseen environments and (2) in composition with training concepts.

paragraphs: A few demonstrations may show what an agent does without explicitly stating its goal or motion style. FTL-IGM treats learning that underlying intent as task concept learning. It first trains an invertible generative model on basic concepts and demonstrations, establishing a reusable relationship between task concepts and the behavior they produce.

For a new concept, the method works backward from a small set of demonstrations. Backpropagation adjusts the inferred concept while leaving the pretrained model's weights unchanged. The model's invertibility enables this inference procedure. Once a concept has been learned, the generative model can use it to produce corresponding plans or motions.

The authors evaluate the approach in five domains: object rearrangement, goal-oriented navigation, human-action motion caption, autonomous driving, and real-world tabletop manipulation. Their experiments show successful learning of novel concepts and generation in unseen environments or in combination with training concepts. The central finding is that a pretrained generative model can support both inferring intent from sparse examples and reusing that intent to generate behavior in these tested settings.
summary.tldr: FTL-IGM infers new task concepts from a few demonstrations through a fixed invertible generative model, then generates corresponding plans or motions.

title: Few-Shot Task Learning through Inverse Generative Modeling

abstract: Credal sets are sets of probability distributions that are considered as candidates for an imprecisely known ground-truth distribution. In machine learning, they have recently attracted attention as an appealing formalism for uncertainty representation, in particular, due to their ability to represent both the aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in a prediction. However, the design of methods for learning credal set predictors remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we make use of conformal prediction for this purpose. More specifically, we propose a method for predicting credal sets in the classification task, given training data labeled by probability distributions. Since our method inherits the coverage guarantees of conformal prediction, our conformal credal sets are guaranteed to be valid with high probability (without any assumptions on model or distribution). We demonstrate the applicability of our method on ambiguous classification tasks for uncertainty quantification.

In machine learning, they have recently attracted attention as an appealing formalism for uncertainty representation, in particular, due to their ability to represent both the aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in a prediction. However, the design of methods for learning credal set predictors remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we make use of conformal prediction for this purpose. paragraphs: A classifier can express uncertainty by assigning probabilities to possible classes. A credal set goes further: it contains several probability distributions that could plausibly describe an imprecisely known target distribution. This lets the representation accommodate both uncertainty inherent in the outcome and uncertainty about which probability distribution is appropriate.

The paper proposes learning these sets through conformal prediction. Its setting is classification with training examples labeled by probability distributions, rather than only individual class labels. The predictor therefore aims to return a set of candidate distributions for a new example. This matches the form of uncertainty in the training labels and gives the method a way to preserve ambiguity instead of collapsing it into one probability assignment.

The resulting sets inherit conformal coverage guarantees, providing high-probability validity without specifying a particular model or distribution. The authors demonstrate the approach on ambiguous classification tasks. Its contribution is to combine a richer uncertainty representation with a calibration mechanism that gives a formal validity guarantee, rather than relying only on how convincing the predicted probabilities appear.
summary.tldr: The paper uses conformal prediction to learn sets of class-probability distributions with high-probability validity guarantees.

title: Conformalized Credal Set Predictors

abstract: Iteratively improving and repairing source code with large language models (LLMs), known as refinement, has emerged as a popular way of generating programs that would be too complex to construct in one shot. Given a bank of test cases, together with a candidate program, an LLM can improve that program by being prompted with failed test cases. But it remains an open question how to best iteratively refine code, with prior work employing simple greedy or breadth-first strategies. We show here that refinement exposes an explore-exploit tradeoff: exploit by refining the program that passes the most test cases, or explore by refining a lesser considered program. We frame this as an arm-acquiring bandit problem, which we solve with Thompson Sampling. The resulting LLM-based program synthesis algorithm is broadly applicable: Across loop invariant synthesis, visual reasoning puzzles, and competition programming problems, we find that our new method can solve more problems using fewer language model calls.

paragraphs: Generating a difficult program can involve repeated repair: an LLM produces code, tests reveal failures, and the model uses those failures to propose improvements. Once several candidate programs exist, deciding which one to repair becomes a separate problem. The candidate passing the most tests looks promising, but another candidate may offer a better route to a solution.

The paper treats this choice as an exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Exploitation means investing more effort in the strongest current candidate; exploration means trying a candidate that has received less attention. The authors formulate the process as an arm-acquiring bandit problem and use Thompson Sampling to decide where further refinement effort should go.

The resulting program-synthesis method is evaluated on loop invariant synthesis, visual reasoning puzzles, and competition programming. Across these settings, the authors find that it solves more problems with fewer language-model calls. The contribution is therefore a strategy for allocating repair attempts, showing that how candidates are selected can materially affect the effectiveness of iterative code generation.
summary.tldr: Treating code repair as a bandit problem helps an LLM choose which candidate to refine, solving more evaluated problems with fewer calls.

title: Code Repair with LLMs gives an Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff

abstract: In real-world applications, the distribution of the data, and our goals, evolve over time. The prevailing theoretical framework for studying machine learning, namely probably approximately correct (PAC) learning, largely ignores time. As a consequence, existing strategies to address the dynamic nature of data and goals exhibit poor real-world performance. This paper develops a theoretical framework called"Prospective Learning" that is tailored for situations when the optimal hypothesis changes over time. In PAC learning, empirical risk minimization (ERM) is known to be consistent. We develop a learner called Prospective ERM, which returns a sequence of predictors that make predictions on future data. We prove that the risk of prospective ERM converges to the Bayes risk under certain assumptions on the stochastic process generating the data. Prospective ERM, roughly speaking, incorporates time as an input in addition to the data. We show that standard ERM as done in PAC learning, without incorporating time, can result in failure to learn when distributions are dynamic. Numerical experiments illustrate that prospective ERM can learn synthetic and visual recognition problems constructed from MNIST and CIFAR-10. Code at https://github.com/neurodata/prolearn.

paragraphs: Learning problems can change because both data distributions and goals evolve over time. Prospective Learning develops a theoretical framework for this setting, where the best prediction rule may itself change. The paper contrasts this with the largely time-independent treatment in probably approximately correct learning and examines what it means to learn for future data.

The proposed Prospective Empirical Risk Minimization learner returns a sequence of predictors. Roughly, it includes time alongside the usual data inputs, allowing predictions to account for when they will be used. Under specified assumptions on the stochastic process generating the data, the authors prove that its risk converges to Bayes risk.

The paper also shows that standard empirical risk minimization without time can fail to learn under dynamic distributions. Numerical experiments illustrate prospective learning on synthetic problems and visual recognition problems constructed from MNIST and CIFAR-10. The results combine a conditional theoretical guarantee with examples showing why time can be a meaningful part of the prediction problem.
summary.tldr: Prospective Learning incorporates time into prediction and proves convergence to Bayes risk under assumptions about the evolving data process.

title: Prospective Learning: Learning for a Dynamic Future

abstract: *Constrained Reinforcement Learning* (CRL) tackles sequential decision-making problems where agents are required to achieve goals by maximizing the expected return while meeting domain-specific constraints, which are often formulated on expected costs. In this setting, *policy-based* methods are widely used since they come with several advantages when dealing with continuous-control problems. These methods search in the policy space with an *action-based* or *parameter-based* exploration strategy, depending on whether they learn directly the parameters of a stochastic policy or those of a stochastic hyperpolicy. In this paper, we propose a general framework for addressing CRL problems via *gradient-based primal-dual* algorithms, relying on an alternate ascent/descent scheme with dual-variable regularization. We introduce an exploration-agnostic algorithm, called C-PG, which exhibits global last-iterate convergence guarantees under (weak) gradient domination assumptions, improving and generalizing existing results. Then, we design C-PGAE and C-PGPE, the action-based and the parameter-based versions of C-PG, respectively, and we illustrate how they naturally extend to constraints defined in terms of *risk measures* over the costs, as it is often requested in safety-critical scenarios. Finally, we numerically validate our algorithms on constrained control problems, and compare them with state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating their effectiveness.

paragraphs: Constrained reinforcement learning seeks policies that earn high expected returns while satisfying requirements on costs. They also show how these methods extend to constraints expressed through risk measures on costs, which are relevant to safety-critical control. Numerical comparisons on constrained control problems support their effectiveness. The theoretical convergence claim remains tied to the stated gradient-domination assumptions.
summary.tldr: C-PG unifies constrained policy-gradient methods and provides global last-iterate convergence under weak gradient-domination assumptions.

title: Last-Iterate Global Convergence of Policy Gradients for Constrained Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent advancements in generative models have highlighted the crucial role of image tokenization in the efficient synthesis of high-resolution images. Tokenization, which transforms images into latent representations, reduces computational demands compared to directly processing pixels and enhances the effectiveness and efficiency of the generation process. Prior methods, such as VQGAN, typically utilize 2D latent grids with fixed downsampling factors. However, these 2D tokenizations face challenges in managing the inherent redundancies present in images, where adjacent regions frequently display similarities. To overcome this issue, we introduce **T**ransformer-based 1-D**i**mensional **Tok**enizer (TiTok), an innovative approach that tokenizes images into 1D latent sequences. TiTok provides a more compact latent representation, yielding substantially more efficient and effective representations than conventional techniques. For example, a 256 × 256 × 3 image can be reduced to just **32** discrete tokens, a significant reduction from the 256 or 1024 tokens obtained by prior methods. Despite its compact nature, TiTok achieves competitive performance to state-of-the-art approaches. Specifically, using the same generator framework, TiTok attains **1.97** gFID, outperforming MaskGIT baseline significantly by 4.21 at ImageNet 256 × 256 benchmark. The advantages of TiTok become even more significant when it comes to higher resolution. At ImageNet 512 × 512 benchmark, TiTok not only outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion model DiT-XL/2 (gFID 2.74 vs. 3.04), but also reduces the image tokens by 64×, leading to **410× faster** generation process. Our best-performing variant can significantly surpasses DiT-XL/2 (gFID **2.13** vs. 3.04) while still generating high-quality samples **74× faster**. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/bytedance/1d-tokenizer

title: An Image is Worth 32 Tokens for Reconstruction and Generation

abstract: Accurate temporal prediction is the bridge between comprehensive scene understanding and embodied artificial intelligence. However, predicting multiple fine-grained states of scene at multiple temporal scales is difficult for vision-language models. We formalize the Multi‐Scale Temporal Prediction (MSTP) task in general and surgical scene by decomposing multi‐scale into two orthogonal dimensions: the temporal scale, forecasting states of human and surgery at varying look‐ahead intervals, and the state scale, modeling a hierarchy of states in general and surgical scene. For instance in general scene, states of contacting relationship are finer-grained than states of spatial relationship. For instance in surgical scene, medium‐level steps are finer‐grained than high‐level phases yet remain constrained by their encompassing phase. To support this unified task, we introduce the first MSTP Benchmark, featuring synchronized annotations across multiple state scales and temporal scales. We further propose a novel method, Incremental Generation and Multi‐agent Collaboration (IG-MC), which integrates two key innovations. Firstly, we propose an plug-and-play incremental generation to keep high-quality temporal prediction that continuously synthesizes up-to-date visual previews at expanding temporal scales to inform multiple decision-making agents, ensuring decision content and generated visuals remain synchronized and preventing performance degradation as look‐ahead intervals lengthen. Secondly, we propose a decision‐driven multi‐agent collaboration framework for multiple states prediction, comprising generation, initiation, and multi‐state assessment agents that dynamically triggers and evaluates prediction cycles to balance global coherence and local fidelity. Extensive experiments on the MSTP Benchmark in general and surgical scene show that IG‐MC is a generalizable plug-and-play method for MSTP, demonstrating the effectiveness of incremental generation and the stability of decision‐driven multi‐agent collaboration.

paragraphs: Predicting a scene’s future involves both how far ahead to look and how detailed the prediction should be. The paper formalizes these as separate dimensions of Multi-Scale Temporal Prediction. It covers general and surgical scenes, where detailed states belong within broader structures, such as surgical steps within phases. A new benchmark provides synchronized annotations across both dimensions.

Generation continually updates visual previews as the prediction horizon expands, keeping those previews synchronized with decisions. This component is intended to maintain prediction quality as forecasts reach further into the future and to provide current visual information to the agents.

A second component coordinates generation, initiation, and multi-state assessment agents to trigger and evaluate prediction cycles. Their collaboration balances consistency across the overall scene with accuracy in detailed states. title: Multi-scale Temporal Prediction via Incremental Generation and Multi-agent Collaboration

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the de facto parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method for large language models (LLMs) by constraining weight updates to low-rank matrices. Recent works such as Tied-LoRA, VeRA, and VB-LoRA push efficiency further by introducing additional constraints to reduce the trainable parameter space. In this paper, we show that the parameter space reduction strategies employed by these LoRA variants can be formulated within a unified framework, Uni-LoRA, where the LoRA parameter space, flattened as a high-dimensional vector space R^D, can be reconstructed through a projection from a subspace R^d, with d << D. We demonstrate that the fundamental difference among various LoRA methods lies in the choice of the projection matrix, P ∈ R^{D×d}. Most existing LoRA variants rely on layer-wise or structure-specific projections that limit cross-layer parameter sharing, thereby compromising parameter efficiency. In light of this, we introduce an efficient and theoretically grounded projection matrix that is isometric, enabling global parameter sharing and reducing computation overhead. Furthermore, under the unified view of Uni-LoRA, this design requires only a single trainable vector to reconstruct LoRA parameters for the entire LLM -- making Uni-LoRA both a unified framework and a “one-vector-only” solution. Extensive experiments on GLUE, mathematical reasoning, and instruction tuning benchmarks demonstrate that Uni-LoRA achieves state-of-the-art parameter efficiency while outperforming or matching prior approaches in predictive performance.

summary.tldr: Uni-LoRA unifies compact LoRA variants through projections and introduces global sharing that reconstructs all LoRA parameters from one trainable vector.

title: Uni-LoRA: One Vector is All You Need

abstract: Open-weight large language model (LLM) zoos provide access to numerous high-quality models, but selecting the appropriate model for specific tasks remains challenging and requires technical expertise. Most users simply want factually correct, safe, and satisfying responses without concerning themselves with model technicalities, while inference service providers prioritize minimizing operating costs. These competing interests are typically mediated through service level agreements (SLAs) that guarantee minimum service quality. We introduce MESS+, a stochastic optimization algorithm for cost-optimal LLM request routing while providing rigorous SLA compliance guarantees. MESS+ learns request satisfaction probabilities of LLMs in real-time as users interact with the system, based on which model selection decisions are made by solving a per-request optimization problem. Our algorithm includes a novel combination of virtual queues and request satisfaction prediction, along with a theoretical analysis of cost optimality and constraint satisfaction. Across a wide range of state-of-the-art LLM benchmarks, MESS+ achieves an average of $2\times$ cost savings compared to existing LLM routing techniques.

paragraphs: MESS+ chooses which language model should handle each incoming request while balancing operating cost against service-quality requirements. A collection of available models offers many choices, but users generally care about response quality rather than model selection. The paper frames this decision around service level agreements that specify minimum acceptable service.

The algorithm learns each model’s probability of satisfying requests as users interact with the system. It combines those predictions with virtual queues and solves an optimization problem for each request. This makes routing responsive to learned satisfaction probabilities while incorporating the service constraints into the selection process.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of cost optimality and constraint satisfaction, including rigorous guarantees for SLA compliance. Across the evaluated language-model benchmarks, MESS+ achieves average cost savings of twofold relative to existing routing methods. The contribution combines online learning about request satisfaction with constrained routing decisions. The reported savings concern the benchmark comparison; the service guarantees concern the algorithm’s analyzed constraints, rather than a promise that every individual answer is correct.
summary.tldr: MESS+ learns model satisfaction probabilities online and routes requests to reduce cost while providing analyzed service-level guarantees.

title: MESS+: Dynamically Learned Inference-Time LLM Routing in Model Zoos with Service Level Guarantees

abstract: Despite Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP)'s remarkable capability to retrieve content across modalities, a substantial modality gap persists in its feature space. Intriguingly, we discover that off-the-shelf MLLMs (Multimodal Large Language Models) demonstrate powerful inherent modality alignment properties. While recent MLLM-based retrievers with unified architectures partially mitigate this gap, their reliance on coarse modality alignment mechanisms fundamentally limits their potential. In this work, We introduce MAPLE (Modality-Aligned Preference Learning for Embeddings), a novel framework that leverages the fine-grained alignment priors inherent in MLLM to guide cross-modal representation learning. MAPLE formulates the learning process as reinforcement learning with two key components: (1) Automatic preference data construction using off-the-shelf MLLM, and (2) a new Relative Preference Alignment (RPA) loss, which adapts Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to the embedding learning setting. Experimental results show that our preference-guided alignment achieves substantial gains in fine-grained cross-modal retrieval, underscoring its effectiveness in handling nuanced semantic distinctions.

The stated findings suggest that a multimodal model's alignment knowledge can serve as training supervision for embeddings, helping retrieval systems distinguish closely related meanings rather than merely recognize broad correspondence between images and text.
summary.tldr: MAPLE transfers multimodal language models' alignment knowledge into retrieval embeddings through automatically generated preferences and a specialized alignment loss.

title: Guiding Cross-Modal Representations with MLLM Priors via Preference Alignment

abstract: Contrastive learning is a powerful framework for learning discriminative representations from image-text pairs. Despite its success, its theoretical foundations, especially when the image-text pair exhibits misalignment, remain underexplored. This paper provides the first theoretical analysis of contrastive learning under data misalignment, proving how the ground-truth modality-paired features are amplified while spurious features are suppressed through the training dynamics analysis. Specifically, we study two nonlinear encoders trained jointly with a contrastive loss and demonstrate that noisy (or misaligned) data pairs result in mixed representations and degrade the model's generalization ability. In contrast, recaptioning and filtering improve the data alignment, which in turn purifies the features learned by neurons and subsequently enhances generalization. Our analysis identifies feature purity as a key factor in the success of contrastive learning and offers insights into how data quality and training procedures impact representation learning and downstream generalization. Theoretical insights are supported by experiments on standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses image–text pairs to learn representations that connect the two modalities. When an image and its caption do not match well, the training signal can mix useful relationships with misleading ones. This paper examines that problem theoretically, studying two nonlinear encoders that are trained together using a contrastive loss.

The analysis follows how features change during training. It establishes how genuinely paired features become stronger while spurious features are suppressed, and shows how noisy or misaligned pairs produce mixed representations that harm generalization. The authors identify feature purity—the extent to which neurons learn the relevant features without this mixing—as a central factor in the analyzed learning process.

Recaptioning and filtering improve alignment between training images and text. Within the analysis, better alignment leads to purer learned features and improved generalization. Experiments on standard benchmarks support these theoretical insights. The contribution is an explanation connecting data-cleaning choices to internal representation learning and downstream performance, rather than treating data quality only as an empirical observation.
summary.tldr: The paper links image–text alignment to feature purity, explaining theoretically why recaptioning and filtering can improve contrastive-learning generalization.

title: Contrastive Learning with Data Misalignment: Feature Purity, Training Dynamics and Theoretical Generalization Guarantees

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have shown an impressive ability to generate high-quality images from input textual descriptions/prompts. However, concerns have been raised about the potential for these models to create content that infringes on copyrights or depicts disturbing subject matter. Removing specific concepts from these models is a promising solution to this issue. However, existing methods for concept removal do not work well in practical but challenging scenarios where concepts need to be continuously removed. Specifically, these methods lead to poor alignment between the text prompts and the generated image after the continuous removal process. To address this issue, we propose a novel concept removal approach called CCRT that includes a designed knowledge distillation paradigm. CCRT constrains the text-image alignment behavior during the continuous concept removal process by using a set of text prompts. These prompts are generated through our genetic algorithm, which employs a designed fuzzing strategy. To evaluate the effectiveness of CCRT, we conduct extensive experiments involving the removal of various concepts, algorithmic metrics, and human studies. The results demonstrate that CCRT can effectively remove the targeted concepts from the model in a continuous manner while maintaining the high image generation quality (e.g., text-image alignment). The code of CCRT is available at https://github.com/wssun/CCRT.

The evaluation covers multiple removed concepts and includes both algorithmic measures and human studies. The authors report that CCRT can remove targeted concepts continuously while retaining high image-generation quality, including alignment with text. The stated contribution is therefore sustained editing of a model's concepts while preserving its usefulness across the successive changes examined.
summary.tldr: CCRT uses knowledge distillation and generated prompts to remove concepts repeatedly while preserving text-image alignment in the reported evaluations.

title: Continuous Concepts Removal in Text-to-image Diffusion Models

abstract: Subgraph matching in logic circuits is foundational for numerous Electronic Design Automation (EDA) applications, including datapath optimization, arithmetic verification, and hardware trojan detection. However, existing techniques rely primarily on structural graph isomorphism and thus fail to identify function-related subgraphs when synthesis transformations substantially alter circuit topology. To overcome this critical limitation, we introduce the concept of functional subgraph matching, a novel approach that identifies whether a given logic function is implicitly present within a larger circuit, irrespective of structural variations induced by synthesis or technology mapping. Specifically, we propose a two-stage multi-modal framework: (1) learning robust functional embeddings across AIG and post-mapping netlists for functional subgraph detection, and (2) identifying fuzzy boundaries using a graph segmentation approach. Evaluations on standard benchmarks (ITC99, OpenABCD, ForgeEDA) demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing structural methods, with average 93.8% accuracy in functional subgraph detection and a dice score of 91.3% in fuzzy boundary identification.

paragraphs: Circuit synthesis can change how logic gates are connected while preserving the computation they perform. This makes structural subgraph matching inadequate for finding some functionally related circuit regions. The paper introduces functional subgraph matching: determining whether a specified logic function is present inside a larger circuit despite changes in its visible graph structure.

The proposed framework separates detection from localization. First, it learns functional representations across AIG circuit representations and post-mapping netlists to detect whether the relevant function is present. Second, graph segmentation identifies its fuzzy boundaries. This separation addresses both the existence of a function and the region associated with it.

On ITC99, OpenABCD, and ForgeEDA benchmarks, the authors report an average functional detection accuracy of 93.8% and a boundary-identification Dice score of 91.3%, improving significantly over structural methods. The findings support using learned functional information when synthesis obscures structural similarity, with relevance to the paper's motivating applications in datapath optimization, arithmetic verification, and hardware trojan detection.
summary.tldr: The paper detects and localizes logic functions inside circuits using learned functional representations, overcoming structural changes caused by synthesis.

title: Functional Matching of Logic Subgraphs: Beyond Structural Isomorphism

abstract: Recent results show that modern Large Language Models (LLM) are indeed capable of understanding and answering questions about structured data such as graphs. This new paradigm can lead to solutions that require less supervision while, at the same time, providing a model that can generalize and answer questions beyond the training labels. Existing proposals often use some description of the graph to create an ``augmented'' prompt fed to the LLM. For a chosen class of graphs, if a well-tailored graph encoder is deployed to play together with a pre-trained LLM, the model can answer graph-related questions well. Existing solutions to graph-based prompts range from graph serialization to graph transformers. In this work, we show that the use of a parameter-free graph encoder based on Fock space representations, a concept borrowed from mathematical physics, is remarkably versatile in this problem setting. The simple construction, inherited directly from the theory with a few small adjustments, can provide rich and informative graph encodings, for a wide range of different graphs. We investigate the use of this idea for prefix-tuned prompts leveraging the capabilities of a pre-trained, frozen LLM. The modifications lead to a model that can answer graph-related questions -- from simple graphs to proteins to hypergraphs -- effectively and with minimal, if any, adjustments to the architecture. Our work significantly simplifies existing solutions and generalizes well to multiple different graph-based structures effortlessly.
originalAbstract: Recent results show that modern Large Language Models (LLM) are indeed capable of understanding and answering questions about structured data such as graphs. This new paradigm can lead to solutions that require less supervision while, at the same time, providing a model that can generalize and answer questions beyond the training labels. Existing proposals often use some description of the graph to create an ``augmented'' prompt fed to the LLM. For a chosen class of graphs, if a well-tailored graph encoder is deployed to play together with a pre-trained LLM, the model can answer graph-related questions well. Existing solutions to graph-based prompts range from graph serialization to graph transformers. In this work, we show that the use of a parameter-free graph encoder based on Fock space representations, a concept borrowed from mathematical physics, is remarkably versatile in this problem setting. The simple construction, inherited directly from the theory with a few small adjustments, can provide rich and informative graph encodings, for a wide range of different graphs. We investigate the use of this idea for prefix-tuned prompts leveraging the capabilities of a pre-trained, frozen LLM. The modifications lead to a model that can answer graph-related questions -- from simple graphs to proteins to hypergraphs -- effectively and with minimal, if any, adjustments to the architecture. Our work significantly simplifies existing solutions and generalizes well to multiple different graph-based structures effortlessly.

paragraphs: Language models can answer questions about graphs when graph structure is represented in a suitable prompt. Designing that representation can involve specialized encoders tailored to particular graph types. FoGE investigates whether a simple construction inspired by Fock space, a mathematical framework from physics, can provide useful graph representations across a wider range of structures.

Its graph encoder has no learned parameters. With a few adjustments to the underlying mathematical construction, it produces encodings intended to retain rich structural information. The authors use these encodings in prefix-tuned prompts for a pretrained language model whose own parameters remain frozen. This separates graph representation from changes to the language model itself.

The resulting approach answers questions involving simple graphs, proteins, and hypergraphs effectively, with minimal architectural changes and sometimes none. The reported versatility matters because these structures need not all demand a separately designed prompting architecture. The paper's contribution is a simpler graph-encoding route that works across the investigated structures while drawing on the capabilities of an existing language model.
summary.tldr: FoGE uses a parameter-free graph encoder inspired by Fock space to support graph question answering with a frozen language model.

title: FoGE: Fock Space inspired encoding for graph prompting

abstract: Language models trained via outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) to reason using chain-of-thought (CoT) have shown remarkable performance. Monitoring such a model's CoT may allow us to understand its intentions and detect potential malicious behavior. However, to be effective, this requires that CoTs are legible and faithful. We evaluate the legibility of CoTs in state-of-the-art reasoning models. We find that R1, R1-Zero, and QwQ often produce illegible CoTs (mixing nonsensical phrases, random words, and non-English characters) before returning to perfect coherence in their final responses, while Claude models notably exhibit higher legibility. Across 14 models, we observe that larger models within the same training paradigm tend to produce more illegible reasoning. Prefill experiments show that truncating reasoning at a legibility threshold reduces accuracy by 53\%, suggesting that illegible portions contribute to performance despite being difficult to monitor. Illegibility increases with question difficulty, suggesting that CoT monitoring may be less reliable precisely when most needed. We discuss potential hypotheses for these results, including steganography, vestigial tokens, and training artifacts. Our findings suggest that current approaches to CoT monitoring may be vulnerable to the emergence of outcome-based RL, particularly as models face increasingly complex tasks.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether reasoning models' written chains of thought remain understandable enough to support monitoring. Such monitoring may help reveal intentions or detect problematic behavior, but it depends on reasoning traces being legible and faithful. The study focuses on legibility, including cases where confusing intermediate text precedes a coherent final answer.

Across 14 models, the authors find that R1, R1-Zero, and QwQ often produce traces containing nonsensical phrases, random words, and non-English characters, while Claude models show greater legibility. Within the same training paradigm, larger models tend to produce more illegible reasoning. Illegibility also increases with question difficulty, connecting the problem to more demanding tasks.

In prefill experiments, cutting reasoning off at a legibility threshold reduces accuracy by 53%. This suggests that difficult-to-read portions contribute to performance. The authors discuss possible explanations, including steganography, vestigial tokens, and training artifacts, without establishing one as the cause. The findings raise a qualified concern that chain-of-thought monitoring may become less reliable as outcome-trained models tackle increasingly complex problems.
summary.tldr: Some reasoning models produce illegible intermediate text that appears useful for accuracy, potentially weakening chain-of-thought monitoring.

title: Reasoning Models Sometimes Output Illegible Chains of Thought

abstract: Score-based Generative Models (SGMs) have achieved impressive performance in data generation across a wide range of applications and benefit from strong theoretical guarantees. Recently, methods inspired by statistical mechanics, in particular, Hamiltonian dynamics, have introduced Critically-damped Langevin Diffusions (CLDs), which define diffusion processes on extended spaces by coupling the data with auxiliary variables. These approaches, along with their associated score-matching and sampling procedures, have been shown to outperform standard diffusion-based samplers numerically. In this paper, we analyze a generalized dynamic that extends classical CLDs by introducing an additional hyperparameter controlling the noise applied to the data coordinate, thereby better exploiting the extended space. We further derive a novel upper bound on the sampling error of CLD-based generative models in the Wasserstein metric. This additional hyperparameter influences the smoothness of sample paths, and our discretization error analysis provides practical guidance for its tuning, leading to improved sampling performance.

paragraphs: Critically damped Langevin diffusion models extend a generative process by coupling data coordinates with auxiliary variables. Inspired by Hamiltonian dynamics, these methods have shown numerical advantages over standard diffusion samplers. This paper studies a generalized version of those dynamics, aiming to understand sampling error and how the extended space can be used more effectively.

The generalization adds a hyperparameter controlling the noise applied directly to the data coordinate. This parameter affects the smoothness of sample paths, making it relevant to the behavior of the continuous process and its numerical approximation. The authors derive a new upper bound on sampling error measured in the Wasserstein metric, which compares generated and target distributions.

Their discretization analysis connects the added parameter to errors arising when continuous dynamics are implemented through numerical steps. This connection supplies practical guidance for choosing the parameter and leads to improved sampling performance. The contribution therefore combines a more flexible diffusion process with a theoretical analysis that informs a concrete sampling-design choice.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds sampling error for generalized critically damped Langevin diffusions and uses discretization analysis to guide noise-parameter tuning.

title: Wasserstein Convergence of Critically Damped Langevin Diffusions

abstract: Searching through chemical space is an exceptionally challenging problem because the number of possible molecules grows combinatorially with the number of atoms. Large, autoregressive models trained on databases of chemical compounds have yielded powerful generators, but we still lack robust strategies for generating molecules with desired properties. This molecular search problem closely resembles the "alignment" problem for large language models, though for many chemical tasks we have a specific and easily evaluable reward function. Here, we introduce an algorithm called energy rank alignment (ERA) that leverages an explicit reward function to produce a gradient-based objective that we use to optimize autoregressive policies. We show theoretically that this algorithm is closely related to proximal policy optimization (PPO) and direct preference optimization (DPO), but has a minimizer that converges to an ideal Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution with the reward playing the role of an energy function. Furthermore, this algorithm is highly scalable, does not require reinforcement learning, and performs well relative to DPO when the number of preference observations per pairing is small. We deploy this approach to align molecular transformers and protein language models to generate molecules and protein sequences, respectively, with externally specified properties and find that it does so robustly, searching through diverse parts of chemical space.

paragraphs: Generating a chemically valid molecule is only part of molecular design: the molecule must also have desired properties. The search is difficult because possible structures multiply rapidly as atoms are added. This paper approaches that challenge as an alignment problem, using an explicit reward function to steer an autoregressive generator toward externally specified goals.

The proposed energy rank alignment algorithm, ERA, converts that reward into an objective suitable for gradient-based optimization without requiring reinforcement learning. The authors establish theoretical connections to proximal policy optimization and direct preference optimization. They also show that the objective's minimizer converges to an ideal Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution, with the reward acting as an energy function that shapes which outputs are favored.

The authors apply ERA to molecular transformers and protein language models, reporting robust generation with requested properties while exploring diverse regions of chemical space. They also report favorable performance relative to direct preference optimization when each pairing has few preference observations. Together, these findings support using explicit, evaluable rewards to guide chemical generation while retaining diversity.
summary.tldr: ERA uses explicit rewards to align molecular and protein generators toward desired properties through a scalable objective that does not require reinforcement learning.

title: Aligning Transformers with Continuous Feedback via Energy Rank Alignment

abstract: The Schrödinger bridge problem seeks the optimal stochastic process that connects two given probability distributions with minimal energy modification. While the Sinkhorn algorithm is widely used to solve the static optimal transport problem, a recent work (Pooladian and Niles-Weed, 2024) proposed the *Sinkhorn bridge*, which estimates Schrödinger bridges by plugging optimal transport into the time-dependent drifts of SDEs, with statistical guarantees in the one-sample estimation setting where the true source distribution is fully accessible. In this work, to further justify this method, we study the statistical performance of intermediate Sinkhorn iterations in the two-sample estimation setting, where only finite samples from both source and target distributions are available. Specifically, we establish a statistical bound on the squared total variation error of Sinkhorn bridge iterations: $\mathcal{O}(1/m+1/n + r^{2k})~(r \in (0,1))$, where $m$ and $n$ are the sample sizes from the source and target distributions, respectively, and $k$ is the number of Sinkhorn iterations. This result provides a theoretical guarantee for the finite-sample performance of the Schrödinger bridge estimator and offers practical guidance for selecting sample sizes and the number of Sinkhorn iterations. Notably, our theoretical results apply to several representative methods such as [SF]$^2$M, DSBM-IMF, BM2, and lightSB(-M) under specific settings, through the previously unnoticed connection between these estimators.

paragraphs: A Schrödinger bridge connects two probability distributions through a stochastic process with minimal energy modification. The Sinkhorn bridge estimates such a process using optimal transport inside time-dependent stochastic dynamics. This paper studies the practical setting where neither endpoint distribution is fully known and only finite samples from each are available.

The main result bounds squared total variation error at intermediate Sinkhorn iterations by O(1/m + 1/n + r^(2k)), where m and n are endpoint sample sizes, k is the iteration count, and r lies between zero and one. The expression separates finite-sample contributions from a term that decreases geometrically as the algorithm runs.

This separation gives guidance on allocating effort: more iterations reduce the iteration term, while larger datasets reduce the sampling terms. The authors also identify connections that extend their results to several representative bridge estimators under specific settings. The contribution supplies finite-sample justification for partially completed Sinkhorn computations and clarifies how data quantity and iteration count jointly affect the statistical guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds Sinkhorn bridge estimation error using both endpoint sample sizes and the number of algorithm iterations.

title: Statistical Analysis of the Sinkhorn Iterations for Two-Sample Schr\"{o}dinger Bridge Estimation

abstract: When applicants get rejected by a high-stakes algorithmic decision system, recourse explanations provide actionable suggestions for applicants on how to change their input features to get a positive evaluation. A crucial yet overlooked phenomenon is that recourse explanations are *performative*: When many applicants act according to their recommendations, their collective behavior may shift the data distribution and, once the model is refitted, also the decision boundary. Consequently, the recourse algorithm may render its own recommendations *invalid*, such that applicants who make the effort of implementing their recommendations may be rejected again when they reapply. In this work, we formally characterize the conditions under which recourse explanations remain valid under their own performative effects. In particular, we prove that recourse actions may become invalid if they are influenced by or if they intervene on non-causal variables. Based on this analysis, we caution against the use of standard counterfactual explanations and causal recourse methods, and instead advocate for recourse methods that recommend actions exclusively on causal variables.

paragraphs: Recourse explanations tell people rejected by an algorithm what they could change to receive a positive decision. This paper examines a feedback problem: when many people follow that advice, their collective actions can alter the data used to retrain the decision model. The resulting decision boundary may move, leaving people rejected again despite having made the recommended changes.

The authors formally characterize conditions under which recourse remains valid after these effects occur. Their analysis shows that recommendations may become invalid when they depend on non-causal variables or instruct people to change them. The concern therefore involves both the information used to choose an action and the variables the action directly changes.

Based on this analysis, the authors caution against standard counterfactual explanations and causal recourse methods, and advocate recommendations acting exclusively on causal variables. The result identifies a possible failure mechanism, rather than asserting that every recommendation involving a non-causal variable must fail. It makes the consequences of collective compliance and subsequent retraining central to evaluating whether recourse advice remains useful.
summary.tldr: Recourse advice can invalidate itself after collective behavior changes and model retraining, particularly when non-causal variables influence recommended actions.

title: Performative Validity of Recourse Explanations

abstract: Detecting AI-involved text is essential for combating misinformation, plagiarism, and academic misconduct. However, AI text generation includes diverse collaborative processes (AI-written text edited by humans, human-written text edited by AI, and AI-generated text refined by other AI), where various or even new LLMs could be involved. Texts generated through these varied processes exhibit complex characteristics, presenting significant challenges for detection. Current methods model these processes rather crudely, primarily employing binary classification (purely human vs. AI-involved) or multi-classification (treating human-AI collaboration as a new class). We observe that representations of texts generated through different processes exhibit inherent clustering relationships. Therefore, we propose DETree, a novel approach that models the relationships among different processes as a Hierarchical Affinity Tree structure, and introduces a specialized loss function that aligns text representations with this tree. To facilitate this learning, we developed RealBench, a comprehensive benchmark dataset that automatically incorporates a wide spectrum of hybrid texts produced through various human-AI collaboration processes. Our method improves performance in hybrid text detection tasks and significantly enhances robustness and generalization in out-of-distribution scenarios, particularly in few-shot learning conditions, further demonstrating the promise of training-based approaches in OOD settings. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/heyongxin233/DETree.

paragraphs: Text can involve AI in several ways: a person may edit an AI draft, an AI may revise human writing, or one AI may refine another’s output. These processes produce different but related textual characteristics. DETree addresses the difficulty of detecting such mixtures, including cases involving unfamiliar language models.

The authors observe clustering relationships among representations of texts produced through different processes. They organize those relationships into a Hierarchical Affinity Tree and introduce a loss function that trains text representations to follow its structure. This gives the detector a richer description of collaboration than either a human-versus-AI label or a single additional category for mixed authorship.

To support this training, the authors build RealBench, a benchmark that automatically incorporates a broad range of hybrid texts. They report improved hybrid-text detection and stronger robustness and generalization outside the training distribution, particularly when few examples are available. The findings suggest that explicitly learning relationships among production processes can help trained detectors handle more varied forms of AI involvement.
summary.tldr: DETree organizes relationships among human–AI writing processes into a hierarchy to improve hybrid-text detection and generalization.

title: DETree: DEtecting Human-AI Collaborative Texts via Tree-Structured Hierarchical Representation Learning

abstract: We introduce UniGen, a unified multimodal large language model (MLLM) capable of image understanding and generation. We study the full training pipeline of UniGen from a data-centric perspective, including multi-stage pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and direct preference optimization. More importantly, we propose a new Chain-of-Thought Verification (CoT-V) strategy for test-time scaling, which significantly boosts UniGen’s image generation quality using a simple Best-of-N test-time strategy. Specifically, CoT-V enables UniGen to act as both image generator and verifier at test time, assessing the semantic alignment between a text prompt and its generated image in a step-by-step CoT manner. Trained entirely on open-source datasets across all stages, UniGen achieves state-of-the-art performance on a range of image understanding and generation benchmarks, with a final score of 0.78 on GenEval and 85.19 on DPG-Bench. Through extensive ablation studies, our work provides actionable insights and addresses key challenges in the full life cycle of building unified MLLMs, contributing meaningful directions to future research.

paragraphs: UniGen is a single multimodal language model designed for both understanding images and generating them. The paper studies its full training process from a data-centered perspective, covering multiple pretraining stages, supervised fine-tuning, and direct preference optimization. All training stages use open-source datasets, making the data choices part of the overall contribution.

The authors also introduce Chain-of-Thought Verification, a method for improving generation through additional computation at test time. UniGen generates candidate images and then serves as its own verifier, assessing step by step how well each image matches the meaning of the text prompt. This assessment supports a Best-of-N selection strategy, connecting the model’s understanding ability to its generation ability.

The model achieves reported state-of-the-art results across a range of image-understanding and image-generation benchmarks, including 0.78 on GenEval and 85.19 on DPG-Bench. Verification significantly improves generation quality in the reported evaluations. Extensive ablations examine the training and test-time choices, providing evidence about building a unified system across its full development process rather than considering generation and understanding separately.
summary.tldr: UniGen combines open-data multimodal training with self-verification of candidate images to improve unified understanding and generation.

title: UniGen: Enhanced Training & Test-Time Strategies for Unified Multimodal Understanding and Generation

abstract: Starting from flow- and diffusion-based transformers, Multi-modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have reshaped text-to-vision generation, gaining acclaim for exceptional visual fidelity. As these models advance, users continually push the boundary with imaginative or rare prompts, which advanced models still falter in generating, since their concepts are often too scarce to leave a strong imprint during pre-training. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective intervention that surfaces rare semantics inside MM-DiTs without additional training steps, data, denoising-time optimization, or reliance on external modules (e.g., large language models). In particular, the joint-attention mechanism intrinsic to MM-DiT sequentially updates text embeddings alongside image embeddings throughout transformer blocks. We find that by mathematically expanding representational basins around text token embeddings via variance scale-up before the joint-attention blocks, rare semantics clearly emerge in MM-DiT’s outputs. Furthermore, our results generalize effectively across text-to-vision tasks, including text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-driven image editing. Our work invites generative models to reveal the semantics that users intend, once hidden yet ready to surface.

paragraphs: Text-to-vision models can produce highly realistic outputs while struggling to express unusual concepts in a prompt. This paper investigates whether rare meanings can be brought out through a small intervention inside multimodal diffusion transformers. The method requires no additional training, new data, denoising-time optimization, or external language model.

The intervention targets the text embeddings processed by joint-attention blocks. In these models, text and image embeddings are updated together throughout the transformer. The authors increase the variance of text-token embeddings before joint attention, describing this as expanding the representational regions around those tokens. They find that this adjustment makes rare semantics more apparent in generated outputs.

The reported results extend across text-to-image generation, text-to-video generation, and text-guided image editing. This suggests that the intervention addresses a mechanism shared across several text-conditioned visual tasks. The contribution is a way to expose meanings already represented within the model through a change to its internal text representations, with demonstrated improvements across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Scaling text-embedding variance before joint attention helps multimodal diffusion transformers express rare prompt concepts without additional training.

title: Rare Text Semantics Were Always There in Your Diffusion Transformer

abstract: Causality discovery without manipulation is considered a crucial problem to a variety of applications, such as genetic therapy. The state-of-the-art solutions, e.g. LiNGAM, return accurate results when the number of labeled samples is larger than the number of variables. These approaches are thus applicable only when large numbers of samples are available or the problem domain is sufficiently small. Motivated by the observations of the local sparsity properties on causal structures, we propose a general Split-and-Merge strategy, named SADA, to enhance the scalability of a wide class of causality discovery algorithms. SADA is able to accurately identify the causal variables, even when the sample size is significantly smaller than the number of variables. In SADA, the variables are partitioned into subsets, by finding cuts on the sparse probabilistic graphical model over the variables. By running mainstream causation discovery algorithms, e.g. LiNGAM, on the subproblems, complete causality can be reconstructed by combining all the partial results. SADA benefits from the recursive division technique, since each small subproblem generates more accurate result under the same number of samples. We theoretically prove that SADA always reduces the scale of problems without significant sacrifice on result accuracy, depending only on the local sparsity condition over the variables. Experiments on real-world datasets verify the improvements on scalability and accuracy by applying SADA on top of existing causation algorithms.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships without manipulating variables becomes difficult when there are fewer samples than variables. The paper describes existing methods whose accuracy depends on having sufficiently many samples relative to the problem size. SADA addresses this challenge by reducing the number of variables handled together while retaining the available samples.

Its split-and-merge strategy partitions variables by finding cuts in a sparse probabilistic graphical model. Existing causal-discovery algorithms then solve the smaller subproblems, and their partial results are combined to reconstruct the full causal structure. Recursive division makes each local problem smaller, allowing the same sample collection to support more accurate local estimation.

The theoretical guarantee depends on a local sparsity condition: under that condition, SADA reduces problem scale without a significant sacrifice in accuracy. The paper also reports accurate identification when samples are substantially fewer than variables. Experiments on real datasets show improvements in scalability and accuracy when SADA is added to existing algorithms, supporting its role as a framework for extending their usable scale.
summary.tldr: SADA uses locally sparse structure to split causal-discovery problems into smaller tasks, improving reported scalability and accuracy.

title: SADA: A General Framework to Support Robust Causation Discovery

abstract: Sum-product networks (SPNs) are a deep probabilistic representation that allows for efficient, exact inference. SPNs generalize many other tractable models, including thin junction trees, latent tree models, and many types of mixtures. Previous work on learning SPN structure has mainly focused on using top-down or bottom-up clustering to find mixtures, which capture variable interactions indirectly through implicit latent variables. In contrast, most work on learning graphical models, thin junction trees, and arithmetic circuits has focused on finding direct interactions among variables. In this paper, we present ID-SPN, a new algorithm for learning SPN structure that unifies the two approaches. In experiments on 20 benchmark datasets, we find that the combination of direct and indirect interactions leads to significantly better accuracy than several state-of-the-art algorithms for learning SPNs and other tractable models.

title: Learning Sum-Product Networks with Direct and Indirect Variable Interactions

abstract: Although recent work in non-linear dimensionality reduction investigates multiple choices of divergence measure during optimization \citeyang2013icml,bunte2012neuro, little work discusses the direct effects that divergence measures have on visualization. We study this relationship, theoretically and through an empirical analysis over 10 datasets. Our works shows how the αand βparameters of the generalized alpha-beta divergence can be chosen to discover hidden macro-structures (categories, e.g. birds) or micro-structures (fine-grained classes, e.g. toucans). Our method, which generalizes t-SNE \citetsne, allows us to discover such structure without extensive grid searches over (α, β) due to our theoretical analysis: such structure is apparent with particular choices of (α, β) that generalize across datasets. We also discuss efficient parallel CPU and GPU schemes which are non-trivial due to the tree-structures employed in optimization and the large datasets that do not fully fit into GPU memory. Our method runs 20x faster than the fastest published code \citefmm. We conclude with detailed case studies on the following very large datasets: ILSVRC 2012, a standard computer vision dataset with 1.2M images; SUSY, a particle physics dataset with 5M instances; and HIGGS, another particle physics dataset with 11M instances. This represents the largest published visualization attained by SNE methods. We have open-sourced our visualization code: \texttthttp://rll.berkeley.edu/absne/.

summary.tldr: A generalization of t-SNE uses alpha-beta divergence parameters to reveal broad or fine-grained structure while supporting large-scale visualization.

title: Alpha-Beta Divergences Discover Micro and Macro Structures in Data

abstract: Gaussian vector autoregressive (VAR) processes have been extensively studied in the literature. However, Gaussian assumptions are stringent for heavy-tailed time series that frequently arises in finance and economics. In this paper, we develop a unified framework for modeling and estimating heavy-tailed VAR processes. In particular, we generalize the Gaussian VAR model by an elliptical VAR model that naturally accommodates heavy-tailed time series. Under this model, we develop a quantile-based robust estimator for the transition matrix of the VAR process. We show that the proposed estimator achieves parametric rates of convergence in high dimensions. This is the first work in analyzing heavy-tailed high dimensional VAR processes. As an application of the proposed framework, we investigate Granger causality in the elliptical VAR process, and show that the robust transition matrix estimator induces sign-consistent estimators of Granger causality. The empirical performance of the proposed methodology is demonstrated by both synthetic and real data. We show that the proposed estimator is robust to heavy tails, and exhibit superior performance in stock price prediction.
