paragraphs: Vector autoregressive models describe how several time series evolve together through a transition matrix. Gaussian assumptions can be restrictive when observations have heavy tails, as often occurs in finance and economics. This paper introduces an elliptical VAR model that extends the Gaussian formulation to accommodate such data.

Within that model, the authors develop a robust transition-matrix estimator based on quantiles. They prove parametric convergence rates in high dimensions, providing a theoretical account of how accurately the matrix can be estimated as data accumulate. The framework therefore addresses both a broader model of temporal variation and a method for estimating its dynamics.

The paper also studies Granger causality within the elliptical VAR setting. It shows that the robust transition estimator yields sign-consistent estimators of those relationships, preserving the relevant signs under the stated theoretical result. Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate robustness to heavy tails and superior stock-price prediction performance. These findings concern the proposed model and evaluations, linking robust estimation to temporal interpretation and prediction.
summary.tldr: An elliptical VAR model and quantile-based estimator support robust high-dimensional time-series estimation and Granger-causality analysis.

title: Robust Estimation of Transition Matrices in High Dimensional Heavy-tailed Vector Autoregressive Processes

abstract: We propose an efficient method for approximating natural gradient descent in neural networks which we call Kronecker-factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC). K-FAC is based on an efficiently invertible approximation of a neural network’s Fisher information matrix which is neither diagonal nor low-rank, and in some cases is completely non-sparse. It is derived by approximating various large blocks of the Fisher (corresponding to entire layers) as being the Kronecker product of two much smaller matrices. While only several times more expensive to compute than the plain stochastic gradient, the updates produced by K-FAC make much more progress optimizing the objective, which results in an algorithm that can be much faster than stochastic gradient descent with momentum in practice. And unlike some previously proposed approximate natural-gradient/Newton methods which use high-quality non-diagonal curvature matrices (such as Hessian-free optimization), K-FAC works very well in highly stochastic optimization regimes. This is because the cost of storing and inverting K-FAC’s approximation to the curvature matrix does not depend on the amount of data used to estimate it, which is a feature typically associated only with diagonal or low-rank approximations to the curvature matrix.

paragraphs: Natural-gradient optimization uses the Fisher information matrix to shape neural-network updates, but handling that matrix efficiently is a major computational challenge. K-FAC addresses this by approximating large blocks associated with entire layers as Kronecker products of two much smaller matrices. This structure makes the approximation efficiently invertible while retaining relationships beyond a diagonal representation.

The resulting curvature approximation is neither diagonal nor low-rank and can even be fully non-sparse. The authors report that computing an update costs only several times as much as an ordinary stochastic gradient, while each update makes substantially more progress on the objective. That tradeoff can make K-FAC much faster in practice than SGD with momentum.

The method also performs well in highly stochastic optimization regimes. A central explanation is that the storage and inversion costs of its curvature approximation do not depend on how much data is used to estimate it. K-FAC therefore combines a richer curvature representation with a cost property often associated with simpler approximations, supporting useful updates even when estimates use limited data.
summary.tldr: K-FAC uses Kronecker-factored Fisher approximations to make natural-gradient neural-network training computationally practical.

title: Optimizing Neural Networks with Kronecker-factored Approximate Curvature

abstract: We introduce anytime Explore-m, a pure exploration problem for multi-armed bandits (MAB) that requires making a prediction of the top-m arms at every time step. Anytime Explore-m is more practical than fixed budget or fixed confidence formulations of the top-m problem, since many applications involve a finite, but unpredictable, budget. However, the development and analysis of anytime algorithms present many challenges. We propose AT-LUCB (AnyTime Lower and Upper Confidence Bound), the first nontrivial algorithm that provably solves anytime Explore-m. Our analysis shows that the sample complexity of AT-LUCB is competitive to anytime variants of existing algorithms. Moreover, our empirical evaluation on AT-LUCB shows that AT-LUCB performs as well as or better than state-of-the-art baseline methods for anytime Explore-m.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit problem, a learner gathers observations from different options, called arms. This paper studies pure exploration: identifying the best options rather than focusing on rewards collected while learning. Its proposed anytime Explore-m problem requires a prediction of the best m arms at every step, so an answer remains available whenever exploration stops.

That requirement fits settings where the available budget is finite but its eventual size is unpredictable. A method designed around a predetermined budget or confidence target does not directly express this same requirement. The authors introduce AT-LUCB, an algorithm based on lower and upper confidence bounds, and establish that it provably solves the anytime problem.

Their analysis finds its sample complexity competitive with anytime versions of existing algorithms. Experiments also show performance matching or exceeding the compared leading baselines. These are complementary findings: the analysis supports its observation requirements, while the experiments show how it behaves in the evaluated settings where predictions must remain available throughout exploration.
summary.tldr: AT-LUCB identifies promising arms while maintaining a prediction of the best m options at every time step.

title: Anytime Exploration for Multi-armed Bandits using Confidence Information

abstract: We design a new nonparametric method that allows one to estimate the matrix of integrated kernels of a multivariate Hawkes process. This matrix not only encodes the mutual influences of each node of the process, but also disentangles the causality relationships between them. Our approach is the first that leads to an estimation of this matrix without any parametric modeling and estimation of the kernels themselves . A consequence is that it can give an estimation of causality relationships between nodes (or users), based on their activity timestamps (on a social network for instance), without knowing or estimating the shape of the activities lifetime. For that purpose, we introduce a moment matching method that fits the second-order and the third-order integrated cumulants of the process. A theoretical analysis allows to prove that this new estimation technique is consistent. Moreover, we show on numerical experiments that our approach is indeed very robust to the shape of the kernels, and gives appealing results on the MemeTracker database and on financial order book data.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover relationships among event streams modeled by a multivariate Hawkes process. Its target is the matrix of integrated kernels, which summarizes mutual influences among nodes and encodes causal relationships within the process. The observations can be activity timestamps, such as the times at which users act on a social network.

The authors propose estimating this matrix directly without specifying parametric kernel shapes or estimating the kernels themselves. Their method matches the process's second- and third-order integrated cumulants. This focuses estimation on the aggregate influence relationships, avoiding the need to know or reconstruct the detailed time course of each activity's influence.

A theoretical analysis proves consistency of the estimator. Numerical experiments show robustness to kernel shape, and the paper reports appealing results on MemeTracker and financial order book data. The central contribution is a nonparametric route from timestamp data to the Hawkes process's influence matrix, with both a consistency result and empirical support for reducing dependence on assumptions about kernel shape.
summary.tldr: A consistent moment-matching method estimates Hawkes influence relationships directly from timestamps without estimating kernel shapes.

title: Uncovering Causality from Multivariate Hawkes Integrated Cumulants

abstract: We consider the online one-class collaborative filtering (CF) problem that consist of recommending items to users over time in an online fashion based on positive ratings only. This problem arises when users respond only occasionally to a recommendation with a positive rating, and never with a negative one. We study the impact of the probability of a user responding to a recommendation, $p_f$, on the sample complexity, and ask whether receiving positive and negative ratings, instead of positive ratings only, improves the sample complexity. Both questions arise in the design of recommender systems. We introduce a simple probabilistic user model, and analyze the performance of an online user-based CF algorithm. We prove that after an initial cold start phase, where recommendations are invested in exploring the user’s preferences, this algorithm makes—up to a fraction of the recommendations required for updating the user’s preferences—perfect recommendations. The number of ratings required for the cold start phase is nearly proportional to $1/p_f$, and that for updating the user’s preferences is essentially independent of $p_f$. As a consequence we find that, receiving positive and negative ratings instead of only positive ones improves the number of ratings required for initial exploration by a factor of $1/p_f$, which can be significant.

paragraphs: The paper studies online recommendation when users occasionally provide positive ratings and never provide negative ones. It asks how the response probability, p_f, affects the amount of feedback needed to learn preferences. It also examines the benefit of receiving both positive and negative ratings instead.

Under a simple probabilistic user model, the authors analyze a user-based collaborative filtering algorithm. After a cold-start phase devoted to exploring preferences, the algorithm makes perfect recommendations apart from a fraction used to update those preferences. The number of ratings needed for cold start is nearly proportional to 1/p_f, whereas the number needed for updates is essentially independent of p_f.

The analysis therefore separates the feedback burden of initial exploration from that of continued preference updating. It further shows that receiving both rating types improves the number of ratings required for initial exploration by a factor of 1/p_f. This can be a substantial benefit when responses are rare, within the assumptions of the analyzed user model.
summary.tldr: Under a probabilistic user model, sparse positive feedback mainly increases recommendation cold-start requirements, while preference-update requirements are largely unaffected.

title: The Sample Complexity of Online One-Class Collaborative Filtering

abstract: Motivated by applications in computational advertising and systems biology, we consider the problem of identifying the best out of several possible soft interventions at a source node $V$ in an acyclic causal directed graph, to maximize the expected value of a target node $Y$ (located downstream of $V$). Our setting imposes a fixed total budget for sampling under various interventions, along with cost constraints on different types of interventions. We pose this as a best arm identification bandit problem with $K$ arms, where each arm is a soft intervention at $V$ and leverage the information leakage among the arms to provide the first gap dependent error and simple regret bounds for this problem. Our results are a significant improvement over the traditional best arm identification results. We empirically show that our algorithms outperform the state of the art in the Flow Cytometry data-set, and also apply our algorithm for model interpretation of the Inception-v3 deep net that classifies images.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to choose among several soft interventions at one source node in an acyclic causal graph. The objective is to maximize the expected value of a downstream target node. Sampling has a fixed overall budget, and different intervention types also face cost constraints, making efficient use of observations essential.

The authors formulate the choice as a best-arm identification problem, with each intervention treated as an arm. Their approach uses information shared across interventions, so observations associated with one arm can inform comparisons involving others. Exploiting this information produces gap-dependent bounds on selection error and simple regret, improving on traditional best-arm identification results for this problem.

Experiments on a Flow Cytometry dataset show the algorithms outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The authors also apply the algorithm to interpreting the Inception-v3 image classifier. These applications accompany the theoretical contribution: accounting for relationships among interventions can improve how a limited sampling budget is used to identify a promising causal intervention.
summary.tldr: Sharing information across causal interventions improves best-intervention identification under sampling and cost constraints.

title: Identifying Best Interventions through Online Importance Sampling

abstract: Recent deep networks are capable of memorizing the entire data even when the labels are completely random. To overcome the overfitting on corrupted labels, we propose a novel technique of learning another neural network, called MentorNet, to supervise the training of the base deep networks, namely, StudentNet. During training, MentorNet provides a curriculum (sample weighting scheme) for StudentNet to focus on the sample the label of which is probably correct. Unlike the existing curriculum that is usually predefined by human experts, MentorNet learns a data-driven curriculum dynamically with StudentNet. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can significantly improve the generalization performance of deep networks trained on corrupted training data. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, we achieve the best-published result on WebVision, a large benchmark containing 2.2 million images of real-world noisy labels.

paragraphs: Deep networks can memorize training examples even when their labels are random, so fitting the training data does not necessarily mean learning useful patterns. MentorNet addresses this problem by adding a second neural network that supervises the training of the main network, called StudentNet. Its purpose is to reduce overfitting to corrupted labels.

MentorNet supplies a curriculum in the form of weights assigned to training samples. These weights encourage StudentNet to focus on examples whose labels are probably correct. The curriculum is learned from data and changes dynamically with StudentNet's training, giving the sample-weighting process an adaptive role instead of relying on a schedule predefined by human experts.

Experiments show that this approach can significantly improve generalization when deep networks train on corrupted data. The authors also report what, to their knowledge, was the best published result on WebVision, a benchmark containing 2.2 million images with real-world noisy labels. The evidence supports learning how strongly to trust training examples as part of the overall training process.
summary.tldr: MentorNet learns adaptive sample weights that help a student network generalize better from training data with corrupted labels.

title: MentorNet: Learning Data-Driven Curriculum for Very Deep Neural Networks on Corrupted Labels

abstract: We present an extension to the Tacotron speech synthesis architecture that learns a latent embedding space of prosody, derived from a reference acoustic representation containing the desired prosody. We show that conditioning Tacotron on this learned embedding space results in synthesized audio that matches the prosody of the reference signal with fine time detail even when the reference and synthesis speakers are different. Additionally, we show that a reference prosody embedding can be used to synthesize text that is different from that of the reference utterance. We define several quantitative and subjective metrics for evaluating prosody transfer, and report results with accompanying audio samples from single-speaker and 44-speaker Tacotron models on a prosody transfer task.

Additionally, we show that a reference prosody embedding can be used to synthesize text that is different from that of the reference utterance. paragraphs: Speech synthesis must capture how words are delivered as well as which words are spoken. This paper extends Tacotron so that a reference recording can supply the desired prosody. The system learns a latent embedding from an acoustic representation of that reference, then conditions speech generation on the learned embedding.

The authors show that synthesized speech can follow the reference prosody in fine temporal detail even when the reference speaker and the synthesis speaker differ. This means that the transferred delivery is not restricted to reproducing the same speaker. They also demonstrate synthesis of text different from the reference utterance, showing that a reference embedding can be reused beyond its original words.

The evaluation introduces quantitative and subjective measures of prosody transfer and includes audio examples from single-speaker and 44-speaker Tacotron models. Together, these results support using a learned reference representation to guide expressive speech synthesis across changes in speaker and text. The contribution is a mechanism for transferring aspects of delivery through a learned conditioning space.
summary.tldr: A reference-derived prosody embedding lets Tacotron transfer expressive delivery across speakers and to different text.

title: Towards End-to-End Prosody Transfer for Expressive Speech Synthesis with Tacotron

abstract: Large neural models have demonstrated human-level performance on language and vision benchmarks, while their performance degrades considerably on adversarial or out-of-distribution samples. This raises the question of whether these models have learned to solve a dataset rather than the underlying task by overfitting to spurious dataset biases. We investigate one recently proposed approach, AFLITE, which adversarially filters such dataset biases, as a means to mitigate the prevalent overestimation of machine performance. We provide a theoretical understanding for AFLITE, by situating it in the generalized framework for optimum bias reduction. We present extensive supporting evidence that AFLITE is broadly applicable for reduction of measurable dataset biases, and that models trained on the filtered datasets yield better generalization to out-of-distribution tasks. Finally, filtering results in a large drop in model performance (e.g., from 92% to 62% for SNLI), while human performance still remains high. Our work thus shows that such filtered datasets can pose new research challenges for robust generalization by serving as upgraded benchmarks.

paragraphs: High benchmark accuracy can give an inflated impression of a model's ability when the dataset contains convenient but misleading patterns. This paper investigates AFLITE, an adversarial filtering approach intended to reduce such biases. The motivating question is whether strong models have learned the underlying task or have become particularly effective at exploiting the dataset used to measure them.

The authors place AFLITE within a broader mathematical framework for optimal bias reduction, providing a theoretical account of the approach. They also present extensive empirical evidence that filtering reduces measurable biases across datasets. Models trained using the filtered data generalize better to tasks outside their training distribution in the reported evaluations.

Filtering also makes existing benchmarks substantially harder for models while leaving human performance high. On SNLI, the reported model performance drops from 92% to 62%. This combination matters because increased difficulty alone would not establish that a benchmark remains meaningful. The results support using filtered datasets as stronger tests of robust generalization and as a check on overly optimistic assessments of machine performance.
summary.tldr: AFLITE reduces measurable dataset biases, producing harder benchmarks and improving the reported generalization of models trained on filtered data.

title: Adversarial Filters of Dataset Biases

abstract: The performance of standard learning procedures has been observed to differ widely across groups. Recent studies usually attribute this loss discrepancy to an information deficiency for one group (e.g., one group has less data). In this work, we point to a more subtle source of loss discrepancy—feature noise. Our main result is that even when there is no information deficiency specific to one group (e.g., both groups have infinite data), adding the same amount of feature noise to all individuals leads to loss discrepancy. For linear regression, we thoroughly characterize the effect of feature noise on loss discrepancy in terms of the amount of noise, the difference between moments of the two groups, and whether group information is used or not. We then show this loss discrepancy does not vanish immediately if a shift in distribution causes the groups to have similar moments. On three real-world datasets, we show feature noise increases the loss discrepancy if groups have different distributions, while it does not affect the loss discrepancy on datasets where groups have similar distributions.

For linear regression, we thoroughly characterize the effect of feature noise on loss discrepancy in terms of the amount of noise, the difference between moments of the two groups, and whether group information is used or not. On three real-world datasets, we show feature noise increases the loss discrepancy if groups have different distributions, while it does not affect the loss discrepancy on datasets where groups have similar distributions.

paragraphs: Performance gaps between groups are often explained by one group having less useful training information. This paper identifies another mechanism: noise in the input features. It shows that equal amounts of feature noise can produce unequal losses even without a group-specific information shortage, including situations where both groups have infinite data.

For linear regression, the authors characterize how this discrepancy depends on noise magnitude, differences in the groups' distributional moments, and whether the model uses group information. This connects unequal outcomes to the interaction between noisy measurements and underlying group distributions. They also show that the discrepancy need not disappear immediately after a distribution shift makes those moments similar.

Results on three real-world datasets support the importance of distributional differences. Adding feature noise increases loss discrepancy when group distributions differ, while the reported datasets with similar distributions show no change in discrepancy. The findings identify feature quality as a source of unequal performance that additional data alone does not necessarily resolve.
summary.tldr: Equal feature noise can produce unequal group losses even with unlimited data, with the effect depending on group distributions.

title: Feature Noise Induces Loss Discrepancy Across Groups

abstract: Graph representation learning serves as the core of important prediction tasks, ranging from product recommendation to fraud detection. Real-life graphs usually have complex information in the local neighborhood, where each node is described by a rich set of features and connects to dozens or even hundreds of neighbors. Despite the success of neighborhood aggregation in graph neural networks, task-irrelevant information is mixed into nodes’ neighborhood, making learned models suffer from sub-optimal generalization performance. In this paper, we present NeuralSparse, a supervised graph sparsification technique that improves generalization power by learning to remove potentially task-irrelevant edges from input graphs. Our method takes both structural and non-structural information as input, utilizes deep neural networks to parameterize sparsification processes, and optimizes the parameters by feedback signals from downstream tasks. Under the NeuralSparse framework, supervised graph sparsification could seamlessly connect with existing graph neural networks for more robust performance. Experimental results on both benchmark and private datasets show that NeuralSparse can yield up to 7.2% improvement in testing accuracy when working with existing graph neural networks on node classification tasks.

Rich node features and many connections do not ensure that every edge helps. This paper proposes NeuralSparse, a supervised method that learns which potentially irrelevant edges to remove before they affect graph-based learning.

The sparsification process is parameterized by deep neural networks and uses both structural and non-structural information. Feedback from the downstream task trains those parameters, making edge removal responsive to the prediction objective. NeuralSparse can connect with existing graph neural networks, so the learned sparsification becomes part of how those models obtain useful neighborhood information.

Experiments on benchmark and private datasets show test-accuracy improvements of up to 7.2% for node classification when NeuralSparse is combined with existing graph neural networks. That figure is a reported maximum, rather than a gain promised for every dataset or model. The findings support the idea that selectively removing connections can improve generalization when neighborhood information includes task-irrelevant content.
summary.tldr: NeuralSparse learns task-guided edge removal to improve graph neural network generalization.

title: Robust Graph Representation Learning via Neural Sparsification

abstract: An open question in systems and computational neuroscience is how neural circuits accumulate evidence towards a decision. Fitting models of decision-making theory to neural activity helps answer this question, but current approaches limit the number of these models that we can fit to neural data. Here we propose a general framework for modeling neural activity during decision-making. The framework includes the canonical drift-diffusion model and enables extensions such as multi-dimensional accumulators, variable and collapsing boundaries, and discrete jumps. Our framework is based on constraining the parameters of recurrent state space models, for which we introduce a scalable variational Laplace EM inference algorithm. We applied the modeling approach to spiking responses recorded from monkey parietal cortex during two decision-making tasks. We found that a two-dimensional accumulator better captured the responses of a set of parietal neurons than a single accumulator model, and we identified a variable lower boundary in the responses of a parietal neuron during a random dot motion task. We expect this framework will be useful for modeling neural dynamics in a variety of decision-making settings.

Existing fitting approaches restrict which decision theories researchers can investigate. This paper introduces a recurrent state space framework that accommodates several theories within a common modeling approach, making a wider range of explanations accessible to analysis.

The framework includes the standard drift-diffusion model and supports multiple evidence accumulators, changing decision boundaries, and discrete jumps. These alternatives are expressed through constraints on model parameters. The authors also introduce a scalable variational Laplace EM algorithm for fitting the models, connecting the broader modeling language to a practical inference procedure.

Applied to monkey parietal cortex recordings from two decision tasks, a two-dimensional accumulator described a set of neurons better than a single accumulator. The analysis also identified a variable lower boundary in one neuron's responses during a random dot motion task. These findings support the usefulness of richer decision models for those recordings; broader usefulness across decision settings remains the authors' expectation.
summary.tldr: A flexible state space framework fits richer evidence-accumulation models to neural recordings and reveals structure missed by simpler models in the studied data.

title: A general recurrent state space framework for modeling neural dynamics during decision-making

abstract: Feature attribution is often loosely presented as the process of selecting a subset of relevant features as a rationale of a prediction. Task-dependent by nature, precise definitions of "relevance" encountered in the literature are however not always consistent. This lack of clarity stems from the fact that we usually do not have access to any notion of ground-truth attribution and from a more general debate on what good interpretations are. In this paper we propose to formalise feature selection/attribution based on the concept of relaxed functional dependence. In particular, we extend our notions to the instance-wise setting and derive necessary properties for candidate selection solutions, while leaving room for task-dependence. By computing ground-truth attributions on synthetic datasets, we evaluate many state-of-the-art attribution methods and show that, even when optimised, some fail to verify the proposed properties and provide wrong solutions.

paragraphs: Feature attribution aims to identify inputs relevant to a prediction, but relevance does not always have a consistent meaning across methods. Evaluation is also difficult when there is no known correct attribution. This paper addresses those problems by giving feature selection and attribution a formal foundation based on relaxed functional dependence.

The authors extend the framework to explanations of individual instances and derive necessary properties for candidate feature selections. Their formulation still allows relevance to depend on the task. This matters because a rigorous evaluation need not impose one identical notion of explanation on every application; it can specify required properties while preserving task-specific choices.

The paper constructs ground-truth attributions on synthetic datasets and uses them to evaluate several leading attribution methods. Some methods produce incorrect selections and fail the proposed properties even after optimization. The finding concerns those methods under the paper's formal criteria and synthetic evaluations. Its broader contribution is to make attribution claims testable against explicit requirements, providing a clearer basis for judging whether selected features form an acceptable explanation.
summary.tldr: A formal account of feature relevance enables ground-truth attribution tests that expose failures in some leading explanation methods.

title: Towards Rigorous Interpretations: a Formalisation of Feature Attribution

abstract: In recent years, federated learning has been embraced as an approach for bringing about collaboration across large populations of learning agents. However, little is known about how collaboration protocols should take agents’ incentives into account when allocating individual resources for communal learning in order to maintain such collaborations. Inspired by game theoretic notions, this paper introduces a framework for incentive-aware learning and data sharing in federated learning. Our stable and envy-free equilibria capture notions of collaboration in the presence of agents interested in meeting their learning objectives while keeping their own sample collection burden low. For example, in an envy-free equilibrium, no agent would wish to swap their sampling burden with any other agent and in a stable equilibrium, no agent would wish to unilaterally reduce their sampling burden. In addition to formalizing this framework, our contributions include characterizing the structural properties of such equilibria, proving when they exist, and showing how they can be computed. Furthermore, we compare the sample complexity of incentive-aware collaboration with that of optimal collaboration when one ignores agents’ incentives.

paragraphs: Federated learning enables agents to collaborate, but that collaboration depends on how the work of collecting data is shared. Each agent may want to achieve a learning objective while contributing as few samples as possible. This paper develops a framework that makes those incentives explicit when deciding how individual sampling effort supports communal learning.

The framework defines two equilibrium notions. In a stable equilibrium, no agent wants to reduce its own sampling burden unilaterally. In an envy-free equilibrium, no agent wants to exchange its sampling burden with another agent. These notions capture different reasons a contribution arrangement might be acceptable to its participants, linking learning requirements with incentives around data collection.

The authors characterize structural properties of these equilibria, establish conditions for their existence, and show how to compute them. They also compare the sample complexity of incentive-aware collaboration with optimal collaboration that ignores incentives. This comparison provides a way to assess how accounting for participants' preferences affects the total data requirements of a collaborative learning arrangement.
summary.tldr: An incentive-aware federated-learning framework analyzes stable and envy-free allocations of data-collection effort and their sample requirements.

title: One for One, or All for All: Equilibria and Optimality of Collaboration in Federated Learning

abstract: We consider the task of learning to control a linear dynamical system under fixed quadratic costs, known as the Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) problem. While model-free approaches are often favorable in practice, thus far only model-based methods, which rely on costly system identification, have been shown to achieve regret that scales with the optimal dependence on the time horizon T. We present the first model-free algorithm that achieves similar regret guarantees. Our method relies on an efficient policy gradient scheme, and a novel and tighter analysis of the cost of exploration in policy space in this setting.

paragraphs: The linear quadratic regulator problem asks how to control a linear dynamical system when costs are fixed quadratic functions. This paper studies learning that control policy online. The central performance question is how regret grows with the time horizon as the learner explores and improves its decisions.

Previously, the optimal dependence on the time horizon had been established only for model-based methods, which require costly system identification. The authors present a model-free algorithm with comparable regret guarantees, achieving square-root dependence on the horizon. This establishes that obtaining that time scaling does not require the model-based route in the studied LQR setting.

The method uses an efficient policy gradient scheme together with a new, tighter analysis of exploration costs in policy space. That analysis matters because trying alternative policies contributes to the cost of learning. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and theoretical: a direct policy-learning procedure and an accounting of exploration sharp enough to support the stated regret guarantee.
summary.tldr: An efficient model-free policy gradient method achieves square-root-horizon regret for learning linear quadratic control.

title: Online Policy Gradient for Model Free Learning of Linear Quadratic Regulators with $\sqrt$T Regret

abstract: Anomaly estimation, or the problem of finding a subset of a dataset that differs from the rest of the dataset, is a classic problem in machine learning and data mining. In both theoretical work and in applications, the anomaly is assumed to have a specific structure defined by membership in an anomaly family. For example, in temporal data the anomaly family may be time intervals, while in network data the anomaly family may be connected subgraphs. The most prominent approach for anomaly estimation is to compute the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) of the anomaly; however, it was recently observed that for normally distributed data, the MLE is a biased estimator for some anomaly families. In this work, we demonstrate that in the normal means setting, the bias of the MLE depends on the size of the anomaly family. We prove that if the number of sets in the anomaly family that contain the anomaly is sub-exponential, then the MLE is asymptotically unbiased. We also provide empirical evidence that the converse is true: if the number of such sets is exponential, then the MLE is asymptotically biased. Our analysis unifies a number of earlier results on the bias of the MLE for specific anomaly families. Next, we derive a new anomaly estimator using a mixture model, and we prove that our anomaly estimator is asymptotically unbiased regardless of the size of the anomaly family. We illustrate the advantages of our estimator versus the MLE on disease outbreak data and highway traffic data.

paragraphs: Structured anomaly estimation searches for an unusual subset within a permitted family, such as time intervals or connected network regions. Maximum likelihood is a prominent way to choose that subset, but it can be biased for normally distributed data. This paper studies how that bias relates to the number of candidate sets containing the true anomaly.

In the normal-means setting, the authors prove that maximum likelihood is asymptotically unbiased when this number grows sub-exponentially. They also present empirical evidence for the converse: exponential growth is associated with asymptotic bias. The distinction matters because the first direction is a theorem, while the reverse direction is supported experimentally. The analysis brings earlier family-specific findings into a common account.

The authors then construct a mixture-model estimator and prove that it is asymptotically unbiased regardless of anomaly-family size within the studied setting. Applications to disease outbreaks and highway traffic illustrate its advantages over maximum likelihood. The work both explains a source of estimation bias and supplies an alternative whose asymptotic guarantee avoids that dependence on family size.
summary.tldr: Anomaly-family size helps explain maximum-likelihood bias, and a mixture-model estimator achieves asymptotic unbiasedness across family sizes in the studied setting.

title: Quantifying and Reducing Bias in Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Structured Anomalies

abstract: Learning models that gracefully handle distribution shifts is central to research on domain generalization, robust optimization, and fairness. A promising formulation is domain-invariant learning, which identifies the key issue of learning which features are domain-specific versus domain-invariant. An important assumption in this area is that the training examples are partitioned into “domains” or “environments”. Our focus is on the more common setting where such partitions are not provided. We propose EIIL, a general framework for domain-invariant learning that incorporates Environment Inference to directly infer partitions that are maximally informative for downstream Invariant Learning. We show that EIIL outperforms invariant learning methods on the CMNIST benchmark without using environment labels, and significantly outperforms ERM on worst-group performance in the Waterbirds dataset. Finally, we establish connections between EIIL and algorithmic fairness, which enables EIIL to improve accuracy and calibration in a fair prediction problem.

paragraphs: Invariant learning aims to identify features that remain useful when the data distribution changes, rather than relying on features tied to a particular environment. Many approaches assume training examples already have environment labels. This paper addresses the more common situation in which those labels are unavailable, making the relevant partition of the training data part of the learning problem.

EIIL combines environment inference with subsequent invariant learning. It seeks partitions that are maximally informative for the downstream learning objective. The inferred groups therefore serve a specific purpose: helping the learner distinguish environment-specific relationships from relationships that can remain useful across environments.

On CMNIST, EIIL outperforms invariant learning methods without using environment labels. On Waterbirds, it significantly improves worst-group performance over empirical risk minimization, highlighting performance for the least well-served group rather than only aggregate accuracy. The authors also connect the framework to algorithmic fairness and demonstrate improved accuracy and calibration in a fair prediction problem. These results show how inferring environments can make invariant learning useful when explicit domain annotations are absent.
summary.tldr: EIIL infers useful training environments without environment labels and improves reported invariant-learning, worst-group, and fair-prediction results.

title: Environment Inference for Invariant Learning

abstract: The Bayesian paradigm has the potential to solve core issues of deep neural networks such as poor calibration and data inefficiency. Alas, scaling Bayesian inference to large weight spaces often requires restrictive approximations. In this work, we show that it suffices to perform inference over a small subset of model weights in order to obtain accurate predictive posteriors. The other weights are kept as point estimates. This subnetwork inference framework enables us to use expressive, otherwise intractable, posterior approximations over such subsets. In particular, we implement subnetwork linearized Laplace as a simple, scalable Bayesian deep learning method: We first obtain a MAP estimate of all weights and then infer a full-covariance Gaussian posterior over a subnetwork using the linearized Laplace approximation. We propose a subnetwork selection strategy that aims to maximally preserve the model’s predictive uncertainty. Empirically, our approach compares favorably to ensembles and less expressive posterior approximations over full networks.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty about model weights, potentially improving calibration and data efficiency. Applying expressive inference to every weight in a large network, however, can be computationally prohibitive. This paper investigates concentrating the uncertainty calculation on a small subset of weights while keeping the remaining weights fixed at point estimates.

The proposed subnetwork inference framework makes richer posterior approximations feasible within that smaller space. Its concrete implementation first obtains a maximum a posteriori estimate for all weights. It then applies a linearized Laplace approximation to infer a full-covariance Gaussian posterior over the selected subnetwork. Full covariance allows the approximation to represent dependencies among those uncertain weights.

The authors also propose selecting weights with the aim of preserving as much predictive uncertainty as possible. Their results show that inference over a small subset can yield accurate predictive posteriors, and their empirical method compares favorably with ensembles and less expressive full-network approximations. The findings support allocating inference capacity selectively rather than spreading a simpler approximation across every parameter.
summary.tldr: Expressive Bayesian inference over a selected subset of network weights can produce accurate predictive uncertainty at a more manageable scale.

title: Bayesian Deep Learning via Subnetwork Inference

abstract: Many problems in engineering design and simulation require balancing competing objectives under the presence of uncertainty. Sample-efficient multiobjective optimization methods focus on the objective function values in metric space and ignore the sampling behavior of the design configurations in parameter space. Consequently, they may provide little actionable insight on how to choose designs in the presence of metric uncertainty or limited precision when implementing a chosen design. We propose a new formulation that accounts for the importance of the parameter space and is thus more suitable for multiobjective design problems; instead of searching for the Pareto-efficient frontier, we solicit the desired minimum performance thresholds on all objectives to define regions of satisfaction. We introduce an active search algorithm called Expected Coverage Improvement (ECI) to efficiently discover the region of satisfaction and simultaneously sample diverse acceptable configurations. We demonstrate our algorithm on several design and simulation domains: mechanical design, additive manufacturing, medical monitoring, and plasma physics.

paragraphs: Engineering design often involves competing goals, uncertain performance measurements, and limits on how precisely a design can be built. Methods that search for the best tradeoffs usually emphasize objective values. That emphasis can leave a designer with little guidance about the range of actual configurations that would meet practical needs.

This paper changes the search target by asking for minimum acceptable performance on every objective. Those thresholds define a region of satisfaction in the space of design parameters. The task becomes finding configurations throughout that acceptable region, making the variety and location of workable designs part of the search itself.

The proposed Expected Coverage Improvement algorithm actively selects evaluations to discover this region efficiently while also sampling diverse acceptable configurations. The authors demonstrate it in mechanical design, additive manufacturing, medical monitoring, and plasma physics. The contribution is a formulation and search method that connect performance requirements to choices in parameter space, addressing the practical importance of uncertainty and implementation precision.
summary.tldr: Expected Coverage Improvement searches for diverse designs that meet all performance thresholds, making acceptable regions in parameter space the goal.

title: Beyond the Pareto Efficient Frontier: Constraint Active Search for Multiobjective Experimental Design

abstract: Meta-learning of shared initialization parameters has shown to be highly effective in solving few-shot learning tasks. However, extending the framework to many-shot scenarios, which may further enhance its practicality, has been relatively overlooked due to the technical difficulties of meta-learning over long chains of inner-gradient steps. In this paper, we first show that allowing the meta-learners to take a larger number of inner gradient steps better captures the structure of heterogeneous and large-scale task distributions, thus results in obtaining better initialization points. Further, in order to increase the frequency of meta-updates even with the excessively long inner-optimization trajectories, we propose to estimate the required shift of the task-specific parameters with respect to the change of the initialization parameters. By doing so, we can arbitrarily increase the frequency of meta-updates and thus greatly improve the meta-level convergence as well as the quality of the learned initializations. We validate our method on a heterogeneous set of large-scale tasks, and show that the algorithm largely outperforms the previous first-order meta-learning methods in terms of both generalization performance and convergence, as well as multi-task learning and fine-tuning baselines.

paragraphs: Initialization-based meta-learning learns a shared starting point from which models adapt to individual tasks. Extending it to many-shot learning creates a difficulty: task adaptation can require long sequences of gradient updates. The authors first show that allowing more of these inner steps better captures heterogeneous, large-scale task distributions and produces better starting parameters.

Their method addresses the resulting tension between long task-specific training trajectories and frequent updates to the shared initialization. When that initialization changes, they estimate how the task-specific parameters should shift in response. This allows the method to increase the frequency of meta-updates even while working with long inner optimization trajectories.

The paper reports that this approach greatly improves convergence at the meta-learning level and the quality of the learned initializations. Evaluations on heterogeneous large-scale tasks show substantial advantages over previous first-order meta-learning methods in generalization and convergence, as well as over multi-task learning and fine-tuning baselines. The practical contribution is a way to combine deeper task adaptation with more frequent learning of the shared starting point.
summary.tldr: Continual trajectory shifting enables frequent meta-updates during long task adaptation sequences, improving learned initializations in large-scale experiments.

title: Large-Scale Meta-Learning with Continual Trajectory Shifting

abstract: Current state-of-the-art algorithms for training robust decision trees have high runtime costs and require hours to run. We present GROOT, an efficient algorithm for training robust decision trees and random forests that runs in a matter of seconds to minutes. Where before the worst-case Gini impurity was computed iteratively, we find that we can solve this function analytically to improve time complexity from O(n) to O(1) in terms of n samples. Our results on both single trees and ensembles on 14 structured datasets as well as on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that GROOT runs several orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art works and also shows better performance in terms of adversarial accuracy on structured data.

We present GROOT, an efficient algorithm for training robust decision trees and random forests that runs in a matter of seconds to minutes. Where before the worst-case Gini impurity was computed iteratively, we find that we can solve this function analytically to improve time complexity from O(n) to O(1) in terms of n samples. Our results on both single trees and ensembles on 14 structured datasets as well as on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that GROOT runs several orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art works and also shows better performance in terms of adversarial accuracy on structured data.

paragraphs: Training decision trees to resist adversarial examples can be computationally expensive. The paper introduces GROOT, an algorithm for robust decision trees and random forests, to reduce that expense. It reports training times of seconds to minutes where existing leading approaches require hours, making training speed a central contribution.

The main technical change concerns the worst-case Gini impurity calculation used during robust training. Earlier methods compute this quantity iteratively. The authors derive an analytical solution, reducing the calculation's complexity from linear in the number of samples to constant time. This claim applies to that computation, rather than implying that an entire tree can be trained in constant time.

The evaluation covers individual trees and ensembles on 14 structured datasets, alongside MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. GROOT runs several orders of magnitude faster than the compared leading methods and achieves better adversarial accuracy on structured data. The stated results therefore combine a substantial efficiency improvement with improved robustness performance in the structured-data evaluations.
summary.tldr: GROOT accelerates robust tree training with an analytical impurity calculation and reports better adversarial accuracy on structured data.

title: Efficient Training of Robust Decision Trees Against Adversarial Examples

abstract: Adaptive first-order methods in optimization have widespread ML applications due to their ability to adapt to non-convex landscapes. However, their convergence guarantees are typically stated in terms of vanishing gradient norms, which leaves open the issue of converging to undesirable saddle points (or even local maxima). In this paper, we focus on the AdaGrad family of algorithms - from scalar to full-matrix preconditioning - and we examine the question of whether the method’s trajectories avoid saddle points. A major challenge that arises here is that AdaGrad’s step-size (or, more accurately, the method’s preconditioner) evolves over time in a filtration-dependent way, i.e., as a function of all gradients observed in earlier iterations; as a result, avoidance results for methods with a constant or vanishing step-size do not apply. We resolve this challenge by combining a series of step-size stabilization arguments with a recursive representation of the AdaGrad preconditioner that allows us to employ center-stable techniques and ultimately show that the induced trajectories avoid saddle points from almost any initial condition.

paragraphs: A small gradient does not necessarily mean an optimization algorithm has found a useful minimum. It can also occur at a saddle point, where there are directions of improvement that a first-order stopping criterion does not reveal. This paper asks whether AdaGrad avoids such points, strengthening the understanding provided by guarantees about shrinking gradients alone.

The analysis covers AdaGrad variants ranging from scalar scaling to full-matrix preconditioning.

The authors combine arguments about stabilization of the update scale with a recursive description of the preconditioner. This lets them apply mathematical techniques for studying trajectories near stationary points. They show that AdaGrad trajectories avoid saddle points from almost every initial condition. The qualifier matters: the result concerns almost all starting points, rather than every possible initialization.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that AdaGrad avoids saddle points from almost every initial condition despite its history-dependent updates.

title: AdaGrad Avoids Saddle Points

abstract: Recent years have seen advances in generalization bounds for noisy stochastic algorithms, especially stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) based on stability (Mou et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020) and information theoretic approaches (Xu & Raginsky, 2017; Negrea et al., 2019; Steinke & Zakynthinou, 2020). In this paper, we unify and substantially generalize stability based generalization bounds and make three technical contributions. First, we bound the generalization error in terms of expected (not uniform) stability which arguably leads to quantitatively sharper bounds. Second, as our main contribution, we introduce Exponential Family Langevin Dynamics (EFLD), a substantial generalization of SGLD, which includes noisy versions of Sign-SGD and quantized SGD as special cases. We establish data dependent expected stability based generalization bounds for any EFLD algorithm with a O(1/n) sample dependence and dependence on gradient discrepancy rather than the norm of gradients, yielding significantly sharper bounds. Third, we establish optimization guarantees for special cases of EFLD. Further, empirical results on benchmarks illustrate that our bounds are non-vacuous, quantitatively sharper than existing bounds, and behave correctly under noisy labels.

paragraphs: This paper studies generalization guarantees for noisy stochastic learning algorithms through stability. It bounds generalization error using expected stability rather than uniform stability, aiming for quantitatively sharper results. The distinction shifts the analysis toward expected behavior instead of requiring the same stability control uniformly.

The main framework, Exponential Family Langevin Dynamics, generalizes stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics and includes noisy forms of Sign-SGD and quantized SGD. For this family, the authors establish data-dependent generalization bounds with a 1/n sample dependence. The bounds depend on gradient discrepancy rather than gradient norms, providing a different way to quantify the sensitivity relevant to generalization.

The authors also prove optimization guarantees for special cases of the framework, keeping that result distinct from the broader generalization analysis. Benchmark experiments show that the bounds are non-vacuous, sharper than existing bounds, and behave appropriately under noisy labels. Together, the contributions expand the algorithms covered by stability analysis and make its estimates more informative in the evaluated settings, connecting a broader theoretical framework with empirical bound quality.
summary.tldr: Expected-stability analysis yields sharper data-dependent generalization bounds for a broad family of noisy optimization algorithms.

title: Stability Based Generalization Bounds for Exponential Family Langevin Dynamics

abstract: Generative models which use explicit density modeling (e.g., variational autoencoders, flow-based generative models) involve finding a mapping from a known distribution, e.g. Gaussian, to the unknown input distribution. This often requires searching over a class of non-linear functions (e.g., representable by a deep neural network). While effective in practice, the associated runtime/memory costs can increase rapidly, usually as a function of the performance desired in an application. We propose a substantially cheaper (and simpler) forward operator estimation strategy based on adapting known results on kernel transfer operators. We show that our formulation enables highly efficient distribution approximation and sampling, and offers surprisingly good empirical performance that compares favorably with powerful baselines, but with significant runtime savings. We show that the algorithm also performs well in small sample size settings (in brain imaging).

paragraphs: Some generative models learn a mapping from a familiar distribution, such as a Gaussian, to the unknown distribution represented by observed data. Finding that mapping can involve searching through a large class of nonlinear functions implemented by neural networks. Although effective, this process can demand increasing runtime and memory as applications require better performance.

The paper proposes a simpler and substantially cheaper strategy based on forward operator estimation. It adapts existing results about kernel transfer operators to the generative modeling problem. The resulting formulation supports both approximating a data distribution and drawing samples from it, making the operator approach useful for the central tasks expected of a generative model.

The authors report favorable empirical comparisons with powerful baselines alongside substantial runtime savings. They also demonstrate good performance with small samples in a brain-imaging setting. These findings make computational efficiency a central part of the contribution: the proposed formulation offers a different way to obtain useful distribution approximations and samples with lower reported computational cost.
summary.tldr: Kernel transfer operators provide a simpler generative modeling approach with favorable empirical performance and substantial runtime savings.

title: Forward Operator Estimation in Generative Models with Kernel Transfer Operators

abstract: We propose Guided-TTS, a high-quality text-to-speech (TTS) model that does not require any transcript of target speaker using classifier guidance. Guided-TTS combines an unconditional diffusion probabilistic model with a separately trained phoneme classifier for classifier guidance. Our unconditional diffusion model learns to generate speech without any context from untranscribed speech data. For TTS synthesis, we guide the generative process of the diffusion model with a phoneme classifier trained on a large-scale speech recognition dataset. We present a norm-based scaling method that reduces the pronunciation errors of classifier guidance in Guided-TTS. We show that Guided-TTS achieves a performance comparable to that of the state-of-the-art TTS model, Grad-TTS, without any transcript for LJSpeech. We further demonstrate that Guided-TTS performs well on diverse datasets including a long-form untranscribed dataset.

paragraphs: Guided-TTS addresses speech synthesis when recordings of the target speaker have no transcripts. Its approach separates learning how that speaker's speech sounds from guiding the generated speech toward the requested content. This allows the target speaker's untranscribed audio to support a text-to-speech system.

The system combines an unconditional diffusion model with a separately trained phoneme classifier. The diffusion model learns to generate speech from untranscribed recordings without conditioning on text. During synthesis, the phoneme classifier guides generation toward the desired speech content. That classifier is trained on a large speech-recognition dataset, so the absence of target-speaker transcripts does not mean the entire system avoids transcribed training resources.

The authors introduce norm-based scaling to reduce pronunciation errors arising from classifier guidance. They report performance comparable to Grad-TTS on LJSpeech without using its transcripts for the target speaker. Further experiments show good performance across diverse datasets, including long-form untranscribed speech. The findings support separating speech generation and linguistic guidance when target-speaker transcription is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Guided-TTS combines diffusion speech generation with phoneme-classifier guidance to synthesize speech without target-speaker transcripts.

title: Guided-TTS: A Diffusion Model for Text-to-Speech via Classifier Guidance

abstract: High-quality data plays a central role in ensuring the accuracy of policy evaluation. This paper initiates the study of efficient and safe data collection for bandit policy evaluation. We formulate the problem and investigate its several representative variants. For each variant, we analyze its statistical properties, derive the corresponding exploration policy, and design an efficient algorithm for computing it. Both theoretical analysis and experiments support the usefulness of the proposed methods.
originalAbstract: High-quality data plays a central role in ensuring the accuracy of policy evaluation. This paper initiates the study of efficient and safe data collection for bandit policy evaluation. We formulate the problem and investigate its several representative variants. Both theoretical analysis and experiments support the usefulness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Accurately evaluating a policy depends on the data available about its decisions and outcomes. This paper studies how to collect that data efficiently and safely in bandit settings. It places the data-collection policy itself at the center of the problem, connecting exploration choices to the quality of later policy evaluation and comparison.

The authors formulate the problem and examine several representative variants. For each variant, they analyze statistical properties and derive a corresponding exploration policy. They also provide an efficient algorithm for computing that policy, linking the desired statistical behavior to a procedure that can actually choose how data should be gathered.

Both theoretical analysis and experiments support the usefulness of the methods. The contribution is a framework for treating evaluation data as something to design deliberately, with safety and efficiency considered together. Its emphasis on multiple variants also makes clear that the appropriate exploration policy depends on the particular evaluation problem being posed, rather than assuming one collection strategy fits every case.
summary.tldr: The paper formulates safe, efficient data collection for bandit policy evaluation and derives computable exploration policies for several variants.

title: Safe Exploration for Efficient Policy Evaluation and Comparison

abstract: Learning dynamics models accurately is an important goal for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL), but most MBRL methods learn a dense dynamics model which is vulnerable to spurious correlations and therefore generalizes poorly to unseen states. In this paper, we introduce Causal Dynamics Learning for Task-Independent State Abstraction (CDL), which first learns a theoretically proved causal dynamics model that removes unnecessary dependencies between state variables and the action, thus generalizing well to unseen states. A state abstraction can then be derived from the learned dynamics, which not only improves sample efficiency but also applies to a wider range of tasks than existing state abstraction methods. Evaluated on two simulated environments and downstream tasks, both the dynamics model and policies learned by the proposed method generalize well to unseen states and the derived state abstraction improves sample efficiency compared to learning without it.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning depends on predicting how actions change an environment. A densely connected dynamics model can learn relationships that happen to occur in its training data without representing useful causal dependencies. Such spurious relationships make prediction less reliable when the agent encounters unfamiliar states, even if the training observations were modeled accurately.

Causal Dynamics Learning addresses this problem by first learning a dynamics model that removes unnecessary dependencies among state variables and actions. The paper provides theoretical support for this causal model. It then derives a state abstraction from the learned dynamics, giving the learner a reduced representation that can support a wider range of tasks than the existing abstraction methods considered.

Evaluations in two simulated environments and downstream tasks show that both the dynamics predictions and the learned policies generalize well to unseen states. Using the derived abstraction also improves sample efficiency compared with learning without it. The contribution connects two goals: learning which dependencies matter for environmental change, and using that structure to make subsequent policy learning more efficient.
summary.tldr: CDL learns causal dynamics and derives reusable state abstractions that improve sample efficiency and generalization in simulated tasks.

title: Causal Dynamics Learning for Task-Independent State Abstraction

abstract: In this paper, we study contrastive learning from an optimization perspective, aiming to analyze and address a fundamental issue of existing contrastive learning methods that either rely on a large batch size or a large dictionary of feature vectors. We consider a global objective for contrastive learning, which contrasts each positive pair with all negative pairs for an anchor point. From the optimization perspective, we explain why existing methods such as SimCLR require a large batch size in order to achieve a satisfactory result. In order to remove such requirement, we propose a memory-efficient Stochastic Optimization algorithm for solving the Global objective of Contrastive Learning of Representations, named SogCLR. We show that its optimization error is negligible under a reasonable condition after a sufficient number of iterations or is diminishing for a slightly different global contrastive objective. Empirically, we demonstrate that SogCLR with small batch size (e.g., 256) can achieve similar performance as SimCLR with large batch size (e.g., 8192) on self-supervised learning task on ImageNet-1K. We also attempt to show that the proposed optimization technique is generic and can be applied to solving other contrastive losses, e.g., two-way contrastive losses for bimodal contrastive learning. The proposed method is implemented in our open-sourced library LibAUC (www.libauc.org).

paragraphs: Contrastive learning trains representations by comparing positive pairs with negative pairs. This paper studies a global objective that compares each positive pair against all negatives associated with an anchor. From an optimization perspective, it explains why methods such as SimCLR need large batches to obtain satisfactory results and seeks to remove that requirement.

The proposed algorithm, SogCLR, is a memory-efficient stochastic method for optimizing this global objective. The analysis shows that its optimization error becomes negligible after sufficiently many iterations under a stated reasonable condition. For a slightly different global contrastive objective, the authors instead establish diminishing optimization error. These are distinct guarantees tied to the objective and conditions analyzed.

On ImageNet-1K self-supervised learning, SogCLR with a batch size of 256 achieves performance similar to SimCLR with a batch size of 8192. This demonstrates that small batches can work well with the proposed optimization approach. The paper also explores applying the technique to other contrastive losses, including two-way losses for bimodal learning.
summary.tldr: SogCLR optimizes a global contrastive objective and empirically matches large-batch SimCLR performance using much smaller batches.

title: Provable Stochastic Optimization for Global Contrastive Learning: Small Batch Does Not Harm Performance

abstract: We present a general causal generative modelling framework for accurate estimation of high fidelity image counterfactuals with deep structural causal models. Estimation of interventional and counterfactual queries for high-dimensional structured variables, such as images, remains a challenging task. We leverage ideas from causal mediation analysis and advances in generative modelling to design new deep causal mechanisms for structured variables in causal models. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed mechanisms are capable of accurate abduction and estimation of direct, indirect and total effects as measured by axiomatic soundness of counterfactuals.
originalAbstract: We present a general causal generative modelling framework for accurate estimation of high fidelity image counterfactuals with deep structural causal models. Estimation of interventional and counterfactual queries for high-dimensional structured variables, such as images, remains a challenging task. We leverage ideas from causal mediation analysis and advances in generative modelling to design new deep causal mechanisms for structured variables in causal models. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed mechanisms are capable of accurate abduction and estimation of direct, indirect and total effects as measured by axiomatic soundness of counterfactuals.

paragraphs: An image counterfactual asks how an observed image would change under a different causal circumstance. Answering this requires more than producing a plausible image: the change must follow the relationships represented by the causal model. This paper develops a general generative framework for estimating such counterfactuals with deep structural causal models.

The authors combine ideas from causal mediation analysis with advances in generative modeling. Their new causal mechanisms handle structured, high-dimensional variables such as images. Mediation gives the framework a way to distinguish direct effects from effects transmitted indirectly through other variables, alongside the total effect of a change.

The experiments demonstrate accurate abduction and estimation of direct, indirect, and total effects. Here, abduction is the inference step needed to connect an observed case with the model’s counterfactual reasoning. The authors assess these capabilities through the axiomatic soundness of the resulting counterfactuals. The stated contribution therefore joins high-fidelity image generation with a causal evaluation criterion, examining whether generated alternatives behave consistently with the counterfactual properties being tested.
summary.tldr: New deep causal mechanisms support high-fidelity image counterfactuals and accurate effect estimation under axiomatic counterfactual evaluation.

title: High Fidelity Image Counterfactuals with Probabilistic Causal Models

abstract: The sampling process of diffusion models can be interpreted as solving the reverse stochastic differential equation (SDE) or the ordinary differential equation (ODE) of the diffusion process, which often requires up to thousands of discretization steps to generate a single image. This has sparked a great interest in developing efficient integration techniques for reverse-S/ODEs. Here, we propose an orthogonal approach to accelerating score-based sampling: Denoising MCMC (DMCMC). DMCMC first uses MCMC to produce initialization points for reverse-S/ODE in the product space of data and diffusion time. Then, a reverse-S/ODE integrator is used to denoise the initialization points. Since MCMC traverses close to the data manifold, the cost of producing a clean sample for DMCMC is much less than that of producing a clean sample from noise. Denoising Langevin Gibbs, an instance of DMCMC, successfully accelerates all six reverse-S/ODE integrators considered in this work, and achieves state-of-the-art results: in the limited number of score function evaluation (NFE) setting on CIFAR10, we have $3.25$ FID with $\approx 10$ NFE and $2.49$ FID with $\approx 16$ NFE. On CelebA-HQ-256, we have $6.99$ FID with $\approx 160$ NFE, which beats the current best record of Kim et al. (2022) among score-based models, $7.16$ FID with $4000$ NFE. Code: https://github.com/1202kbs/DMCMC

paragraphs: Generating an image with a diffusion model can require many steps of a reverse stochastic or ordinary differential equation. Much work speeds up the numerical integration of that equation. Denoising MCMC takes a complementary approach: it changes the starting points supplied to the integrator, reducing how much denoising those points need.

The method first runs Markov chain Monte Carlo in a space that includes both the data and diffusion time. It then applies a reverse-equation integrator to the resulting initialization points. Because the MCMC process moves near the data manifold, producing a clean sample from these points costs much less than starting from noise.

The tested instance, Denoising Langevin Gibbs, accelerates all six integrators considered. On CIFAR10, it achieves FID values of 3.25 with approximately 10 score evaluations and 2.49 with approximately 16. On CelebA-HQ-256, it achieves 6.99 FID with approximately 160 evaluations, compared with the cited prior score-based result of 7.16 using 4,000. These findings show that better initialization can complement improvements to the integrator itself.
summary.tldr: Denoising MCMC accelerates diffusion sampling by supplying starting points near the data manifold before numerical denoising.

title: Denoising MCMC for Accelerating Diffusion-Based Generative Models

abstract: With growing attention to tabular data these days, the attempt to apply a synthetic table to various tasks has been expanded toward various scenarios. Owing to the recent advances in generative modeling, fake data generated by tabular data synthesis models become sophisticated and realistic. However, there still exists a difficulty in modeling discrete variables (columns) of tabular data. In this work, we propose to process continuous and discrete variables separately (but being conditioned on each other) by two diffusion models. The two diffusion models are co-evolved during training by reading conditions from each other. In order to further bind the diffusion models, moreover, we introduce a contrastive learning method with a negative sampling method. In our experiments with 11 real-world tabular datasets and 8 baseline methods, we prove the efficacy of the proposed method, called $\texttt{CoDi}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChaejeongLee/CoDi.
