paragraphs: Synthetic tables need to represent both individual columns and the relationships between them. Mixed-type tables make this difficult because continuous values and discrete categories have different structures. The paper focuses on the remaining difficulty of modeling discrete columns, even as generative models have become better at producing realistic-looking tabular data.

CoDi divides the work between two diffusion models: one handles continuous variables and the other handles discrete variables. The models remain connected because each receives conditioning information from the other during training. This arrangement gives each variable type a separate modeling process while allowing information about the other type to influence what it learns.

The authors further connect the two models using contrastive learning with negative sampling. This adds a training mechanism for coordinating the models beyond their exchange of conditioning information. Experiments across 11 real-world tabular datasets, with eight baseline methods, support the effectiveness of CoDi. The central contribution is a way to combine separate treatment of different column types with joint learning of their relationships, addressing both parts of the mixed-type synthesis problem.
summary.tldr: CoDi synthesizes mixed-type tables using mutually conditioned diffusion models for continuous and discrete variables, further linked through contrastive learning.

title: CoDi: Co-evolving Contrastive Diffusion Models for Mixed-type Tabular Synthesis

abstract: The hyperbolic space is widely used for representing hierarchical datasets due to its ability to embed trees with small distortion. However, this property comes at a price of numerical instability such that training hyperbolic learning models will sometimes lead to catastrophic NaN problems, encountering unrepresentable values in floating point arithmetic. In this work, we analyze the limitations of two popular models for the hyperbolic space, namely, the Poincaré ball and the Lorentz model. We find that, under the 64-bit arithmetic system, the Poincaré ball has a relatively larger capacity than the Lorentz model for correctly representing points. However, the Lorentz model is superior to the Poincaré ball from the perspective of optimization, which we theoretically validate. To address these limitations, we identify one Euclidean parametrization of the hyperbolic space which can alleviate these issues. We further extend this Euclidean parametrization to hyperbolic hyperplanes and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of hyperbolic SVM.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic geometry is useful for representing hierarchical data because it can embed trees with little distortion. Its numerical implementation can nevertheless be fragile. During training, floating-point arithmetic may encounter values it cannot represent, producing NaNs that disrupt the learning process.

The paper analyzes two common representations of hyperbolic space: the Poincaré ball and the Lorentz model. Under 64-bit arithmetic, the Poincaré ball can correctly represent a relatively larger range of points. The Lorentz model, however, has an optimization advantage that the authors establish theoretically. The comparison therefore separates representational capacity in finite arithmetic from optimization behavior.

To alleviate these issues, the authors identify a Euclidean parameterization of hyperbolic space. They also extend that parameterization to hyperbolic hyperplanes and demonstrate improved hyperbolic support-vector-machine performance. The work connects numerical representation choices to practical learning outcomes, while presenting the proposed parameterization as a way to reduce the identified problems rather than a guarantee that numerical instability disappears entirely.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes numerical trade-offs between hyperbolic models and proposes a Euclidean parameterization that alleviates instability and improves hyperbolic SVM performance.

title: The Numerical Stability of Hyperbolic Representation Learning

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to find an optimal policy for sequential decision-making using a pre-collected dataset, without further interaction with the environment. Recent theoretical progress has focused on developing sample-efficient offline RL algorithms with various relaxed assumptions on data coverage and function approximators, especially to handle the case with excessively large state-action spaces. Among them, the framework based on the linear-programming (LP) reformulation of Markov decision processes has shown promise: it enables sample-efficient offline RL with function approximation, under only partial data coverage and realizability assumptions on the function classes, with favorable computational tractability. In this work, we revisit the LP framework for offline RL, and provide a new reformulation that advances the existing results in several aspects, relaxing certain assumptions and achieving optimal statistical rates in terms of sample size. Our key enabler is to introduce proper constraints in the reformulation, instead of using any regularization as in the literature, also with careful choices of the function classes and initial state distributions. We hope our insights bring into light the use of LP formulations and the induced primal-dual minimax optimization, in offline RL.

In this work, we revisit the LP framework for offline RL, and provide a new reformulation that advances the existing results in several aspects, relaxing certain assumptions and achieving optimal statistical rates in terms of sample size. Our key enabler is to introduce proper constraints in the reformulation, instead of using any regularization as in the literature, also with careful choices of the function classes and initial state distributions. We hope our insights bring into light the use of LP formulations and the induced primal-dual minimax optimization, in offline RL.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a good decision-making policy from previously collected data, without additional environment interaction. Large state-action spaces make both data coverage and function approximation important. Linear-programming formulations have offered a promising route, supporting sample-efficient learning under partial coverage and assumptions that the chosen function classes can represent the needed quantities.

This paper introduces a new formulation that relaxes certain assumptions in earlier results and achieves optimal statistical rates as a function of sample size. Its central design change is to impose suitable constraints in the optimization problem. Careful choices of function classes and initial-state distributions are also essential parts of the construction.

The authors use these constraints in place of the regularization employed in prior formulations. The resulting perspective clarifies how the structure of the optimization problem can improve statistical guarantees for offline learning. The contribution is theoretical: it advances the linear-programming framework and its associated primal-dual minimax optimization while retaining explicit attention to the assumptions needed for learning from limited existing data.
summary.tldr: A constrained linear-programming formulation relaxes some offline RL assumptions and achieves optimal statistical rates in sample size.

title: Revisiting the Linear-Programming Framework for Offline RL with General Function Approximation

abstract: The manifold hypothesis, which assumes that data lies on or close to an unknown manifold of low intrinsic dimension, is a staple of modern machine learning research. However, recent work has shown that real-world data exhibits distinct non-manifold structures, i.e. singularities, that can lead to erroneous findings. Detecting such singularities is therefore crucial as a precursor to interpolation and inference tasks. We address this issue by developing a topological framework that (i) quantifies the local intrinsic dimension, and (ii) yields a Euclidicity score for assessing the ’manifoldness’ of a point along multiple scales. Our approach identifies singularities of complex spaces, while also capturing singular structures and local geometric complexity in image data.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning methods assume that data lies near a low-dimensional manifold, a structure that behaves locally like an ordinary Euclidean space. Real data can also contain singularities where this local description fails. Such departures can lead to erroneous findings, making their detection relevant before interpolation or inference.

The paper introduces a topological framework with two complementary outputs. One quantifies local intrinsic dimension, describing the dimensional complexity near a point. The other is a Euclidicity score that assesses how closely the neighborhood resembles a manifold. Evaluating across multiple scales makes the assessment sensitive to the size of the neighborhood being examined.

The approach identifies singularities in complex spaces and captures singular structures and local geometric complexity in image data. Its contribution is a way to examine the manifold assumption locally instead of treating it as a single property of an entire dataset. The resulting dimension and Euclidicity assessments provide distinct information about where a manifold-based description may be inadequate.
summary.tldr: A multiscale topological framework estimates local dimension and Euclidicity to detect departures from manifold structure.

title: Topological Singularity Detection at Multiple Scales

abstract: Model-based imitation learning (MBIL) is a popular reinforcement learning method that improves sample efficiency on high-dimension input sources, such as images and videos. Following the convention of MBIL research, existing algorithms are highly deceptive by task-irrelevant information, especially moving distractors in videos. To tackle this problem, we propose a new algorithm - named Separated Model-based Adversarial Imitation Learning (SeMAIL) - decoupling the environment dynamics into two parts by task-relevant dependency, which is determined by agent actions, and training separately. In this way, the agent can imagine its trajectories and imitate the expert behavior efficiently in task-relevant state space. Our method achieves near-expert performance on various visual control tasks with complex observations and the more challenging tasks with different backgrounds from expert observations.

paragraphs: Learning to imitate from images or video requires separating useful information from visual distractions. Model-based imitation learning can use high-dimensional observations efficiently, but existing methods can be misled by task-irrelevant content, particularly moving distractors. This paper proposes SeMAIL to address that problem through the structure of its environment model.

The authors report near-expert performance on several visual control tasks with complex observations. They also evaluate harder tasks where the learner’s backgrounds differ from those in the expert observations. Those results support separating the modeled dynamics as a way to make visual imitation less vulnerable to distractors. The approach ties the representation used for imagined experience to action-related task structure.
summary.tldr: SeMAIL separates task-relevant and irrelevant dynamics so visual imitation can focus on expert behavior despite distracting or changed backgrounds.

title: SeMAIL: Eliminating Distractors in Visual Imitation via Separated Models

abstract: The studies on adversarial attacks and defenses have greatly improved the robustness of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). Most advanced approaches have been overwhelmingly designed for continuous data such as images. However, these achievements are still hard to be generalized to categorical data. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework, Probabilistic Categorical Adversarial Attack (or PCAA). It transfers the discrete optimization problem of finding categorical adversarial examples to a continuous problem that can be solved via gradient-based methods. We analyze the optimality (attack success rate) and time complexity of PCAA to demonstrate its significant advantage over current search-based attacks. More importantly, through extensive empirical studies, we demonstrate that the well-established defenses for continuous data, such as adversarial training and TRADES, can be easily accommodated to defend DNNs for categorical data.

paragraphs: Many successful adversarial attack and defense techniques were developed for continuous inputs such as images. Categorical inputs present a different optimization problem because changes involve discrete choices. This paper introduces Probabilistic Categorical Adversarial Attack, or PCAA, to make attacks on such data amenable to gradient-based optimization.

PCAA transforms the discrete search for categorical adversarial examples into a continuous problem. This gives gradient methods a route into a setting otherwise handled by search-based attacks. The authors analyze attack success and computational complexity, reporting significant advantages over existing search approaches. The contribution concerns both finding effective adversarial examples and the computational effort needed to find them.

The framework also supports studying defenses for categorical data. Extensive empirical evaluations show that adversarial training and TRADES, established approaches for continuous inputs, can be adapted to defend categorical-input neural networks. These results connect the attack formulation to practical robustness training. They support the usefulness of adapting existing defense ideas through the proposed framework, rather than implying universal protection against categorical attacks.
summary.tldr: PCAA turns categorical adversarial search into continuous optimization and enables established robustness-training methods to be adapted to categorical data.

title: Probabilistic Categorical Adversarial Attack and Adversarial Training

abstract: Ensuring alignment of language model’s outputs with human preferences is critical to guarantee a useful, safe, and pleasant user experience. Thus, human alignment has been extensively studied recently and several methods such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), Direct Policy Optimisation (DPO) and Sequence Likelihood Calibration (SLiC) have emerged. In this paper, our contribution is two-fold. First, we show the equivalence between two recent alignment methods, namely Identity Policy Optimisation (IPO) and Nash Mirror Descent (Nash-MD). Second, we introduce a generalisation of IPO, named IPO-MD, that leverages the regularised sampling approach proposed by Nash-MD. This equivalence may seem surprising at first sight, since IPO is an offline method whereas Nash-MD is an online method using a preference model. However, this equivalence can be proven when we consider the online version of IPO, that is when both generations are sampled by the online policy and annotated by a trained preference model. Optimising the IPO loss with such a stream of data becomes then equivalent to finding the Nash equilibrium of the preference model through self-play. Building on this equivalence, we introduce the IPO-MD algorithm that generates data with a mixture policy (between the online and reference policy) similarly as the general Nash-MD algorithm. We compare online-IPO and IPO-MD to different online versions of existing losses on preference data such as DPO and SLiC on a summarisation task.

paragraphs: Preference optimization trains language models to produce outputs people favor. This paper connects two methods that initially appear different: Identity Policy Optimisation, or IPO, is an offline method, while Nash Mirror Descent, or Nash-MD, operates online using a preference model. The connection emerges when IPO is placed in a particular online setting.

The authors compare online IPO and IPO-MD with online versions of DPO and SLiC on summarization. The stated contribution is the theoretical connection and the resulting algorithm, with an empirical comparison on that task.
summary.tldr: The paper proves an online IPO–Nash-MD equivalence under specified sampling conditions and introduces the mixture-policy algorithm IPO-MD.

title: Human Alignment of Large Language Models through Online Preference Optimisation

abstract: Diffusion models create data from noise by inverting the forward paths of data towards noise and have emerged as a powerful generative modeling technique for high-dimensional, perceptual data such as images and videos. Rectified flow is a recent generative model formulation that connects data and noise in a straight line. Despite its better theoretical properties and conceptual simplicity, it is not yet decisively established as standard practice. In this work, we improve existing noise sampling techniques for training rectified flow models by biasing them towards perceptually relevant scales. Through a large-scale study, we demonstrate the superior performance of this approach compared to established diffusion formulations for high-resolution text-to-image synthesis. Additionally, we present a novel transformer-based architecture for text-to-image generation that uses separate weights for the two modalities and enables a bidirectional flow of information between image and text tokens, improving text comprehension, typography, and human preference ratings. We demonstrate that this architecture follows predictable scaling trends and correlates lower validation loss to improved text-to-image synthesis as measured by various metrics and human evaluations. Our largest models outperform state-of-the-art models. Stability AI is considering making experimental data, code, and model weights publicly available.

summary.tldr: Improved rectified-flow training and a bidirectional text–image transformer deliver strong high-resolution image generation with predictable scaling trends.

title: Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis

abstract: Opponent exploitation is an important task for players to exploit the weaknesses of others in games. Existing approaches mainly focus on balancing between exploitation and exploitability but are often vulnerable to modeling errors and deceptive adversaries. To address this problem, our paper offers a novel perspective on the safety of opponent exploitation, named Adaptation Safety. This concept leverages the insight that strategies, even those not explicitly aimed at opponent exploitation, may inherently be exploitable due to computational complexities, rendering traditional safety overly rigorous. In contrast, adaptation safety requires that the strategy should not be more exploitable than it would be in scenarios where opponent exploitation is not considered. Building on such adaptation safety, we further propose an Opponent eXploitation Search (OX-Search) framework by incorporating real-time search techniques for efficient online opponent exploitation. Moreover, we provide theoretical analyses to show the adaptation safety and robust exploitation of OX-Search, even with inaccurate opponent models. Empirical evaluations in popular poker games demonstrate OX-Search’s superiority in both exploitability and exploitation compared to previous methods.

paragraphs: Exploiting an opponent's weaknesses can make a game-playing strategy vulnerable, especially when the opponent model is inaccurate or the opponent is deceptive. This paper introduces adaptation safety as a way to define the acceptable risk of exploitation. Its starting point is that computationally limited strategies may already be exploitable before any opponent-specific adaptation.

Adaptation safety requires that exploiting the opponent should not make a strategy more exploitable than it would have been without that adaptation. The reference point is therefore the strategy's existing vulnerability. This definition makes the safety requirement directly about the additional risk introduced by trying to take advantage of an opponent.

The authors build Opponent eXploitation Search, or OX-Search, around this principle, incorporating real-time search for efficient online exploitation. Their theoretical analysis establishes adaptation safety and robust exploitation even with inaccurate opponent models. Evaluations in poker games show improvements over earlier methods in both exploitation and exploitability. Together, the definition and algorithm connect opponent-specific gains to an explicit bound on added strategic vulnerability.
summary.tldr: OX-Search exploits opponents while satisfying adaptation safety: exploitation should not increase vulnerability relative to the strategy without adaptation.

title: Safe and Robust Subgame Exploitation in Imperfect Information Games

abstract: What do different contrastive learning (CL) losses actually optimize for? Although multiple CL methods have demonstrated remarkable representation learning capabilities, the differences in their inner workings remain largely opaque. In this work, we analyse several CL families and prove that, under certain conditions, they admit the same minimisers when optimizing either their batch-level objectives or their expectations asymptotically. In both cases, an intimate connection with the hyperspherical energy minimisation (HEM) problem resurfaces. Drawing inspiration from this, we introduce a novel CL objective, coined Decoupled Hyperspherical Energy Loss (DHEL). DHEL simplifies the problem by decoupling the target hyperspherical energy from the alignment of positive examples while preserving the same theoretical guarantees. Going one step further, we show the same results hold for another relevant CL family, namely kernel contrastive learning (KCL), with the additional advantage of the expected loss being independent of batch size, thus identifying the minimisers in the non-asymptotic regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved downstream performance and robustness across combinations of different batch sizes and hyperparameters and reduced dimensionality collapse, on several computer vision datasets.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning can produce useful representations through several different training losses, yet it is not always clear how their preferred solutions differ. This paper compares families of these losses at the level of individual batches and their asymptotic expected objectives. Under specified conditions, the authors prove that these formulations share the same minimizers.

The analysis connects those solutions to arranging representations on a hypersphere through energy minimization. This motivates Decoupled Hyperspherical Energy Loss, which separates the energy objective from the alignment of positive examples while retaining the theoretical guarantees. The separation makes the two aims easier to distinguish within the training objective.

The authors extend the results to kernel contrastive learning, whose expected loss has the additional property of being independent of batch size. This permits identification of minimizers without relying on an asymptotic regime. Computer-vision experiments report better downstream performance, greater robustness across batch sizes and hyperparameters, and less dimensionality collapse. The empirical findings complement the conditional equivalence results rather than making all contrastive losses universally interchangeable.
summary.tldr: A conditional analysis links contrastive losses through hyperspherical energy and motivates objectives with improved empirical performance and reduced dimensionality collapse.

title: Bridging Mini-Batch and Asymptotic Analysis in Contrastive Learning: From InfoNCE to Kernel-Based Losses

abstract: Recent advances in knowledge graph embedding (KGE) rely on Euclidean/hyperbolic orthogonal relation transformations to model intrinsic logical patterns and topological structures. However, existing approaches are confined to rigid relational orthogonalization with restricted dimension and homogeneous geometry, leading to deficient modeling capability. In this work, we move beyond these approaches in terms of both dimension and geometry by introducing a powerful framework named GoldE, which features a universal orthogonal parameterization based on a generalized form of Householder reflection. Such parameterization can naturally achieve dimensional extension and geometric unification with theoretical guarantees, enabling our framework to simultaneously capture crucial logical patterns and inherent topological heterogeneity of knowledge graphs. Empirically, GoldE achieves state-of-the-art performance on three standard benchmarks. Codes are available at https://github.com/xxrep/GoldE.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embedding represents entities and relations geometrically so that the representation can capture logical patterns and graph structure. This paper focuses on methods that express relations through orthogonal transformations. The authors argue that existing formulations are constrained by restricted dimensions and a single kind of geometry, limiting the structures they can model.

Their framework, GoldE, uses a generalized Householder reflection to parameterize orthogonal transformations. The construction supports both extending the dimension and unifying geometric settings, with theoretical guarantees. Its purpose is to give relation transformations enough flexibility to capture logical regularities while accommodating differences in the graph's underlying topology.

GoldE reports state-of-the-art performance on three standard benchmarks. The empirical results support the value of broadening the mathematical form of relation representations. The main contribution is therefore a more general parameterization connecting dimension and geometry within one framework, alongside evidence that this additional modeling capacity benefits the evaluated knowledge graph tasks.
summary.tldr: GoldE generalizes orthogonal relation transformations across dimensions and geometries to improve knowledge graph representations.

title: Generalizing Knowledge Graph Embedding with Universal Orthogonal Parameterization

abstract: Automated red teaming holds substantial promise for uncovering and mitigating the risks associated with the malicious use of large language models (LLMs), yet the field lacks a standardized evaluation framework to rigorously assess new methods. To address this issue, we introduce HarmBench, a standardized evaluation framework for automated red teaming. We identify several desirable properties previously unaccounted for in red teaming evaluations and systematically design HarmBench to meet these criteria. Using HarmBench, we conduct a large-scale comparison of 18 red teaming methods and 33 target LLMs and defenses, yielding novel insights. We also introduce a highly efficient adversarial training method that greatly enhances LLM robustness across a wide range of attacks, demonstrating how HarmBench enables codevelopment of attacks and defenses. We open source HarmBench at https://github.com/centerforaisafety/HarmBench.

paragraphs: Automated red teaming tests whether language models can be induced to produce harmful responses. Its usefulness depends partly on whether different testing methods and defenses can be compared fairly. HarmBench addresses the lack of a standardized evaluation framework, giving this research area a shared basis for assessing progress.

The authors identify desirable evaluation properties that earlier red-teaming assessments had not accounted for and design the framework around them. They then use HarmBench to compare 18 red-teaming methods against 33 target language models and defenses. This broad comparison makes the framework an instrument for studying both the effectiveness of attacks and the behavior of the systems they target.

The paper also introduces an efficient adversarial training method that substantially improves robustness across a wide range of tested attacks. This connects evaluation to model improvement: the same framework supports developing attacks and defenses together. The reported contribution therefore includes a shared evaluation approach, a large comparative study, and a training method whose robustness gains are demonstrated through that approach.
summary.tldr: HarmBench standardizes automated red-teaming evaluation and supports an efficient adversarial training method that improves robustness across many attacks.

title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal

abstract: Graph clustering is a fundamental problem in machine learning. Deep learning methods achieve the state-of-the-art results in recent years, but they still cannot work without predefined cluster numbers. Such limitation motivates us to pose a more challenging problem of graph clustering with unknown cluster number. We propose to address this problem from a fresh perspective of graph information theory (i.e., structural information). In the literature, structural information has not yet been introduced to deep clustering, and its classic definition falls short of discrete formulation and modeling node features. In this work, we first formulate a differentiable structural information (DSI) in the continuous realm, accompanied by several theoretical results. By minimizing DSI, we construct the optimal partitioning tree where densely connected nodes in the graph tend to have the same assignment, revealing the cluster struc- ture. DSI is also theoretically presented as a new graph clustering objective, not requiring the pre-defined cluster number. Furthermore, we design a neural LSEnet in the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space, where we integrate node features to structural information via manifold-valued graph convolution. Extensive empirical results on real graphs show the superiority of our approach.

paragraphs: LSEnet addresses graph clustering when the number of clusters is unknown. Many deep clustering methods require that number beforehand, making it an input to the method rather than something discovered from the graph. The paper approaches this challenge through structural information, an information-theoretic description of graph organization.

The authors develop a continuous, differentiable form of structural information and provide theoretical results for it. Minimizing this quantity constructs an optimal partitioning tree in which densely connected nodes tend to receive the same assignment. They also establish it as a graph clustering objective that does not require a predefined cluster count.

LSEnet implements this approach in the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space. Its graph convolution operates on that geometry and incorporates node features into the structural information framework. Experiments on real graphs report superiority over the evaluated alternatives. The contribution brings together an objective for discovering cluster structure, a differentiable formulation suitable for deep learning, and a neural architecture that uses both graph connections and node attributes.
summary.tldr: LSEnet combines differentiable structural information with hyperbolic graph learning to cluster graphs without a predefined number of clusters.

title: LSEnet: Lorentz Structural Entropy Neural Network for Deep Graph Clustering

abstract: Reconstructing high-resolution (HR) images from low-resolution (LR) inputs poses a significant challenge in image super-resolution (SR). While recent approaches have demonstrated the efficacy of intricate operations customized for various objectives, the straightforward stacking of these disparate operations can result in a substantial computational burden, hampering their practical utility. In response, we introduce SeemoRe, an efficient SR model employing expert mining. Our approach strategically incorporates experts at different levels, adopting a collaborative methodology. At the macro scale, our experts address rank-wise and spatial-wise informative features, providing a holistic understanding. Subsequently, the model delves into the subtleties of rank choice by leveraging a mixture of low-rank experts. By tapping into experts specialized in distinct key factors crucial for accurate SR, our model excels in uncovering intricate intra-feature details. This collaborative approach is reminiscent of the concept of “see more", allowing our model to achieve an optimal performance with minimal computational costs in efficient settings.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution reconstructs a high-resolution image from a lower-resolution input. Specialized operations can help recover different kinds of detail, but simply stacking them can make a model computationally expensive. SeemoRe addresses this tension by organizing specialized experts into a collaborative architecture designed for efficient super-resolution.

These levels of specialization are intended to capture distinct factors needed for reconstruction and uncover fine detail within the learned features.

The approach matters because specialization is built into how the model distributes its reconstruction work, instead of merely adding more disparate operations. The authors report an optimal performance outcome with minimal computational costs in efficient settings. The stated finding supports the proposed balance between detailed reconstruction and computational economy in that setting; it does not establish that one expert arrangement is universally optimal for every super-resolution problem.
summary.tldr: SeemoRe combines spatial and rank-focused experts, including low-rank mixtures, to recover image detail with low computational cost.

title: See More Details: Efficient Image Super-Resolution by Experts Mining

abstract: Fine-tuning vision-language models (VLMs) with abundant unlabeled data recently has attracted increasing attention. Existing methods that resort to the pseudolabeling strategy would suffer from heavily incorrect hard pseudolabels when VLMs exhibit low zero-shot performance in downstream tasks. To alleviate this issue, we propose a Candidate Pseudolabel Learning method, termed CPL, to fine-tune VLMs with suitable candidate pseudolabels of unlabeled data in downstream tasks. The core of our method lies in the generation strategy of candidate pseudolabels, which progressively generates refined candidate pseudolabels by both intra- and inter-instance label selection, based on a confidence score matrix for all unlabeled data. This strategy can result in better performance in true label inclusion and class-balanced instance selection. In this way, we can directly apply existing loss functions to learn with generated candidate psueudolabels. Extensive experiments on nine benchmark datasets with three learning paradigms demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Our code can be found here.

paragraphs: Candidate Pseudolabel Learning addresses a weakness in adapting vision-language models with unlabeled examples. Existing approaches often assign each example a single predicted label and train on that assignment. When the model initially performs poorly on the target task, these hard pseudolabels can contain many mistakes and provide misleading training guidance.

CPL instead generates candidate pseudolabels using a matrix of confidence scores across the unlabeled dataset. Its selection process works both within individual examples and across examples, progressively refining the candidates. This connects two objectives: keeping the true label among the possibilities and selecting examples in a more balanced way across classes.

The generated candidates can be used with existing loss functions, making the selection strategy the central contribution. Experiments across nine benchmark datasets and three learning paradigms support its effectiveness. The findings suggest that prompt tuning with unlabeled data can benefit from improving the labels supplied to training, especially when committing immediately to one predicted class would introduce substantial errors.
summary.tldr: CPL improves vision-language model adaptation by refining candidate pseudolabels instead of immediately trusting a single predicted label.

title: Candidate Pseudolabel Learning: Enhancing Vision-Language Models by Prompt Tuning with Unlabeled Data

abstract: Aligning large language models with humans is challenging due to the inherently multifaceted nature of preference feedback. While existing approaches typically frame this as a multi-objective optimization problem, they often overlook how humans actually make decisions. Research on bounded rationality suggests that human decision making follows satisficing strategies- optimizing primary objectives while ensuring others meet acceptable thresholds. To bridge this gap and operationalize the notion of satisficing alignment, we propose SITAlign: an inference-time framework that addresses the multifaceted nature of alignment by maximizing a primary objective while satisfying threshold-based constraints on secondary criteria. We provide theoretical insights by deriving sub-optimality bounds of our satisficing-based inference alignment approach. We empirically validate SITAlign’s performance through extensive experimentation on multiple benchmarks. For instance, on the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset with the primary objective of maximizing helpfulness while ensuring a threshold on harmlessness, SITAlign outperforms the state-of-the-art multi-objective decoding strategy by a margin of 22.3% in terms of GPT-4 win-tie rate for helpfulness reward while adhering to the threshold on harmlessness.

paragraphs: Human preferences involve several criteria, but people do not always try to maximize all of them simultaneously. The paper draws on satisficing: prioritize one objective while keeping other considerations above acceptable thresholds. SITAlign turns this decision-making idea into a framework for aligning language-model outputs during inference.

The framework maximizes a primary objective subject to threshold constraints on secondary criteria. For example, helpfulness can be the quantity to improve while harmlessness must meet a specified standard. This formulation gives the secondary criteria a concrete role in defining acceptable responses. The authors also derive sub-optimality bounds to characterize how the approach compares with an optimum.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks support SITAlign's effectiveness. On PKU-SafeRLHF, the authors report a 22.3% margin over a leading multi-objective decoding strategy in GPT-4 win-tie rate for helpfulness reward, while meeting the harmlessness threshold. This result supports the approach in the evaluated setting: explicitly prioritizing helpfulness within a constrained acceptable set can improve the measured outcome while respecting the selected secondary requirement.
summary.tldr: SITAlign guides inference by maximizing a primary preference while requiring secondary criteria to satisfy acceptable thresholds.

title: Bounded Rationality for LLMs: Satisficing Alignment at Inference-Time

abstract: We study the offline active learning problem on graphs. In this problem, one seeks to select k vertices whose labels are best suited for predicting the labels of all the other vertices in the graph. Guillory and Bilmes (Guillory & Bilmes, 2009) introduced a natural theoretical model motivated by a label smoothness assumption. Prior to our work, algorithms with theoretical guarantees were only known for restricted graph types such as trees (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2010) despite the models simplicity. We present the first O(log n)-resource augmented algorithm for general weighted graphs. To complement our algorithm, we show constant hardness of approximation.

Prior to our work, algorithms with theoretical guarantees were only known for restricted graph types such as trees (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2010) despite the models simplicity. We present the first O(log n)-resource augmented algorithm for general weighted graphs. To complement our algorithm, we show constant hardness of approximation.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose which vertices of a graph should have their labels revealed. The objective is to select k vertices whose labels will be most useful for predicting labels elsewhere in the graph. The setting is offline: the problem centers on selecting a set of vertices, under a theoretical model motivated by smoothness of labels across the graph.

Previously, algorithms with theoretical guarantees in this model were available only for restricted graph families, including trees. The authors extend the algorithmic picture to general weighted graphs. Their result uses O(log n) resource augmentation, meaning the guarantee allows an enlargement of the selection resource that scales logarithmically with graph size. That qualification is central to understanding what the algorithm achieves.

The paper also establishes constant hardness of approximation, identifying an obstacle to obtaining arbitrarily accurate approximation guarantees. The algorithm and hardness result together clarify the computational landscape: useful guarantees extend beyond simple graph structures, while approximation remains constrained by intrinsic difficulty.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a resource-augmented active-learning algorithm for general weighted graphs and establishes a complementary approximation-hardness result.

title: Algorithms and Hardness for Active Learning on Graphs

abstract: We address the regression problem under the constraint of demographic parity, a commonly used fairness definition. Recent studies have revealed fair minimax optimal regression algorithms, the most accurate algorithms that adhere to the fairness constraint. However, these analyses are tightly coupled with specific data generation models. In this paper, we provide meta-theorems that can be applied to various situations to validate the fair minimax optimality of the corresponding regression algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fair minimax optimal regression can be achieved through post-processing methods, allowing researchers and practitioners to focus on improving conventional regression techniques, which can then be efficiently adapted for fair regression.

paragraphs: This paper considers regression subject to demographic parity, a fairness constraint. The objective is to achieve the strongest possible predictive accuracy while satisfying that constraint. Earlier work established fair minimax-optimal methods, but its analyses were closely tied to particular models of how the data were generated, making the conclusions specific to those settings.

The authors develop meta-theorems that can validate fair minimax optimality across a variety of situations. These results provide a reusable level of analysis: instead of deriving every fairness-constrained regression result entirely around one data-generation model, researchers can apply broader theorems to the corresponding algorithms. Minimax optimality concerns the best worst-case accuracy within the setting being analyzed.

The paper also shows that post-processing can achieve fair minimax-optimal regression. This makes improvements to conventional regression methods relevant to fair regression, because their outputs can subsequently be adapted to the constraint. The contribution is a theoretical basis for this workflow, allowing predictive modeling and fairness adaptation to be developed as connected stages.
summary.tldr: Reusable meta-theorems show how post-processing can achieve minimax-optimal regression under demographic parity.

title: Meta Optimality for Demographic Parity Constrained Regression via Post-Processing

abstract: Time series synthesis has become a foundational task in modern society, underpinning decision-making across various scenes. Recent approaches primarily generate time series from structured conditions, such as attribute-based metadata. However, these methods struggle to capture the full complexity of time series, as the predefined structures often fail to reflect intricate temporal dynamics or other nuanced characteristics. Moreover, constructing structured metadata requires expert knowledge, making large-scale data labeling costly and impractical. In this paper, we introduce VerbalTS, a novel framework for generating time series from unstructured textual descriptions, offering a more expressive and flexible solution to time series synthesis. To bridge the gap between unstructured text and time series data, VerbalTS employs a multi-focal alignment and generation framework, effectively modeling their complex relationships. Experiments on two synthetic and four real-world datasets demonstrate that VerbalTS outperforms existing methods in both generation quality and semantic alignment with textual conditions.

paragraphs: Generating a time series often involves specifying structured attributes that describe the desired output. Such predefined fields may miss nuanced temporal behavior, and producing their labels can require expert effort. VerbalTS instead uses unstructured textual descriptions as conditions, aiming to make the requested characteristics more expressive and flexible.

The main technical problem is connecting descriptions in language with patterns in sequential data. VerbalTS introduces a multi-focal alignment and generation framework to model those relationships. Its objective encompasses both generating a time series and making the generated sequence correspond to the meaning of the text that conditions it.

Experiments on two synthetic and four real-world datasets show improvements over existing methods in generation quality and semantic alignment. These two findings address complementary requirements: the output should be a good time series and reflect the requested description. The work supports text as a useful interface for time-series synthesis in the evaluated settings, expanding the kinds of conditions available beyond predefined metadata fields.
summary.tldr: VerbalTS generates time series from free-form descriptions, improving generation quality and textual alignment across six evaluated datasets.

title: VerbalTS: Generating Time Series from Texts

abstract: Conditional flow matching (CFM) stands out as an efficient, simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, achieving remarkable performance for data generation. However, CFM is insufficient to ensure accuracy in learning probability paths. In this paper, we introduce a new partial differential equation characterization for the error between the learned and exact probability paths, along with its solution. We show that the total variation gap between the two probability paths is bounded above by a combination of the CFM loss and an associated divergence loss. This theoretical insight leads to the design of a new objective function that simultaneously matches the flow and its divergence. Our new approach improves the performance of the flow-based generative model by a noticeable margin without sacrificing generation efficiency. We showcase the advantages of this enhanced training approach over CFM on several important benchmark tasks, including generative modeling for dynamical systems, DNA sequences, and videos. Code is available at https://github.com/Utah-Math-Data-Science/Flow_Div_Matching.

paragraphs: Conditional flow matching efficiently trains generative models without simulating the full generation process during training. However, the paper shows that its objective alone is insufficient to ensure accurate probability paths. The issue concerns how the learned distribution evolves, beyond whether the model matches the target flow according to the usual training loss.

The authors derive a partial differential equation describing the discrepancy between learned and exact probability paths, together with its solution. They then bound the total variation gap using a combination of the conditional flow-matching loss and a divergence loss. Divergence describes local expansion or contraction of the flow, providing an additional quantity relevant to the evolution of probability.

This analysis motivates an objective that matches both flow and divergence. Experiments on generative modeling for dynamical systems, DNA sequences, and videos show noticeable improvements without sacrificing generation efficiency. The result gives a mathematical reason for adding the extra training term and empirical evidence that the resulting objective improves the tested generative models.
summary.tldr: Matching flow divergence alongside flow improves generative modeling and yields a bound connecting training losses to probability-path error.

title: Improving Flow Matching by Aligning Flow Divergence

abstract: Medical imaging faces significant challenges in single-domain generalization (SDG) due to the diversity of imaging devices and the variability among data collection centers. To address these challenges, we propose TinyMIG, a framework designed to transfer generalization capabilities from vision foundation models to medical imaging SDG. TinyMIG aims to enable lightweight specialized models to mimic the strong generalization capabilities of foundation models in terms of both global feature distribution and local fine-grained details during training. Specifically, for global feature distribution, we propose a Global Distribution Consistency Learning strategy that mimics the prior distributions of the foundation model layer by layer. For local fine-grained details, we further design a Localized Representation Alignment method, which promotes semantic alignment and generalization distillation between the specialized model and the foundation model. These mechanisms collectively enable the specialized model to achieve robust performance in diverse medical imaging scenarios. Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that TinyMIG, with extremely low computational cost, significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models, showcasing its superior SDG capabilities. All the code and model weights will be publicly available.

paragraphs: Medical images vary across devices and collection centers, making it difficult for a model trained in one domain to generalize elsewhere. TinyMIG aims to transfer the generalization capabilities of vision foundation models into lightweight specialized models. Its training approach asks the smaller model to imitate both broad feature structure and fine-grained local information.

For global structure, Global Distribution Consistency Learning matches the foundation model’s prior feature distributions layer by layer. For local detail, Localized Representation Alignment encourages semantic agreement between the specialized model and the foundation model. The two mechanisms address different scales of representation, so transfer is not limited to matching only an overall distribution or only localized features.

Large-scale benchmark experiments report that TinyMIG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models at extremely low computational cost. The findings support this combination of global and local guidance for single-domain generalization in the evaluated medical-imaging scenarios. The practical aim is to make a lightweight specialized model benefit from a foundation model’s broader representations during training.
summary.tldr: TinyMIG transfers global feature distributions and local semantic details from vision foundation models to lightweight medical-imaging models for stronger single-domain generalization.

title: TinyMIG: Transferring Generalization from Vision Foundation Models to Single-Domain Medical Imaging

abstract: Traditional text-based person ReID assumes that person descriptions from witnesses are complete and provided at once. However, in real-world scenarios, such descriptions are often partial or vague. To address this limitation, we introduce a new task called interactive person re-identification (Inter-ReID). Inter-ReID is a dialogue-based retrieval task that iteratively refines initial descriptions through ongoing interactions with the witnesses. To facilitate the study of this new task, we construct a dialogue dataset that incorporates multiple types of questions by decomposing fine-grained attributes of individuals. We further propose LLaVA-ReID, a question model that generates targeted questions based on visual and textual contexts to elicit additional details about the target person. Leveraging a looking-forward strategy, we prioritize the most informative questions as supervision during training. Experimental results on both Inter-ReID and text-based ReID benchmarks demonstrate that LLaVA-ReID significantly outperforms baselines.

paragraphs: Text-based person re-identification commonly assumes that a witness supplies a complete description in one step. This paper instead starts from partial or vague descriptions and introduces interactive person re-identification. The system refines its retrieval query through a dialogue with the witness, making the acquisition of missing information part of the task itself.

To support this setting, the authors construct a dialogue dataset by breaking person descriptions into fine-grained attributes and incorporating several question types. Their LLaVA-ReID model uses both visual and textual context to generate targeted follow-up questions. The goal is to request additional details that are useful for identifying the intended person.

Training uses a looking-forward strategy to prioritize the most informative questions as supervision. This makes question selection an explicit learning objective, alongside the broader retrieval task. Experiments on both the new interactive benchmark and conventional text-based person re-identification benchmarks show significant improvements over the compared baselines. The findings support learning which details to ask for when the original description is incomplete.
summary.tldr: LLaVA-ReID learns informative follow-up questions to refine incomplete person descriptions and improve retrieval through dialogue.

title: LLaVA-ReID: Selective Multi-image Questioner for Interactive Person Re-Identification

abstract: Random defense represents a promising strategy to protect neural networks from adversarial attacks. Most of these methods enhance robustness by injecting randomness into the data, increasing uncertainty for attackers. However, this randomness could reduce the generalization capacity of defense, as defense performance could be sensitive to the hyperparameters of noise added to the data, making it difficult to generalize across different datasets. Additionally, the involvement of randomness always comes with a reduction of natural accuracy, which leads to a delicate trade-off between them, which is seldom studied in random defense. In this work, we propose incorporating randomness into the network structure instead of data input by designing stochastic deformable convolution, where a random mask replaces the convolutional offset. This process promotes data independence, enhancing generalization across datasets. To study the trade-off, we conduct a theoretical analysis of both robust and clean accuracy, from a perspective of gradient cosine similarity and natural inference. Based on the analysis, we reformulate the adversarial training in our random defense framework. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves SOTA adversarial robustness and clean accuracy compared with other random defense methods.

paragraphs: Randomized defenses aim to make adversarial attacks harder by introducing uncertainty into a neural network’s behavior. Adding noise to input data can help, but its effectiveness may depend heavily on noise settings and the dataset. It can also reduce accuracy on ordinary, unmodified inputs. This paper studies that trade-off while moving randomness into the network structure.

The proposed mechanism is stochastic deformable convolution, in which a random mask replaces the convolutional offset. By introducing randomness through this structural component, the method promotes independence from the input data and aims to generalize better across datasets. The contribution therefore concerns both where randomness enters the model and how the resulting defense is trained.

The authors analyze robust and clean accuracy through gradient cosine similarity and natural inference, then use that analysis to reformulate adversarial training. Experiments report state-of-the-art robustness and clean accuracy relative to other randomized defenses. The stated comparison supports a better balance within that family of methods, rather than establishing superiority over every possible defense.
summary.tldr: Stochastic deformable convolution introduces randomness into network structure and uses a theoretical accuracy analysis to improve adversarial defense training.

title: Adversarial Robustness via Deformable Convolution with Stochasticity

abstract: Real-world multimodal data usually exhibit complex structural relationships beyond traditional one-to-one mappings like image-caption pairs. Entities across modalities interact in intricate ways, with images and text forming diverse interconnections through contextual dependencies and co-references. Graphs provide powerful structural information for modeling intra-modal and inter-modal relationships. However, previous works fail to distinguish multi-hop neighbors and treat the graph as a standalone modality, which fragments the overall understanding. This limitation presents two key challenges in multimodal learning: (1) integrating structural information from multi-hop neighbors into foundational models, and (2) fusing modality-specific information in a principled manner. To address these challenges, we revisit the role of graphs in multimodal learning within the era of foundation models and propose Graph4MM, a graph-based multimodal learning framework. To be specific, we introduce Hop-Diffused Attention, which integrates multi-hop structural information into self-attention through causal masking and hop diffusion. Furthermore, we design MM-QFormer, a multi-mapping querying transformer for cross-modal fusion. Through theoretical and empirical analysis, we show that leveraging structures to integrate both intra- and inter-modal interactions improves multimodal understanding beyond treating them as a standalone modality. Experiments on both generative and discriminative tasks show that Graph4MM outperforms larger VLMs, LLMs, and multimodal graph baselines, achieving a 6.93% average improvement.

paragraphs: Multimodal information often forms a network of relationships more complex than individual image-caption pairs. Images and text can share references and contextual connections both within and across modalities. Graph4MM investigates how these connections can directly shape multimodal learning, addressing approaches that treat graph structure as a separate input modality or fail to distinguish neighbors at different distances.

The framework introduces Hop-Diffused Attention, which incorporates information from multiple graph hops into self-attention using causal masking and hop diffusion. It also introduces MM-QFormer, a querying transformer designed to fuse information across modalities through multiple mappings. Together, these components address structural integration and the combination of modality-specific content.

Theoretical and empirical analyses support using graph relationships to organize interactions within and between modalities. Across generative and discriminative tasks, Graph4MM outperforms the evaluated larger vision-language models, language models, and multimodal graph baselines, with a reported average improvement of 6.93%. The findings indicate that exploiting relationships among inputs can improve multimodal understanding beyond simply supplying graph information as another modality.
summary.tldr: Graph4MM integrates graph relationships into attention and cross-modal fusion, improving performance on evaluated multimodal tasks.

title: Graph4MM: Weaving Multimodal Learning with Structural Information

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful tool for neural combinatorial optimization, enabling models to learn heuristics that solve complex problems without requiring expert knowledge. Despite significant progress, existing RL approaches face challenges such as diminishing reward signals and inefficient exploration in vast combinatorial action spaces, leading to inefficiency. In this paper, we propose Preference Optimization, a novel method that transforms quantitative reward signals into qualitative preference signals via statistical comparison modeling, emphasizing the superiority among sampled solutions. Methodologically, by reparameterizing the reward function in terms of policy and utilizing preference models, we formulate an entropy-regularized RL objective that aligns the policy directly with preferences while avoiding intractable computations. Furthermore, we integrate local search techniques into the fine-tuning rather than post-process to generate high-quality preference pairs, helping the policy escape local optima. Empirical results on various benchmarks, such as the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) and the Flexible Flow Shop Problem (FFSP), demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing RL algorithms, achieving superior convergence efficiency and solution quality.

paragraphs: Neural combinatorial optimization uses learned policies to construct solutions to problems such as routing and scheduling. Reinforcement learning can teach these heuristics without expert demonstrations, but weak reward signals and enormous action spaces can make learning inefficient. This paper changes how the training process represents feedback about solution quality.

Preference Optimization converts numerical rewards into comparisons indicating which sampled solutions are better. Through a policy-based reparameterization of reward and statistical preference models, the authors formulate an entropy-regularized reinforcement learning objective that aligns the policy with those comparisons while avoiding intractable computations. Local search is incorporated into fine-tuning to produce high-quality preference pairs and help the policy escape local optima.

The method significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning algorithms on the evaluated benchmarks, including traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and flexible flow shop problems. The reported benefits cover both convergence efficiency and solution quality. Its central contribution is to make relative solution quality a direct training signal, while using local search to improve the comparisons from which the policy learns.
summary.tldr: Preference Optimization trains combinatorial solvers from solution comparisons and incorporates local search into fine-tuning to improve convergence and solution quality.

title: Preference Optimization for Combinatorial Optimization Problems

abstract: Traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) cannot generalize to new graphs with node attributes different from the training ones, making zero-shot generalization across different node attribute domains an open challenge in graph machine learning. In this paper, we propose STAGE, which encodes statistical dependencies between attributes rather than individual attribute values, which may differ in test graphs. By assuming these dependencies remain invariant under changes in node attributes, STAGE achieves provable generalization guarantees for a family of domain shifts. Empirically, STAGE demonstrates strong zero-shot performance on medium-sized datasets: when trained on multiple graph datasets with different attribute spaces (varying in types and number) and evaluated on graphs with entirely new attributes, STAGE achieves a relative improvement in Hits@1 between 40% to 103% in link prediction and a 10% improvement in node classification compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks face a difficult transfer problem when new graphs describe nodes using entirely different attributes. The meanings and even the number of input features can change. STAGE addresses this by representing statistical dependencies among attributes, using those relationships as the basis for transfer across attribute domains.

The theoretical guarantee assumes that these dependencies remain invariant when node attributes change. Under that assumption, the authors prove generalization for a family of domain shifts. This identifies a specific source of transferable structure: attribute values and identities may differ, while their statistical relationships remain stable enough for the method's analysis to apply.

Experiments train STAGE on multiple graph datasets with differing attribute types and counts, then evaluate graphs with entirely new attributes. On medium-sized datasets, the reported relative improvement in link-prediction Hits@1 ranges from 40% to 103%, alongside a 10% improvement in node classification over state-of-the-art baselines. These results support dependency-based representations for the evaluated zero-shot transfers, while the formal guarantee retains its invariance assumption.
summary.tldr: STAGE transfers across graphs with new node attributes by encoding statistical dependencies, with guarantees when those dependencies remain invariant.

title: Zero-Shot Generalization of GNNs over Distinct Attribute Domains

abstract: We address the problem of extending a pre-trained large language model to a new domain that was not seen during training. Standard techniques, such as fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation (LoRA) are successful at domain adaptation, but do not formally add capacity to the model. This often leads to a trade-off, between performing well on the new domain vs. degrading performance on the original domain. Here, we propose to revisit and improve adapters to extend LLMs. Our paper analyzes this extension problem from three angles: data, architecture and training procedure, which are advantageously considered jointly. The resulting method, called neutral residues, modifies adapters in a way that leads to each new residual block to output near-zeros on the original domain. This solution leads to strong results when adapting a state-of-the-art model originally trained on English to a new language. Neutral residues significantly outperforms competing approaches such as fine-tuning, LoRA or vanilla adapters in terms of the trade-off between learning the new language and not forgetting English.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained language model to an unseen domain can improve new capabilities while degrading existing ones. The paper examines this trade-off through model extension. Its starting point is that standard fine-tuning and LoRA can adapt a model successfully but do not formally add capacity, motivating a renewed look at adapters.

The proposed method, neutral residues, considers training data, architecture, and training procedure jointly. It changes adapters so that each added residual block produces outputs close to zero on the original domain. This makes the new blocks approximately neutral for original-domain inputs while providing added components through which the model can learn the new domain.

The authors evaluate adaptation of a state-of-the-art English-trained model to a new language. Neutral residues significantly improves the trade-off between learning that language and retaining English performance compared with fine-tuning, LoRA, and ordinary adapters. The stated result supports designing added capacity around preservation of existing behavior; the near-zero construction does not itself claim perfect preservation of every original capability.
summary.tldr: Neutral residues add adapters that are nearly inactive on the original domain, improving new-language learning while preserving English performance.

title: Neutral residues: revisiting adapters for model extension

abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler’s predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model’s inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

paragraphs: Strong sequence prediction can suggest that a foundation model has learned the deeper system generating its data, but evaluating that possibility is difficult. This paper introduces an inductive bias probe: a technique that examines how a model adapts to synthetic datasets produced by a proposed world model.

The probe asks whether the foundation model’s tendencies during adaptation align with that underlying model. This shifts evaluation toward what the model carries into new tasks. Across multiple domains, the authors find that models can perform very well on their training tasks while failing to acquire an inductive bias toward the proposed world model.

In the orbital-trajectory study, trained models consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis suggests behavior consistent with task-specific heuristics that do not transfer. These findings show why success on a prediction task alone may provide insufficient evidence of deeper understanding, and the probe supplies a way to investigate that distinction through adaptation.
summary.tldr: Inductive bias probes show that strong training-task performance can coexist with failure to transfer an underlying world model to new tasks.

title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models

abstract: Few-shot point cloud semantic segmentation effectively addresses data scarcity by identifying unlabeled query samples through semantic prototypes generated from a small set of labeled support samples. However, pre-training-based methods suffer from domain shifts and increased training time. Additionally, existing methods using DGCNN as the backbone have limited geometric structure modeling capabilities and struggle to bridge the categorical information gap between query and support sets. To address these challenges, we propose DyPolySeg, a pre-training-free Dynamic Polynomial fitting network for few-shot point cloud semantic segmentation. Specifically, we design a unified Dynamic Polynomial Convolution (DyPolyConv) that extracts flat and detailed features of local geometry through Low-order Convolution (LoConv) and Dynamic High-order Convolution (DyHoConv), complemented by Mamba Block for capturing global context information. Furthermore, we propose a lightweight Prototype Completion Module (PCM) that reduces structural differences through self-enhancement and interactive enhancement between query and support sets. Experiments demonstrate that DyPolySeg achieves state-of-the-art performance on S3DIS and ScanNet datasets.

paragraphs: DyPolySeg tackles semantic segmentation of point clouds when only a small set of labeled support examples is available. These examples provide category prototypes used to identify points in an unlabeled query. The paper targets two difficulties: capturing enough geometric structure and connecting category information between the support and query sets. It also seeks to avoid the domain shifts and additional training time associated with pre-training.

The proposed network learns without a separate pre-training stage. Its dynamic polynomial convolution combines a low-order component for flatter local geometry with a dynamic higher-order component for finer geometric detail. A Mamba block adds global context, allowing the representation to incorporate information beyond individual local neighborhoods.

A lightweight prototype completion module further connects the support and query representations. It uses self-enhancement and interaction between the two sets to reduce structural differences that hinder matching. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on S3DIS and ScanNet. Together, the results support combining richer geometric modeling with prototype refinement for segmentation from limited labeled examples.
summary.tldr: DyPolySeg combines dynamic polynomial geometry features and prototype completion for leading few-shot point cloud segmentation without pre-training.

title: DyPolySeg: Taylor Series-Inspired Dynamic Polynomial Fitting Network for Few-shot Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have showcased remarkable performance across a range of tasks but are hindered by their massive parameter sizes, which impose significant computational and storage demands. Pruning has emerged as an effective solution to reduce model size, but traditional methods often involve inefficient retraining or rely on heuristic-based one-shot approaches that lack theoretical guarantees. In this paper, we reformulate the pruning problem as an $\ell_0$-penalized optimization problem and propose a monotone accelerated Iterative Hard Thresholding (mAIHT) method. Our approach combines solid theoretical foundations with practical effectiveness, offering a detailed theoretical analysis that covers convergence, convergence rates, and risk upper bounds. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that mAIHT outperforms state-of-the-art pruning techniques by effectively pruning the LLaMA-7B model across various evaluation metrics.

paragraphs: Large language models require substantial storage and computation because they contain so many parameters. Pruning reduces this burden by removing parameters, but choosing what to remove presents an optimization problem. The paper targets a gap between expensive methods involving retraining and one-shot heuristics that lack theoretical guarantees about their behavior.

The authors formulate pruning as an optimization problem with an ℓ0 penalty, which penalizes the number of retained nonzero parameters. They propose monotone accelerated Iterative Hard Thresholding, or mAIHT, to solve this formulation. This makes the preference for a smaller model an explicit part of the objective rather than leaving parameter removal entirely to a heuristic rule.

The theoretical analysis addresses whether the method converges, how quickly it converges, and upper bounds on risk. Experiments pruning LLaMA-7B report better performance than state-of-the-art pruning techniques across several evaluation metrics. The contribution therefore combines an analyzed optimization procedure with empirical evidence on a specific language model, supporting a more principled approach to reducing model size.
summary.tldr: mAIHT casts language-model pruning as sparse optimization, combining convergence and risk analysis with improved pruning results on LLaMA-7B.

title: An Efficient Pruner for Large Language Model with Theoretical Guarantee

abstract: Most existing unlearnable strategies focus on preventing unauthorized users from training single-task learning (STL) models with personal data. Nevertheless, the paradigm has recently shifted towards multi-task data and multi-task learning (MTL), targeting generalist and foundation models that can handle multiple tasks simultaneously. Despite their growing importance, MTL data and models have been largely neglected while pursuing unlearnable strategies. This paper presents MTL-UE, the first unified framework for generating unlearnable examples for multi-task data and MTL models. Instead of optimizing perturbations for each sample, we design a generator-based structure that introduces label priors and class-wise feature embeddings which leads to much better attacking performance. In addition, MTL-UE incorporates intra-task and inter-task embedding regularization to increase inter-class separation and suppress intra-class variance which enhances the attack robustness greatly. Furthermore, MTL-UE is versatile with good supports for dense prediction tasks in MTL. It is also plug-and-play allowing integrating existing surrogate-dependent unlearnable methods with little adaptation. Extensive experiments show that MTL-UE achieves superior attacking performance consistently across 4 MTL datasets, 3 base UE methods, 5 model backbones, and 5 MTL task-weighting strategies. Code is available at https://github.com/yuyi-sd/MTL-UE.
