paragraphs: Unlearnable examples modify data to hinder unauthorized model training. Most existing approaches target a single task, leaving a gap for data used to train models on several tasks simultaneously. MTL-UE addresses this gap with a unified framework for generating unlearnable examples for multi-task data and models.

The framework generates perturbations with a shared generator instead of optimizing them separately for every sample. It incorporates label priors and class-specific feature embeddings to improve attack performance. Regularization within and across tasks encourages greater separation between classes while reducing variation within each class, strengthening the attack's robustness. The framework also supports dense prediction tasks and can incorporate existing surrogate-dependent unlearnable methods with limited adaptation.

Experiments report consistently superior attack performance across four multi-task datasets, three base unlearnable-example methods, five model backbones, and five task-weighting strategies. This breadth matters because multi-task training can vary in both architecture and how it balances objectives. The findings support designing data-protection perturbations around shared multi-task structure rather than treating each task in isolation.
summary.tldr: MTL-UE generates perturbations that hinder multi-task model training using label information and regularized class embeddings.

title: MTL-UE: Learning to Learn Nothing for Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Distributed learning methods have gained substantial momentum in recent years, with communication overhead often emerging as a critical bottleneck. Gradient compression techniques alleviate communication costs but involve an inherent trade-off between the empirical efficiency of biased compressors and the theoretical guarantees of unbiased compressors. In this work, we introduce a novel Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) compression scheme that leverages biased compressors to construct statistically unbiased estimates. This approach effectively bridges the gap between biased and unbiased methods, combining the strengths of both. To showcase the versatility of our method, we apply it to popular compressors, like Top-$k$ and bit-wise compressors, resulting in enhanced variants. Furthermore, we derive an adaptive version of our approach to further improve its performance. We validate our method empirically on distributed deep learning tasks.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can spend substantial resources communicating gradients between workers. Compressing those gradients reduces communication, but the choice of compressor creates a trade-off. Biased compressors can work well empirically, while unbiased compressors offer statistical properties that support theoretical guarantees. The paper seeks to combine these advantages within a single compression framework.

The proposed approach uses Multilevel Monte Carlo to construct statistically unbiased estimates from biased compressors. The crucial distinction is between the compression operations used as ingredients and the estimate produced by the overall scheme: biased ingredients can contribute to an unbiased final estimate. This gives the framework a way to retain useful compression methods while addressing their bias.

The authors apply the scheme to Top-k and bit-wise compressors and also derive an adaptive version intended to improve performance further. They evaluate the approach on distributed deep learning tasks. Its stated contribution is therefore both a general construction and implementations for familiar compression choices, with empirical validation supporting its use beyond the statistical formulation.
summary.tldr: A Multilevel Monte Carlo scheme turns biased gradient compressors into statistically unbiased estimators for distributed learning.

title: Beyond Communication Overhead: A Multilevel Monte Carlo Approach for Mitigating Compression Bias in Distributed Learning

abstract: Efficient LLM inference research has largely focused on reducing the cost of each decoding step (e.g., using quantization, pruning, or sparse attention), typically applying a uniform computation budget to every generated token. In practice, token difficulty varies widely, so static compression can over-compute on easy steps and under-compute on hard ones. We study dynamic budget allocation for autoregressive decoding: learning how much computation to spend per token from within a single model. Self-Optimizing Language Models (SOL) pair a frozen LLM with a lightweight policy network that reads the LLM hidden state and selects a discrete efficiency action at each decode step. Actions can jointly control (i) token-level attention sparsity, (ii) structured activation pruning in the MLP, and (iii) activation quantization bit-width, while leaving the base model weights unchanged. We train the policy with group-relative policy optimization on teacher-forced episodes: the token sequence is fixed, while we sample multiple compute schedules (i.e., “counterfactual” schedules that vary only the efficiency actions for the same token path) and compare their likelihoods under the same supervision. Our reward trades off language-model quality against soft penalties that encourage episode-average budget usage to match a requested target. Across model variants and compute regimes, SOL improves quality at matched budget over static allocation and strong random schedule search, offering a complementary axis for inference-efficiency optimization. SOL discovers a better quality-efficiency pareto-front across all our experiments and improves MMLU accuracy by up to 7.3% over uniform budget allocation strategies.

These findings support learning where computation is most useful within a single model.
summary.tldr: A learned policy allocates computation token by token, improving measured language-model quality at matched budgets without changing base weights.

title: Compute Where it Counts: Self Optimizing Language Models

abstract: Humans facing algorithmic decision systems have been found to “game” them by altering their input data (at a cost to them) in order to favorably change the algorithmic outcomes they receive (at a cost to the algorithm). The growing literature on strategic classification seeks to develop robust machine learning algorithms that account for, and reduce, unwanted strategic behavior. A limitation of these existing works is that they assume the cost of strategic behavior to be fixed and independent of the classifier’s decision. In practice, however, manipulation costs evolve and depend on past algorithmic decisions: today’s decisions influence tomorrow’s costs. This paper proposes and analyzes a two-stage robust optimization framework with a decision-dependent uncertainty set to capture such dependencies. We highlight that awareness of policy-dependent costs not only reduces uncertainty, but also better curtails gaming of the algorithmic system over time.

paragraphs: People can respond strategically to an algorithm by changing their inputs to obtain more favorable decisions. Those changes carry costs, and strategic classification tries to account for them when designing the classifier. This paper examines a feedback effect: the algorithm's current decisions can change how costly manipulation becomes in the future.

Existing approaches described in the abstract assume that manipulation costs are fixed and independent of classifier decisions. The authors replace that assumption with a two-stage robust optimization framework. Its uncertainty set depends on the decision, allowing the range of possible future costs to change with the policy chosen today.

This formulation makes the consequences of a policy part of the uncertainty the algorithm must manage. The paper's analysis highlights that recognizing policy-dependent costs can both reduce uncertainty and better restrain gaming over time. The contribution is a model of strategic behavior in which the classifier influences future incentives, rather than treating manipulation costs as an external quantity that stays unchanged as decisions accumulate.
summary.tldr: A two-stage robust framework models how classifier decisions change future manipulation costs and can help curb strategic gaming over time.

title: Robust Strategic Classification under Decision-Dependent Cost Uncertainty

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) commonly boost reasoning via sample-evaluate-ensemble decoders (e.g., majority voting), achieving label free gains without ground truth. However, prevailing strategies score candidates using only external outputs such as token probabilities, entropies, or self evaluations, and these signals can be poorly calibrated after post training. We instead analyze internal behavior based on neuron activations and uncover three findings: (1) external signals are low dimensional projections of richer internal dynamics; (2) correct responses activate substantially fewer unique neurons than incorrect ones throughout generation; and (3) activations from correct responses exhibit stronger cross sample agreement, whereas incorrect ones diverge. Motivated by these observations, we propose Neuron Agreement Decoding (NAD), an unsupervised best of N method that selects candidates using activation sparsity and cross sample neuron agreement, operating solely on internal signals and without requiring comparable textual outputs. NAD enables early correctness prediction within the first 32 generated tokens and supports aggressive early stopping. Across math and science benchmarks with verifiable answers, NAD matches majority voting; on open ended coding benchmarks where majority voting is inapplicable, NAD consistently outperforms Avg@64. By pruning unpromising trajectories early, NAD reduces token usage by 99% with minimal loss in generation quality, showing that internal signals provide reliable, scalable, and efficient guidance for label free ensemble decoding.

paragraphs: Selecting among several generated answers often relies on output probabilities, uncertainty scores, or the model’s own evaluations. These signals can be poorly calibrated after post-training. This paper examines neuron activations instead, arguing that external scores expose only low-dimensional projections of richer internal behavior.

The authors find that correct responses activate fewer distinct neurons during generation and show stronger agreement in activated neurons across samples. Incorrect responses have more divergent activation patterns. Neuron Agreement Decoding uses these observations to select among candidates without labels, combining activation sparsity with cross-sample agreement. Because it uses internal signals, candidates need not have directly comparable text.

On mathematical and scientific tasks with verifiable answers, the method matches majority voting. On open-ended coding tasks, where majority voting is inapplicable, it outperforms Avg@64. The paper also reports correctness prediction within the first 32 generated tokens, enabling early pruning of unpromising trajectories. Its reported 99% token reduction with minimal quality loss shows the potential efficiency benefit in the evaluated setting, alongside the candidate-selection results.
summary.tldr: Neuron Agreement Decoding uses sparse, consistent internal activations to select promising answers and stop weak generations early.

title: Do LLMs Signal When They’re Right? Evidence from Neuron Agreement

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) combining reinforcement learning (RL) ignite remarkable progress in multimodal reasoning, yet still struggle with medical images, which typically exhibit extremely sparse visual evidence to inform clinical decision-making. We recognize that pruning visual tokens outside the grounding region greatly enhances medical reasoning. However, a united RL framework for active visual token pruning (VTP) and medical multimodal reasoning remains unestablished. Here, we propose a dual-stream RL framework, ViToS, to fulfill token pruning and question answering. ViToS trains one policy model with two task branches, where one focuses on grounding while the other conducts token-sparse reasoning after VTP. Furthermore, we solve the coupled policy learning problem by introducing the cross-feedback sequential optimization, avoiding gradient conflict and facilitating convergence of the shared policy model. Evaluated on seven medical benchmarks, our method reduces visual tokens to 77% of the original sequence length while achieving a 108.27% relative performance on Lingshu-7B and 104.16% relative performance on HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B. Overall, ViToS delivers superior performance and inference speedup, establishing an efficient paradigm for medical multimodal reasoning.

ViToS turns that observation into a unified reinforcement learning framework that learns both where to focus and how to answer using the retained visual information.

One shared policy model has two task branches. The grounding branch identifies relevant visual regions, while the reasoning branch answers after visual token pruning. Because these tasks are coupled, their updates can conflict. The proposed cross-feedback sequential optimization coordinates their learning to avoid gradient conflict and facilitate convergence of the shared policy.

Across seven medical benchmarks, ViToS retains 77% of the original visual-token sequence length. It reports relative performance of 108.27% on Lingshu-7B and 104.16% on HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, together with faster inference. These are relative performance levels, rather than gains of 108% and 104%. The findings support learning visual selection jointly with answering to improve the efficiency of medical multimodal reasoning.
summary.tldr: ViToS jointly learns visual grounding and token-pruned medical reasoning, improving reported performance while retaining 77% of visual tokens.

title: Token-Sparse Medical Multimodal Reasoning via Dual-Stream Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion policy sampling enables reinforcement learning (RL) to represent multimodal action distributions beyond suboptimal unimodal Gaussian policies. However, existing diffusion-based RL methods primarily focus on offline setting for reward maximization, with limited consideration of safety in online settings. To address this gap, we propose Augmented Lagrangian-Guided Diffusion (ALGD), a novel algorithm for off-policy safe RL. By revisiting optimization theory and energy-based modeling, we show that the instability of primal–dual methods arises from the non-convex Lagrangian landscape. In diffusion-based safe RL, the Lagrangian can be interpreted as an energy function guiding the denoising dynamics; counter-intuitively, direct usage destabilizes both policy generation and training. ALGD resolves this issue by introducing an augmented Lagrangian that locally convexifies the energy landscape, yielding a stabilized policy generation and training, without altering the distribution of optimal policy. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments demonstrate that ALGD is both theoretically grounded and empirically effective, achieving strong and stable performance across diverse environments.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can represent several distinct modes of action, giving reinforcement learning more flexibility than a unimodal Gaussian policy. This paper investigates how to use that flexibility for safe learning in online settings. It proposes Augmented Lagrangian-Guided Diffusion, or ALGD, as an off-policy algorithm that incorporates safety into diffusion-based policy generation.

The authors interpret the Lagrangian, which combines the optimization objective with constraints, as an energy function guiding denoising. Their analysis traces instability in primal–dual methods to the non-convex shape of that energy landscape. Directly using the Lagrangian as diffusion guidance can therefore destabilize both the generation of actions and the learning process.

ALGD introduces an augmented Lagrangian that locally makes the energy landscape convex, stabilizing generation and training without changing the distribution of the optimal policy. This local modification is central to the method’s theoretical rationale. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments support the approach, with strong and stable performance across diverse environments. The result connects the geometry of constrained optimization to the behavior of a diffusion policy.
summary.tldr: ALGD stabilizes safe diffusion-policy learning by locally convexifying its guiding energy landscape while preserving the optimal policy distribution.

title: How Does the Lagrangian Guide Safe Reinforcement Learning through Diffusion Models?

abstract: Mobile Graphical User Interface (GUI) World Models (WMs) offer a promising path for improving mobile GUI agent performance at train- and inference-time. However, current approaches face a critical trade-off: text-based WMs sacrifice visual fidelity, while the inability of visual WMs in precise text rendering led to their reliance on slow, complex pipelines dependent on numerous external models. We propose a novel paradigm: visual world modeling via renderable code generation, where a single Vision-Language Model (VLM) predicts the next GUI state as executable web code that renders to pixels, rather than generating pixels directly. This combines the strengths of both approaches: VLMs retain their linguistic priors for precise text rendering while their pre-training on structured web code enables high-fidelity visual generation. We introduce gWorld (8B, 32B), the first open-weight visual mobile GUI WMs built on this paradigm, along with a data generation framework (gWorld) that automatically synthesizes code-based training data. In extensive evaluation across 4 in- and 2 out-of-distribution benchmarks, gWorld sets a new pareto frontier in accuracy versus model size, outperforming 8 frontier open-weight models over 50.25x larger. Further analyses show that (1) scaling training data via gWorld yields meaningful gains, (2) each component of our pipeline improves data quality, and (3) stronger world modeling improves downstream mobile GUI policy performance.

paragraphs: A mobile GUI world model predicts what an interface will look like next, helping an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions. Existing approaches face a representation problem: text descriptions lose visual detail, while direct visual generation struggles with precise text and can require complicated pipelines involving multiple models.

The paper proposes predicting executable web code that renders into the next interface image. A single vision-language model supplies both the linguistic structure needed for accurate text and the structured code needed to produce the visual layout. The authors introduce open-weight gWorld models at 8B and 32B sizes, together with a framework that automatically synthesizes code-based training data.

Further analyses find gains from additional generated training data and contributions from each pipeline component to data quality. summary.tldr: gWorld predicts mobile interfaces as renderable web code, combining precise text with visual detail and improving the reported accuracy-versus-model-size trade-off.

title: Generative Visual Code Mobile World Models

abstract: Supervised Graph Outlier Detection has long been constrained by severe class imbalance, and although recent diffusion-based augmentation methods have improved sample quality, their practical utility is hindered by the high computational costs of multi-step iterative sampling and the stochasticity of the generation process. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Graph Outlier Synthesis via Origin Consistency Model (GOCM), a single-step graph outlier synthesis framework based on a consistency model. Theoretically, we pioneer the Origin Consistency (OC) mechanism by employing an “Interval-based Origin Inference” strategy, which mathematically derives a direct mapping from the noise trajectory to the data origin, achieving robust and efficient single-step sample generation. Architecturally, to address the complexity of heterogeneous graphs containing multiple relations, we design the Multi-input Variational Graph Auto-Encoder (MiVGAE), which decouples intricate structures via relation-level message passing and cross-relation fusion, mapping them into a unified latent space, from which GOCM synthesizes high-quality outlier nodes. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that GOCM achieves superior detection performance with significantly improved generation efficiency. The source code is publicly available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RFS-2026-EB63/.

paragraphs: Supervised graph outlier detection often has far fewer anomalous examples than normal ones. Generating additional outliers can help address that imbalance, but diffusion-based generation requires repeated sampling steps and introduces stochastic variation. GOCM proposes a consistency-model approach that synthesizes graph outliers in a single step.

Its Origin Consistency mechanism uses an interval-based inference strategy to derive a direct mapping from a noise trajectory to the data origin. The framework also handles graphs containing multiple kinds of relationships through a Multi-input Variational Graph Auto-Encoder. This component processes relations separately, combines information across them, and maps the resulting structure into a shared latent space. GOCM generates outlier nodes from that representation.

Experiments on multiple real-world datasets report superior detection performance together with significantly better generation efficiency. The contribution combines a faster synthesis mechanism with a representation designed for heterogeneous graph structure. The findings indicate that reducing generation to one step can still produce useful synthetic outliers, improving the downstream detection task while reducing the computational burden of augmentation.
summary.tldr: GOCM synthesizes graph outliers in one step, improving generation efficiency and downstream detection in the reported experiments.

title: GOCM: Single-Step Graph Outlier Synthesis via Origin Consistency Model

abstract: Video predictive models are emerging as a powerful paradigm in robotics, offering a promising path toward task generalization, long-horizon planning, and flexible decision-making. However, prevailing approaches often operate on 2D video sequences, inherently lacking the 3D geometric understanding necessary for precise spatial reasoning and physical consistency. We introduce a Structured 4D Latent Predictive Model, which predicts the evolution of a scene’s 3D structure in a structured latent space conditioned on observations and textual instructions. Our representation encodes the scene holistically and can be decoded into diverse 3D formats, enabling a more complete and 3D consistent scene understanding. This structured 4D latent predictive model serves as a planner, generating future scenes that are translated into executable actions by a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics module. Experiments demonstrate that our model generates futures with strong visual quality, substantially better 3D consistency and multi-view coherence compared to state-of-the-art video-based planners. Consequently, our full planning pipeline achieves superior performance on complex manipulation tasks, exhibits robust generalization to novel visual conditions, and proves effective on real-world robotic platforms. Our website is available at https://structured-4d-model.github.io/.

paragraphs: Robot planners based on predicted video can describe plausible futures, but operating on two-dimensional frames can leave them without the geometric understanding needed for precise spatial reasoning. This paper proposes predicting how a scene’s three-dimensional structure evolves over time. That combination of spatial structure and temporal evolution motivates the model’s four-dimensional representation.

The model predicts within a structured latent space, conditioned on observations and textual instructions. Its representation captures the scene holistically and can be decoded into multiple three-dimensional formats. To use these predictions for control, a goal-conditioned inverse dynamics module converts generated future scenes into executable robot actions. Scene prediction and action generation thus form a complete planning pipeline.

Experiments show strong visual quality and substantially better three-dimensional consistency and agreement across views than state-of-the-art video-based planners. The full system also achieves superior performance on complex manipulation tasks, generalizes robustly to novel visual conditions, and works on real robotic platforms. These findings support explicit evolving scene geometry as a useful foundation for robot planning.
summary.tldr: The model plans robot actions by predicting evolving 3D scenes, improving geometric consistency and manipulation performance.

title: Structured 4D Latent Predictive Model for Robot Planning

abstract: Long-form TV dramas present a formidable challenge for comprehensive video understanding, where deciphering complex storyline often relies on speaker recognition, the task of accurately attributing each spoken utterance to its respective character. In this paper, we advance this field through two primary contributions. (1) We introduce DramaSR-532K, a large-scale benchmark comprising 532K annotated dialogue lines across more than 900 unique characters, necessitating the integration of auditory, linguistic, and visual cues for speaker recognition. (2) We propose DramaSR-LRM, a robust approach built upon a large reasoning model (LRM). DramaSR-LRM is designed to autonomously aggregate contextual evidence via multimodal tool-use, synthesizing diverse inputs to achieve high-fidelity attribution. Experimental results demonstrate that DramaSR-LRM significantly outperforms existing baselines, particularly on short utterances where acoustic biometrics are inherently unreliable. All the data and code will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Following a long television drama requires knowing which character spoke each line. That attribution can be difficult when many characters appear across an extended storyline, particularly when a brief utterance contains little distinctive voice information. This paper develops both an evaluation resource and a reasoning-based method for identifying speakers using several kinds of evidence.

DramaSR-532K contains 532,000 annotated dialogue lines involving more than 900 distinct characters. Its speaker-recognition tasks require combining auditory, linguistic, and visual cues. The proposed DramaSR-LRM system builds on a large reasoning model and uses multimodal tools to gather contextual evidence autonomously. It then combines that evidence to attribute each utterance to a character.

The experiments show significant improvements over existing baselines, especially for short utterances where acoustic biometrics are inherently unreliable. This finding highlights the value of context when voice information alone is weak. The paired contributions provide a large-scale way to evaluate speaker attribution and an approach that treats identification as a multimodal reasoning task within the surrounding drama.
summary.tldr: DramaSR-LRM combines multimodal contextual evidence to improve speaker recognition in TV dramas, especially for short utterances.

title: Reasoning LLM Improves Speaker Recognition in Long-form TV Dramas

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across many tasks but remain vulnerable to hallucinations, making it important to systematically evaluate their reliability under realistic adversarial inputs. We formulate hallucination elicitation as a constrained optimization problem, where the goal is to find semantically coherent adversarial prompts that are equivalent to benign user prompts. Existing attack methods remain limited: discrete prompt-based attacks preserve semantic equivalence and coherence but search only over a limited set of prompt variations, while continuous latent-space attacks explore a richer space but often decode into prompts that are no longer valid rephrasings. To address these limitations, we propose REALISTA, a realistic latent-space attack framework. REALISTA constructs an input-dependent dictionary of valid editing directions, each corresponding to a semantically equivalent and coherent rephrasing, and optimizes continuous combinations of these directions in latent space. This design combines the optimization flexibility of continuous attacks with the semantic realism of discrete rephrasing-based attacks. Experiments demonstrate that REALISTA achieves superior or comparable performance to state-of-the-art realistic attacks on open-source LLMs and, crucially, succeeds in attacking large reasoning models under free-form response settings, where prior realistic attacks fail.

paragraphs: REALISTA studies whether meaning-preserving rephrasings of ordinary prompts can induce language models to hallucinate. The task is framed as constrained optimization: adversarial prompts should remain coherent and semantically equivalent to their benign originals. This makes the evaluation about reliability under realistic wording changes, rather than arbitrary changes to the user's request.

Existing discrete attacks search a limited collection of rephrasings, while continuous latent-space attacks can explore more broadly but may decode into invalid paraphrases. REALISTA builds a dictionary specific to each input, with editing directions corresponding to coherent, equivalent rephrasings. It then optimizes continuous combinations of those directions in latent space, connecting flexible search with a structure grounded in valid edits.

Experiments on open-source language models show performance that is superior or comparable to state-of-the-art realistic attacks. The method also succeeds against large reasoning models in free-form response settings where previous realistic attacks fail. These findings expose reliability weaknesses that can remain hidden when evaluation covers only a narrower set of semantically equivalent prompts.
summary.tldr: REALISTA searches continuous combinations of valid rephrasing directions to find realistic prompts that elicit hallucinations.

title: REALISTA: Realistic Latent Adversarial Attacks that Elicit LLM Hallucinations

abstract: Large-scale web-harvested datasets have fueled the progress of cross-modal retrieval but inevitably suffer from noisy correspondence, which severely degrades model generalization. Existing methods primarily address this by filtering out noise or seeking a substitute label, yet they predominantly remain bound by a “Discrete Selection” paradigm. We argue that relying on a single discrete proxy induces SinglePoint Fragility and Discretization Error. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework, Intra-modal Neighbor-aware Noise Rectification (IN2R), which shifts the paradigm from searching for a substitute to synthesizing a reliable supervision target. Leveraging the intrinsic geometric stability of intra-modal data, IN2R employs a Graph Refiner to perform relational reasoning over neighbors retrieved from a dynamic Cross-Model Memory. Instead of propagating discrete labels, our method synthesizes a continuous, soft prototype that reflects the consensus of the local semantic neighborhood, effectively rectifying inter-modal misalignment. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K, MS-COCO, and CC152K demonstrate that IN2R significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval learns relationships between different kinds of data, but web-collected training pairs can contain incorrect matches. This paper argues that filtering examples or choosing a single replacement target leaves learning vulnerable to a bad individual choice. A discrete replacement also compresses potentially richer neighborhood information into one selected proxy.

Intra-modal Neighbor-aware Noise Rectification, or IN2R, constructs a soft supervision target from multiple related examples. A dynamic Cross-Model Memory supplies neighbors, and a Graph Refiner reasons over their relationships. The resulting continuous prototype represents agreement within a local semantic neighborhood, using structure inside each modality to help repair mismatches between modalities.

This approach makes neighborhood consensus the basis for correcting supervision rather than simply replacing one questionable match with another. Experiments on Flickr30K, MS-COCO, and CC152K report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the usefulness of synthesizing a target from relational evidence when cross-modal pairings are noisy. The method’s rationale rests on the geometric stability available within modalities, which supplies the information used for that synthesis.
summary.tldr: IN2R repairs noisy cross-modal supervision by synthesizing soft targets from graph-based reasoning over neighboring examples.

title: Intra-Modal Neighbors Never Lie: Rectifying Inter-Modal Noisy Correspondence via Graph-Based Intra-Modal Reasoning

abstract: Tool-augmented reasoning has emerged as a promising direction for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing studies mainly focus on enabling models to perform tool invocation, while neglecting the necessity of invoking tools. We argue that tool usage is not always beneficial, as redundant or inappropriate invocations largely increase reasoning overhead and even mislead model predictions. To address this issue, we introduce AutoTool, a model that adaptively decides whether to invoke tools according to the characteristics of each query. Within a reinforcement learning framework, we design an explicit dual-mode reasoning strategy with mode-specific reward functions to guide the model toward producing accurate responses. Moreover, to prevent premature bias toward a single reasoning mode, AutoTool jointly explores and balances tool-assisted and text-centric reasoning throughout training, and promotes free exploration in later stages. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AutoTool exhibits outstanding performance and high efficiency, yielding a 21.8% accuracy gain on V* benchmark compared to the base model, and a 44.9% improvement in efficiency over existing tool-augmented methods on POPE benchmark. Code is available at https://github.com/MQinghe/AutoTool.

paragraphs: Giving a multimodal model access to tools creates another decision: whether a particular question actually needs them. Unnecessary or unsuitable calls can add work and lead the model toward an incorrect answer. AutoTool addresses this decision directly, learning when to use tool assistance and when to rely on text-centric reasoning.

The training framework uses reinforcement learning with two explicit reasoning modes and separate reward functions for each. It encourages exploration of both modes and balances them during training so that the model does not settle prematurely on one approach. Later training allows freer exploration, supporting query-dependent choices rather than a fixed preference for tool use.

The experiments report a 21.8% accuracy gain over the base model on V* and a 44.9% efficiency improvement over existing tool-augmented methods on POPE. These results concern different benchmarks and comparisons. Together, they support treating tool selection as part of the reasoning problem: performance depends on choosing useful assistance as well as knowing how to invoke it.
summary.tldr: AutoTool learns when to use tools or text-centric reasoning, improving reported accuracy and efficiency through adaptive selection.

title: Are Tools Always Beneficial? Learning to Invoke Tools Adaptively for Dual-Mode Multimodal LLM Reasoning

abstract: We present ReflFlow, a novel framework for high-fidelity rendering of dynamic specular scenes by addressing two key challenges: precise reflection direction estimation and physically accurate modeling. To achieve this, we propose a Residual Material-Augmented 2D Gaussian Splatting representation that models dynamic geometry and material properties, allowing accurate reflection ray computation. Furthermore, we introduce a Dynamic Environment Gaussian and a hybrid rendering pipeline that decomposes rendering into diffuse and specular components, enabling physically informed specular synthesis via rasterization and ray tracing. Finally, we devise a coarse-to-fine training strategy to improve optimization stability and promote physically meaningful decomposition. Extensive experiments on dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate that ReflFlow outperforms prior methods quantitatively and qualitatively, producing sharper and more realistic specular reflections in complex dynamic environments.

Furthermore, we introduce a Dynamic Environment Gaussian and a hybrid rendering pipeline that decomposes rendering into diffuse and specular components, enabling physically informed specular synthesis via rasterization and ray tracing. Finally, we devise a coarse-to-fine training strategy to improve optimization stability and promote physically meaningful decomposition. Extensive experiments on dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate that ReflFlow outperforms prior methods quantitatively and qualitatively, producing sharper and more realistic specular reflections in complex dynamic environments.

paragraphs: Reconstructing moving scenes with shiny surfaces requires estimating where reflected rays travel and modeling how materials produce reflections. ReflFlow addresses both challenges in a framework for rendering dynamic specular scenes. Its design connects the representation of changing geometry to the computation of reflection directions.

The method uses a residual, material-augmented 2D Gaussian Splatting representation to model geometry and material properties together. A Dynamic Environment Gaussian and a hybrid rendering pipeline then separate diffuse and specular components. Rasterization and ray tracing support physically informed synthesis of the reflective component. This decomposition gives geometry, materials, and reflection rendering distinct but connected roles.

Training proceeds from coarse to fine to improve optimization stability and encourage a physically meaningful separation of the components. On dynamic-scene benchmarks, the authors report quantitative and qualitative improvements over prior methods, including sharper and more realistic reflections in complex changing environments. The results support combining geometry-guided reflection computation with a rendering pipeline that explicitly accounts for specular appearance.
summary.tldr: ReflFlow combines dynamic geometry and material modeling with hybrid rendering to produce sharper, more realistic reflections in moving scenes.

title: ReflFlow: Learning Geometry-Guided Ray Tracing for Dynamic Specular Reconstruction

abstract: Adversarial Training (AT) is a leading defense against adversarial examples but often suffers from Catastrophic Overfitting (CO) in efficient single-step variants, where robustness to multi-step attacks collapses despite high single-step performance. We address this failure mode with two contributions. First, we formalize Epsilon Overfitting (EO), a perspective in which fixed perturbation magnitudes and directions exacerbate CO, and show that introducing perturbation variability significantly improves robust generalization across different architectures and datasets. Second, we propose PertAlign (Perturbation Alignment), a theoretically grounded, computationally negligible metric that predicts CO onset by measuring gradient alignment across attack stages. Leveraging these insights, we introduce SORA, an adaptive step-size AT method that dynamically adjusts perturbations based on loss surface geometry. SORA consistently prevents CO, achieves state-of-the-art robustness and clean accuracy, and generalizes across datasets and architectures using a single fixed set of hyperparameters, which is essential for applicability in fast AT. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets and architectures show that SORA matches or surpasses the robustness of prior methods while delivering higher clean accuracy and superior efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/SecondOrderAT/SORA.

paragraphs: Fast adversarial training uses inexpensive single-step attacks to train models against adversarial examples. It can suffer catastrophic overfitting, where apparent resistance to those attacks remains high while robustness against multistep attacks collapses. This paper studies that failure through epsilon overfitting, emphasizing how fixed perturbation magnitudes and directions can worsen the problem.

The authors show that varying perturbations improves robust generalization across tested architectures and datasets. They also introduce PertAlign, a computationally negligible measure of gradient alignment across attack stages that predicts the onset of catastrophic overfitting. These ideas motivate SORA, which adapts attack step sizes according to the geometry of the loss surface and thereby changes perturbations during training.

Across the reported experiments, SORA consistently avoids catastrophic overfitting and matches or exceeds prior robustness while improving clean accuracy and efficiency. It works across datasets and architectures with a single fixed set of hyperparameters. The results support geometry-aware perturbation adaptation as a practical way to stabilize fast adversarial training without giving up its computational advantages.
summary.tldr: SORA adapts adversarial perturbations to loss geometry, preventing catastrophic overfitting across the reported fast-training experiments.

title: SORA: Free Second-Order Attacks in Fast Adversarial Training

abstract: We propose a scalable method for training prediction (machine learning) models in the predict-then-optimize paradigm, where model outputs serve as coefficients for a subsequent linear optimization task. Directly minimizing the empirical decision regret is intractable for linear programming and combinatorial optimization since the decision mapping is piecewise constant, and the gradients are zero almost everywhere. While existing methods address this by smoothing the differentiation process, they suffer from scalability issues, since a computationally expensive solver call is required for every gradient evaluation. To address this, we propose a decision-focused learning pipeline based on a measure transformation principle, which yields a new surrogate loss that is completely optimization-solver-free during training. We establish theoretical guarantees, including Fisher consistency and excess risk bounds. Empirically, our method achieves decision quality competitive with state-of-the-art methods while reducing training time by orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: In predict-then-optimize systems, a machine learning model predicts coefficients that a later optimization problem uses to choose a decision. Training should therefore care about the quality of the resulting decision. The difficulty is that small prediction changes often leave the selected decision unchanged, making direct gradients of decision regret zero almost everywhere.

Existing approaches smooth this relationship to obtain useful training signals, but typically require an expensive optimization solver call for every gradient evaluation. This paper introduces a surrogate loss derived through a measure transformation principle. The resulting training pipeline remains focused on decision quality while eliminating optimization solver calls during training, directly addressing a major computational bottleneck.

The authors establish Fisher consistency and excess risk bounds, providing theoretical connections between optimizing the surrogate and improving the target decision objective. Experiments report decision quality competitive with leading methods while reducing training time by orders of magnitude. The solver-free claim concerns training: the overall setting still includes a subsequent optimization task that converts predictions into decisions.
summary.tldr: A theoretically supported surrogate trains decision-focused prediction models without solver calls, substantially reducing reported training costs.

title: A Solver-Free Training Method for Predict-then-Optimize

abstract: Generalization remains a central challenge in offline reinforcement learning (RL), where policies are trained solely from static datasets and must perform reliably under distribution shift. While most existing offline RL methods focus on reducing training loss using standard optimizers such as Adam, the role of loss landscape geometry $-$ particularly sharpness $-$ has received little attention. Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has recently shown strong generalization benefits in supervised learning by favoring flatter minima. However, directly applying SAM to offline RL is non-trivial: unlike supervised settings with ground-truth labels, offline RL relies on bootstrapped targets, making sharpness estimation noisy and often destabilizing optimization. In this paper, we revisit offline RL from an optimization perspective and investigate how sharpness-aware optimization can be made effective in this setting. We propose Q bound weighted SAM (Q-SAM), a robust and scalable framework that treats sharpness as a weighted objective and selectively prioritizes samples that are most suitable for sharpness-aware optimization based on Q bounds. By aligning the SAM objective with the characteristics of bootstrapped value estimation, Q-SAM amplifies the benefits of sharpness minimization while preserving training stability. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks demonstrate that Q-SAM consistently improves generalization performance across diverse datasets and algorithms. Our results highlight the importance of loss sharpness in offline RL and suggest optimizer design as a promising direction for developing more robust offline RL methods.

title: Q-SAM: Unlocking Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Generalization in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent advancements in generative AI have led to image editing models capable of producing realistic forgeries that evade traditional image forgery localization methods, as these approaches depend on physical noise absent in synthetic data. To address this challenge, we theoretically demonstrate that the diffusion process inherently suppresses local high-frequency variance, creating a statistical energy gap that is distinguishable from the natural entropy of optical imaging. Guided by this insight, we propose FLAME, a unified framework that utilizes a LAD map to capture these intrinsic anomalies, coupled with a parameter-efficient adapter for SAM to achieve precise, pixel-level forgery localization. Furthermore, to bridge the lag between forensic benchmarks and evolving generative models, we introduce EditStream, an automated pipeline for continuous, instruction-based training data synthesis. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FLAME establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming previous methods on AI-generated forgery datasets while effectively generalizing to unseen generative architectures. Our code is available at https://github.com/phoenixnir/FLAME.

This paper instead examines a statistical trace associated with diffusion generation. The authors theoretically show that diffusion suppresses local high-frequency variance, producing an energy difference distinguishable from the natural entropy of optical imaging.

FLAME uses a LAD map to expose these anomalies and combines it with a parameter-efficient adapter for SAM. Together, these components identify manipulated regions at pixel level. The approach connects the proposed statistical signal to spatial localization, so the output indicates where a forgery occurs within an image.

The paper also introduces EditStream, an automated pipeline that continuously synthesizes instruction-based training examples to help keep forensic data aligned with evolving editing models. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on AI-generated forgery datasets, significant improvements over previous methods, and generalization to unseen generative architectures. These findings support the usefulness of diffusion-related energy anomalies across the evaluated forgery settings.
summary.tldr: FLAME localizes AI image edits using diffusion-related energy anomalies and reports strong performance on unseen generative architectures.

title: Order within Chaos: Capturing Intrinsic Energy Anomalies for AI-Manipulated Image Forgery Localization

abstract: Building interactive omni-modal assistants often relies on end-to-end multimodal alignment to fuse heterogeneous modalities, which incurs substantial data and compute costs and limits extensibility. We present Training-Free Large Language Model Orchestration (LLM Orchestration), a training-free orchestration framework that integrates off-the-shelf modality experts into a unified multimodal input–output system without additional gradient-based training for integration. LLM Orchestration comprises three components: (1) an LLM controller that infers user intent and emits explicit control tokens for expert selection and sequencing, enabling protocol-constrained and auditable routing; (2) a text-centric cross-modal memory that compresses multimodal evidence into structured records for lightweight retrieval and reuse, reducing redundant expert invocations across turns; and (3) a unified interaction layer that executes routing and memory decisions to support consistent modality transitions, full-duplex streaming, and interruption-aware dialogue. Across diverse multimodal benchmarks, LLM Orchestration achieves strong performance under standard evaluation constraints while maintaining low orchestration overhead and modular upgradeability, providing a practical alternative to costly joint training for omni-modal systems.

paragraphs: This paper builds a multimodal assistant by coordinating existing modality experts. Jointly training an integrated system can demand substantial data and computation and complicate later extensions. The proposed orchestration framework combines off-the-shelf components without additional gradient-based training for their integration, making coordination the central design problem.

An LLM controller interprets user intent and emits explicit control tokens to select and sequence experts. This makes routing constrained by a protocol and available for inspection. A text-centered memory compresses multimodal evidence into structured records that can be retrieved across turns, reducing repeated expert calls. A unified interaction layer executes these decisions and handles modality transitions, simultaneous two-way streaming, and interruptions.

Across diverse multimodal benchmarks, the framework reports strong performance under standard evaluation constraints with low orchestration overhead. Its modular design also supports upgrading components. These findings present orchestration as a practical alternative to costly joint training for the evaluated systems, with memory and interaction management contributing alongside the controller’s choice of experts.
summary.tldr: An LLM controller, structured memory, and interaction layer combine existing modality experts without additional integration training.

title: Training-Free Multimodal Large Language Model Orchestration

abstract: Discrete diffusion models have recently emerged as a compelling alternative for language generation, enabling efficient non-autoregressive sampling while achieving strong empirical performance. A key design choice in discrete diffusion—absent in most continuous diffusion formulations—is the forward corruption kernel, with masked/absorbing corruption now dominating practice. Despite this empirical preference, there is limited statistical theory explaining when and why masking should outperform alternative kernels such as uniform replacement. In this paper, we take a step toward closing this gap from a statistical learning perspective. Our analysis establishes generalization bounds and, through an explicit comparison across different forward corruption kernels, reveals a central advantage of masking: it scales with the effective data support rather than the full ambient state space, thereby mitigating the curse of state space cardinality. We further derive structure-aware refinements that capture how concentration and sparsity in real sequential data sharpen the sample complexities. Together, these results offer a principled explanation for the empirical strength of masked diffusion and provide guidance for forward-kernel design in discrete generative modeling.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion models learn to generate sequences by reversing a corruption process. A major design choice is how that corruption changes the sequence, such as masking symbols or replacing them uniformly. Masking is widely used in practice, and this paper develops statistical theory to help explain its advantage over alternative corruption rules.

The authors derive generalization bounds and explicitly compare forward corruption kernels. Their central finding is that masking's bounds scale with effective data support rather than the entire ambient state space. In plain language, the relevant complexity tracks the portion of possible outcomes supported by the data, instead of charging for every theoretically possible state.

Further refinements incorporate concentration and sparsity in sequential data, showing how such structure can sharpen sample-complexity bounds. These are theoretical statements about learning requirements, providing an explanation for masking's empirical strength. The work matters because the corruption rule influences more than the mechanics of generation: it can also change how the amount and structure of available data enter generalization guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper derives bounds showing how masking can exploit effective data support and sequence structure in discrete diffusion learning.

title: Generalization Bounds for Discrete Diffusion: Statistical Advantage of Masking

abstract: Most evaluations of External Memory Module assume a static setting: memory is built offline and queried at a fixed state. In practice, memory is streaming: new facts arrive continuously, insertions interleave with retrievals, and the memory state evolves while the model is serving queries. In this regime, accuracy and cost are governed by the full memory lifecycle, which encompasses the ingestion, maintenance, retrieval, and integration of information into generation. We present Neuromem, a scalable testbed that benchmarks External Memory Module under an interleaved insertion-and-retrieval protocol and decomposes its lifecycle into five dimensions including memory data structure, normalization strategy, consolidation policy, query formulation strategy, and context integration mechanism. Using three representative datasets LoCoMo, LONGMEMEVAL, and MemAgentBench, Neuromem evaluates interchangeable variants within a shared serving stack, reporting token-level F1 and insertion/retrieval latency.Overall, we observe that performance typically degrades as memory grows across rounds, and time-related queries remain the most challenging category. The memory data structure largely determines the attainable quality frontier, while aggressive compression and generative integration mechanisms mostly shift cost between insertion and retrieval with limited accuracy gain.

paragraphs: An external memory system can behave differently when information keeps arriving during use than when it is built once and queried afterward. Neuromem evaluates this streaming setting by interleaving new insertions with retrieval requests. The aim is to understand how the full memory lifecycle affects answer quality and the time required to serve queries.

The testbed separates five design choices: memory data structure, normalization, consolidation, query formulation, and integration of retrieved information into generation. It compares interchangeable variants within a shared serving stack on LoCoMo, LONGMEMEVAL, and MemAgentBench. Measurements include token-level F1 and insertion and retrieval latency, making both information quality and operational cost visible.

The authors observe that performance typically declines as memory grows across rounds, with time-related questions remaining the hardest category. The data structure largely determines the attainable quality frontier. Aggressive compression and generative integration mostly redistribute costs between inserting and retrieving information, with limited accuracy gains. These findings make evolving memory organization a central consideration when evaluating systems intended for continuous use.
summary.tldr: Neuromem benchmarks continuously growing language-model memory, revealing quality degradation and important trade-offs across the memory lifecycle.

title: Neuromem: A Granular Decomposition of the Streaming Lifecycle in External Memory for LLMs

abstract: "Thinking with images" has emerged as a central research theme in the realm of Vision-Language Models (VLMs). This multimodal reasoning paradigm typically features interleaved images generated via tool use or code execution as part of the Chain-of-Thought (CoT). While reinforcement learning (RL) has driven impressive performance within this paradigm, in this position paper, we argue that current VLMs seldom truly "think" with interleaved images. Through empirical evidence and analysis, we demonstrate that interleaved images do not play a significant role in the success of recent "Thinking with images" methods. Instead, the primary source of performance gains is the improved language generation distribution resulting from fine-tuning. These findings challenge the prevailing belief that "Thinking with images" VLMs actively utilize visual information to complete visual tasks. To improve mechanistic transparency, we suggest that future "Thinking with images" works include lightweight ablation studies to verify the necessity of interleaved images. Furthermore, we call upon the community to develop fundamentally novel benchmarks and advocate for more informative visual tools.

paragraphs: This position paper questions whether vision-language models actually rely on intermediate images in approaches described as thinking with images. These methods insert images produced by tools or code into a reasoning sequence. Their performance improvements, often obtained through reinforcement learning, might appear to show that the model uses those images as part of its reasoning.

The authors present empirical evidence and analysis indicating that intermediate images play little role in the success of the recent methods they examine. They attribute the main gains to changes in language generation produced by fine-tuning. This separates improved task performance from evidence about the mechanism responsible for that improvement.

The authors recommend lightweight ablation studies to test whether the images are necessary, making the contribution of visual information more transparent. They also call for new benchmarks and more informative visual tools. Their position challenges the interpretation of current results: including images within a reasoning sequence does not by itself demonstrate that those images explain the system’s success.
summary.tldr: The authors find that gains in examined image-interleaved reasoning methods mainly come from improved language generation, motivating tests of whether intermediate images matter.

abstract: In this paper we propose a novel, scalable, clustering based Ordinal Regression formulation, which is an instance of a Second Order Cone Program (SOCP) with one Second Order Cone (SOC) constraint. The main contribution of the paper is a fast algorithm, CBOR, which solves the proposed formulation more efficiently than general purpose solvers. Another main contribution of the paper is to pose the problem of focused crawling as a large scale Ordinal Regression problem and solve using the proposed CB-OR. Focused crawling is an efficient mechanism for discovering resources of interest on the web. Posing the problem of focused crawling as an Ordinal Regression problem avoids the need for a negative class and topic hierarchy, which are the main drawbacks of the existing focused crawling methods. Experiments on large synthetic and benchmark datasets show the scalability of CB-OR. Experiments also show that the proposed focused crawler outperforms the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Focused crawling aims to discover web resources relevant to a particular interest. This paper treats that task as a large-scale ordinal regression problem, which uses ordered outcomes. The formulation avoids requiring a negative class or a topic hierarchy, two requirements the authors identify as major drawbacks of existing focused crawling methods.

To support this application, the paper introduces a scalable ordinal regression formulation based on clustering. It is a second-order cone program with one second-order cone constraint. The authors develop a dedicated algorithm, CB-OR, that solves the formulation more efficiently than general-purpose solvers. The modeling contribution and the computational contribution work together to make the large-scale crawling formulation usable.

Experiments on large synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate the solver's scalability. Separate crawling experiments show that the proposed crawler outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluation. These findings support both parts of the contribution: an efficient method for solving the ordinal regression problem and an application that uses it to discover relevant web resources.
summary.tldr: CB-OR efficiently solves a clustering-based ordinal regression formulation and supports a focused crawler that performs strongly in experiments.

title: Focused crawling with scalable ordinal regression solvers

abstract: Clustering with constraints is a developing area of machine learning. Various papers have used constraints to enforce particular clusterings, seed clustering algorithms and even learn distance functions which are then used for clustering. We present intractability results for some constraint combinations and illustrate both formally and experimentally the implications of these results for using constraints with clustering.
originalAbstract: Clustering with constraints is a developing area of machine learning. Various papers have used constraints to enforce particular clusterings, seed clustering algorithms and even learn distance functions which are then used for clustering. We present intractability results for some constraint combinations and illustrate both formally and experimentally the implications of these results for using constraints with clustering.

paragraphs: Clustering constraints provide information about how data should be grouped. The paper places them in several roles: enforcing particular groupings, supplying starting information to clustering algorithms, and learning distance functions that are subsequently used for clustering. These uses make constraints part of both the definition of a grouping problem and the procedure used to solve it.

The authors investigate the computational difficulty created by combining constraints. They establish intractability results for some combinations, showing that additional requirements can make the clustering problem hard to solve. The qualification matters: the stated results concern particular combinations, rather than every use of constraints or every constrained clustering task.

The paper examines the implications through both formal reasoning and experiments. This links complexity results to the practical question of how constraints are used in clustering. Its contribution is to show that guidance about desired groups also has computational consequences. Understanding the interaction among requirements is therefore part of assessing a constrained clustering method, alongside considering what information those requirements convey.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that some combinations of clustering constraints are intractable and examines the consequences formally and experimentally.

title: Intractability and clustering with constraints

abstract: Markov logic networks (MLNs) are an expressive representation for statistical relational learning that generalizes both first-order logic and graphical models. Existing methods for learning the logical structure of an MLN are not discriminative; however, many relational learning problems involve specific target predicates that must be inferred from given background information. We found that existing MLN methods perform very poorly on several such ILP benchmark problems, and we present improved discriminative methods for learning MLN clauses and weights that outperform existing MLN and traditional ILP methods.
originalAbstract: Markov logic networks (MLNs) are an expressive representation for statistical relational learning that generalizes both first-order logic and graphical models. Existing methods for learning the logical structure of an MLN are not discriminative; however, many relational learning problems involve specific target predicates that must be inferred from given background information. We found that existing MLN methods perform very poorly on several such ILP benchmark problems, and we present improved discriminative methods for learning MLN clauses and weights that outperform existing MLN and traditional ILP methods.

paragraphs: Markov logic networks combine the expressive reach of first-order logic with probabilistic graphical modeling. Many relational prediction tasks use this expressiveness for a specific purpose: infer selected target predicates from available background information. The paper argues that learning the model should be directed toward those targets, rather than relying on existing structure learning methods that are not discriminative.

The authors report that existing MLN methods perform very poorly on several benchmark problems from inductive logic programming. They develop improved discriminative methods for learning both clauses and weights. This addresses both the logical relationships included in the network and the numerical parameters attached to them, bringing both parts of model construction into the predictive learning task.

The proposed methods outperform the existing MLN approaches and traditional inductive logic programming methods in the reported comparisons. The finding supports task-directed learning within this expressive representation. Its significance is that changing how the logical structure and parameters are learned can improve prediction on the evaluated relational problems.
summary.tldr: Discriminative learning of MLN clauses and weights improves target-predicate prediction over the methods compared on relational benchmarks.

title: Discriminative structure and parameter learning for Markov logic networks

abstract: A new tree-structured multiplicative gamma process (TMGP) is developed, for inferring the depth of a tree-based factor-analysis model. This new model is coupled with the nested Chinese restaurant process, to nonparametrically infer the depth and width (structure) of the tree. In addition to developing the model, theoretical properties of the TMGP are addressed, and a novel MCMC sampler is developed. The structure of the inferred tree is used to learn relationships between high-dimensional data, and the model is also applied to compressive sensing and interpolation of incomplete images.

This new model is coupled with the nested Chinese restaurant process, to nonparametrically infer the depth and width (structure) of the tree. In addition to developing the model, theoretical properties of the TMGP are addressed, and a novel MCMC sampler is developed. The structure of the inferred tree is used to learn relationships between high-dimensional data, and the model is also applied to compressive sensing and interpolation of incomplete images.

paragraphs: The paper develops a factor-analysis model whose structure is organized as a tree. Its aim is to learn relationships within high-dimensional data while also inferring the tree’s size and shape. Both the number of levels and the branching structure are therefore part of what the model learns.

The central ingredient is a tree-structured multiplicative gamma process, introduced to infer tree depth. The authors combine it with a nested Chinese restaurant process so that the model can infer both depth and width nonparametrically. These two components address complementary aspects of the hierarchy: how far it extends and how it branches. Together, they support learning the overall tree structure from data.

The work also examines theoretical properties of the new process and introduces an MCMC sampler for inference. The inferred tree is used to discover relationships among high-dimensional observations. Applications to compressive sensing and interpolation of incomplete images illustrate how the same structured model can support reconstruction tasks as well as the organization of data.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian tree-based factor model learns both hierarchy depth and branching structure to represent high-dimensional data and support reconstruction tasks.

title: Tree-Structured Infinite Sparse Factor Model

abstract: Feature selection and regularization are becoming increasingly prominent tools in the efforts of the reinforcement learning (RL) community to expand the reach and applicability of RL. One approach to the problem of feature selection is to impose a sparsity-inducing form of regularization on the learning method. Recent work on L_1 regularization has adapted techniques from the supervised learning literature for use with RL. Another approach that has received renewed attention in the supervised learning community is that of using a simple algorithm that greedily adds new features. Such algorithms have many of the good properties of the L_1 regularization methods, while also being extremely efficient and, in some cases, allowing theoretical guarantees on recovery of the true form of a sparse target function from sampled data. This paper considers variants of orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) applied to reinforcement learning. The resulting algorithms are analyzed and compared experimentally with existing L_1 regularized approaches. We demonstrate that perhaps the most natural scenario in which one might hope to achieve sparse recovery fails; however, one variant, OMP-BRM, provides promising theoretical guarantees under certain assumptions on the feature dictionary. Another variant, OMP-TD, empirically outperforms prior methods both in approximation accuracy and efficiency on several benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can benefit from using a small, useful subset of available features. One approach encourages sparsity through L1 regularization. This paper investigates an alternative: greedy algorithms that add features incrementally, adapting variants of orthogonal matching pursuit to reinforcement learning.

The authors analyze these variants and compare them experimentally with existing L1-regularized methods. Their theory shows that sparse recovery fails in a setting that might initially seem natural. However, a variant called OMP-BRM offers promising recovery guarantees under certain assumptions on the feature dictionary. The assumptions are essential to the positive result; the paper does not establish recovery for arbitrary collections of features.

A different variant, OMP-TD, performs better than prior methods in both approximation accuracy and computational efficiency on several benchmark problems. The theoretical and empirical strengths thus belong to distinct variants. Together, the results show why greedy feature selection deserves attention in reinforcement learning, while also demonstrating that guarantees from sparse learning require care when transferred into this setting.
summary.tldr: Greedy feature selection offers promising reinforcement-learning results, with conditional guarantees for OMP-BRM and strong benchmark performance for OMP-TD.

title: Greedy Algorithms for Sparse Reinforcement Learning
Position: No Retroactive Cure for Infringement during Training
